40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: Advanced React APIs
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
Advanced React APIs
Advanced React APIs covers the React hooks and APIs you don’t reach for daily, but need in your toolbelt for specific scenarios: consolidating sprawling component state, sharing values app-wide, rendering UI outside the DOM tree, computing layout before paint, exposing imperative methods through refs, forcing synchronous re-renders for focus management, and syncing with state that lives outside React.
Each topic below has its own note with an API reference (from react.dev) and a Real-World Scenarios section researched from how other developers actually use it in production.
Topics

useReducer — Complex State Management
use and createContext — Context
createPortal — Portals
useLayoutEffect — Layout Computations
useImperativeHandle — Imperative Handles
flushSync — Focus Management
useSyncExternalStore — Sync External Store


My Additional Angles
The common thread: these are all “escape hatches”
Every API here exists because React’s default model (declarative render, automatic batching, one virtual tree) occasionally isn’t enough: useReducer escapes scattered setState calls into one controlled transition function; useImperativeHandle/flushSync escape into imperative DOM territory; createPortal escapes the DOM tree structure; useSyncExternalStore escapes React’s own state model to sync with the outside world. Reaching for any of them is a signal you’re at a genuine boundary — not a default tool.
use unifies two previously separate mental models
Before use, “read context” (useContext) and “read async data” (manual useEffect + loading state, or a data-fetching library) were unrelated patterns. use collapses both into “unwrap this thing” — a context value or a Promise — and because it isn’t bound by the Rules of Hooks, it composes naturally with conditionals in a way no other Hook does.
flushSync and useLayoutEffect solve the same category of problem from different angles
Both exist because “the DOM hasn’t caught up yet” — useLayoutEffect handles the read-measure-before-paint half (so a layout calculation never gets painted with wrong data), while flushSync handles the force-a-write-then-act-imperatively half (so code right after it can trust the DOM reflects the latest state). Seeing them as two sides of the same synchronous-DOM-timing problem makes it easier to recall which one a given bug needs.
Server rendering shows up twice, not once
useSyncExternalStore’s getServerSnapshot and context’s default value (used when no Provider wraps a server-rendered subtree) are both instances of the same requirement: anything read outside a normal client re-render needs an explicit “what do I return when there’s no real browser/store to ask” answer.

Advanced React Patterns
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
Advanced React Patterns
Notes on component API design patterns in React — from EpicWeb’s
Advanced React Patterns
workshop by Kent C. Dodds, plus outside research.
The short version of how the patterns relate: every one of them is a
different answer to the same underlying question — how much control does
a component/hook hand back to whoever’s using it, and how do the pieces find
each other without becoming tightly coupled?
give elements, not data        → Composition and Layout Components
give a stable callback ref     → The Latest Ref Pattern
implicit shared state (tree)   → Compound Components
implicit shared state (context)→ The Slots Pattern
give reusable state + handlers → State Collections and Prop Getters
let the consumer set start state → State Initializers
let the consumer own transitions → The State Reducer Pattern
let the consumer own state itself → Control Props

Later patterns build on earlier ones: compound components and slots are both
composition taken further (implicit wiring instead of an explicit
ReactNode prop); state initializers, the state reducer pattern, and
control props are the same useToggle-style hook progressively handing more
control of its state to the consumer, one exercise at a time.
Notes

Composition and Layout Components — passing React elements instead of
raw data to avoid prop drilling, and when a “layout” component’s prop list
should be children, one named ReactNode prop, or several.
The Latest Ref Pattern — using a ref (not state) so a stable callback
can read the latest render’s values without becoming a
useEffect/useCallback dependency, and where useEffectEvent fits.
Compound Components — sharing implicit state between a component and
its children via React.Children/cloneElement and via context, plus
runtime validation that a compound child isn’t rendered outside its parent.
The Slots Pattern — a context-based alternative to compound components
for deeply nested or reorderable children, generalized into a reusable
hook, plus a render-prop/children-as-function variant.
State Collections and Prop Getters — a custom hook exposing reusable
state + handler props, and the prop-getter functions that fix the
callback-collision bug that appears when a consumer composes their own
handler alongside the hook’s.
State Initializers — an initial* prop so a hook’s consumer can set
the starting state, and keeping that value stable across re-renders with a
ref so reset() doesn’t chase a changing prop.
The State Reducer Pattern — inverting control so a hook’s consumer can
intercept, override, or veto every state transition via a reducer they
supply, plus a default-action-types escape hatch to fall back to the
hook’s own behavior.
Control Props — fully controlled/uncontrolled dual-mode hooks, the
onChange contract that makes controlling one possible, and the dev-mode
warnings for mixing the two incorrectly.

Line-by-line render trace
The notes above explain concepts. Render Trace is a companion set of
notes that instead trace execution order through the actual solution code
of all 8 exercises of the workshop — what renders first, when state/context/
refs get read or written, what re-renders, and why each pattern needed the
specific React primitive it used.

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: Composition and Layout Components
Compound Components
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
Compound Components

Notes from EpicWeb’s Advanced React Patterns
workshop by Kent C. Dodds (exercise 3, “Compound Components,” steps
context and validation) plus his blog post
React Hooks: Compound Components.
Builds on Composition and Layout Components — same “pass elements, not
data” instinct, but the shared state is now implicit instead of an
explicit ReactNode prop. Companion to The Slots Pattern, which is a
context-based alternative for cases compound components handle awkwardly
(deeply nested or reordered children). Notes and clarifications by me are
marked with > 💬.

Interview Q&A
Q: What is a compound component, in one sentence?
A: A set of components that work together to form one complete piece of UI,
sharing state implicitly rather than through props the consumer has to
wire up themselves — the canonical example is HTML’s own <select> and
<option>, where <option> doesn’t need an onClick/selected prop
threaded to it; the <select> just knows about its <option> children.
Q: What’s the alternative, and why is it worse?
A: A single component that accepts a big config prop, e.g.
<CustomSelect options={[{ value: '1', display: 'Option 1' }, ...]} />.
It works, but every new capability (extra attributes per option, a
display that depends on selection state) has to become new API surface on
CustomSelect itself — more for the component author to build, more for
the consumer to learn. Compound components let the consumer compose
arbitrary JSX for each part instead of the author anticipating every
combination up front.
Q: In our Toggle example, what are the pieces and what do they share?
A: Toggle owns the state (on, and a toggle function to flip it).
ToggleOn and ToggleOff each conditionally render their children based on
on. ToggleButton renders the actual clickable Switch, wired to on
and toggle. None of ToggleOn/ToggleOff/ToggleButton receives on or
toggle as an explicit prop from whoever renders them — they pull it from
context that Toggle provides:
export function App() {
  return (
    <Toggle>
      <ToggleOn>The button is on</ToggleOn>
      <ToggleOff>The button is off</ToggleOff>
      <ToggleButton />
    </Toggle>
  )
}
Q: How does the implicit sharing actually work?
A: Toggle creates the state and passes it into a context provider that
wraps whatever children it was given:
type ToggleValue = { on: boolean; toggle: () => void }
const ToggleContext = createContext<ToggleValue | null>(null)
 
export function Toggle({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const [on, setOn] = useState(false)
  const toggle = () => setOn(!on)
  return <ToggleContext value={{ on, toggle }}>{children}</ToggleContext>
}
Each compound child reads that same context with the use hook (React 19’s
context-reading form of useContext):
export function ToggleOn({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const { on } = use(ToggleContext)!
  return <>{on ? children : null}</>
}
ToggleButton reads both fields and forwards them to the actual <Switch>
control:
export function ToggleButton({ ...props }: ToggleButtonProps) {
  const { on, toggle } = use(ToggleContext)!
  return <Switch {...props} on={on} onClick={toggle} />
}

💬 An older, non-context way to do this is React.Children.map +
React.cloneElement over props.children, injecting on/toggle as
props onto each direct child. It works, but only for direct children —
wrap a ToggleOn in an extra <div> and cloneElement never sees it, so
its injected props never arrive. Context has no such depth limit, which is
why this workshop (and Kent’s blog post) lead with context as the default
and mention cloneElement mainly as the pattern’s historical origin.

Q: Why not just require <Toggle on={on} toggle={toggle}> and pass those
down as normal props to each child manually?
A: You could, but then every consumer of Toggle has to manage on state
themselves and thread it through by hand to every compound child — exactly
the prop-drilling problem Composition and Layout Components solves for
data, except here the state is something the component itself should own,
not something the consumer has. Compound components let Toggle keep full
ownership of on/toggle while still giving the consumer total freedom
over which pieces to render and in what order/layout.
Q: What happens if ToggleOn is rendered without a <Toggle> ancestor?
A: In the first pass (step context), use(ToggleContext)! returns null
and the non-null assertion (!) just lies to TypeScript — at runtime you get
a much less helpful error the moment code tries to read .on off null
(“Cannot read properties of null”). Step validation fixes this with a
small internal hook that centralizes the context read and throws a specific,
actionable error:
function useToggle() {
  const context = use(ToggleContext)
  if (!context) {
    throw new Error(
      'Cannot find ToggleContext. All Toggle components must be rendered within <Toggle />',
    )
  }
  return context
}
Every compound child (ToggleOn, ToggleOff, ToggleButton) switches from
use(ToggleContext)! to useToggle(). This also fixes the TypeScript
story: useToggle()’s return type is narrowed to non-null ToggleValue by
the early throw, so no ! assertions are needed anywhere downstream, and
TypeScript itself can verify the narrowing (which it couldn’t verify about
the manual ! — that was a lie to the type checker, not a real guarantee).
What compound components are actually solving, and where the pattern comes from
The workshop frames this around a contrast, not around the Toggle code
first: imagine implementing HTML’s own <select>/<option> as a single
React component. The naive version takes a config prop —
<CustomSelect
  options={[
    { value: '1', display: 'Option 1' },
    { value: '2', display: 'Option 2' },
  ]}
/>
— which works, but every new requirement (per-option attributes, a display
that depends on whether an option is selected) becomes new API surface on
CustomSelect itself: more for the author to build, more for the consumer
to learn, and a config object that’s fundamentally worse at expressing
“here is a tree of related elements” than actual JSX is. <select> and
<option> don’t have this problem — <option> is just markup the browser
already knows how to interpret as a child of <select>. Compound
components are the React-land version of that same relationship: a set of
components that only make sense rendered together, coordinating through
state the parent owns and the children read implicitly, rather than
through a big prop the consumer has to construct.
The pattern itself predates hooks — the workshop credits
Ryan Florence as its originator, and
Kent C. Dodds’s earlier course material taught two implementations: one
using React.Children.map/React.cloneElement to inject props onto direct
children, and one using the (pre-hooks) Context API. His blog post
React Hooks: Compound Components
— written specifically to update that material for a hooks-based world —
uses the same Toggle/ToggleOn/ToggleOff/ToggleButton shape this
exercise does: a ToggleContext.Provider wrapping the children, a custom
useToggleContext()-style hook centralizing the read, and the pieces
consuming it via useContext (this workshop uses React 19’s use instead, which reads
context the same way but — per The use Hook — isn’t restricted to the
Rules of Hooks the way useContext is). The core lesson doesn’t change between
those two eras: pick some implicit channel (props via cloneElement, or
a value via context) so the state lives in one place (Toggle) while the
shape of the UI stays entirely in the consumer’s hands.
Full code walkthrough: from no validation to a real error message
Step context — the complete working implementation, toggle.tsx:
import { createContext, use, useState } from 'react'
import { Switch } from '#shared/switch.tsx'
 
type ToggleValue = { on: boolean; toggle: () => void }
const ToggleContext = createContext<ToggleValue | null>(null)
 
export function Toggle({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const [on, setOn] = useState(false)
  const toggle = () => setOn(!on)
  return <ToggleContext value={{ on, toggle }}>{children}</ToggleContext>
}
 
export function ToggleOn({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const { on } = use(ToggleContext)!
  return <>{on ? children : null}</>
}
 
export function ToggleOff({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const { on } = use(ToggleContext)!
  return <>{on ? null : children}</>
}
 
type ToggleButtonProps = Omit<React.ComponentProps<typeof Switch>, 'on'> & { on?: boolean }
export function ToggleButton({ ...props }: ToggleButtonProps) {
  const { on, toggle } = use(ToggleContext)!
  return <Switch {...props} on={on} onClick={toggle} />
}
and app.tsx, showing what a consumer actually writes — no state, no
wiring, just composition:
import { Toggle, ToggleOn, ToggleOff, ToggleButton } from './toggle.tsx'
 
export function App() {
  return (
    <div>
      <Toggle>
        <ToggleOn>The button is on</ToggleOn>
        <ToggleOff>The button is off</ToggleOff>
        <ToggleButton />
      </Toggle>
    </div>
  )
}
This already works end to end. But the workshop’s own validation step poses
a deliberately broken example: what happens if a consumer writes
export const App = () => <ToggleButton /> — a compound child with no
<Toggle> ancestor at all? At runtime, use(ToggleContext) returns
null (the value the context was createContext’d with), the !
non-null assertion satisfies TypeScript but changes nothing about what
actually happens, and the very next line — const { on, toggle } = null!
— throws Cannot read properties of null (reading 'on'). That message is
technically correct and completely unhelpful: it says nothing about
Toggle, ToggleContext, or what the consumer actually needs to fix.
Step validation replaces every direct use(ToggleContext)! call with
one shared hook:
function useToggle() {
  const context = use(ToggleContext)
  if (!context) {
    throw new Error(
      'Cannot find ToggleContext. All Toggle components must be rendered within <Toggle />',
    )
  }
  return context
}
Same broken example now fails with a message that names the actual
component and the actual fix. And because the throw happens before the
return, TypeScript can see that every code path past this point has a
non-null ToggleValue — useToggle()’s return type is genuinely narrowed,
which is a real guarantee the compiler checked, unlike the ! it was
asked to simply trust before.
Rules and caveats

Prefer context over cloneElement for new code. cloneElement-based
compound components silently break the moment a child is wrapped in
another element (a <div>, a conditional, a custom wrapper) — context
reads work through arbitrary nesting because it isn’t walking
props.children, it’s reading a value provided higher up the tree.
Always centralize the context read behind a validating hook (like
useToggle here) rather than calling use(Context)! at every call site.
One throw site means one error message to get right, and it gives
TypeScript a real narrowing point instead of scattered non-null
assertions.
The context value itself should be memo-safe if it matters. Every
render of Toggle here creates a fresh { on, toggle } object, which
means every consumer re-renders on every Toggle render regardless of
which field they actually read — a real concern for compound components
with many independent children, covered under React Re-rendering’s
context-fan-out notes, not solved by this exercise itself.
Compound components assume a fixed parent/child relationship known at
author time. If children need to be arbitrarily deep, reordered, or
looked up by name/slot rather than by JSX nesting position, reach for
The Slots Pattern instead — same context-sharing idea, different
registration mechanism.

Sources

EpicWeb Advanced React Patterns workshop, exercise 03.compound-components
(steps context, validation)
Kent C. Dodds — React Hooks: Compound Components
Real-world usage: @radix-ui/react-tabs,
@radix-ui/react-accordion,
and most of Radix UI

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: Control Props
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
Control Props

Notes from EpicWeb’s Advanced React Patterns
workshop by Kent C. Dodds (exercise 8, “Control Props”) plus his blog post
When to use Control Props or State Reducers
and react.dev’s controlled <input>
reference. Builds directly on State Initializers and
The State Reducer Pattern — same useToggle hook, one more layer of
control handed to the consumer. Notes and clarifications by me are marked
with > 💬.

Interview Q&A
Q: What does “control props” mean, concretely?
A: It’s the exact same idea as a controlled <input> — <input value={v} onChange={...} />
— applied to a custom hook/component instead of a form element. Normally
useToggle owns its on state internally (uncontrolled). Once a consumer
passes an on prop, the hook stops updating its own state on a toggle
click and instead only calls onChange with the state change it would
have made, trusting the consumer to store that value themselves and feed it
back in as the next on prop:
// Uncontrolled — Toggle owns its own state
<Toggle onChange={(state) => console.info(state)} />
 
// Controlled — the parent owns the state; Toggle only suggests changes
const [bothOn, setBothOn] = useState(false)
<Toggle on={bothOn} onChange={(state) => setBothOn(state.on)} />
Q: How does useToggle know whether it’s controlled?
A: By whether the caller passed an on prop at all — null/undefined
means uncontrolled, any boolean means controlled. The check deliberately
uses != (not !==) so both null and undefined count as “not
controlling”:
export function useToggle({
  initialOn = false,
  reducer = toggleReducer,
  onChange,
  on: controlledOn,
}: {
  initialOn?: boolean
  reducer?: typeof toggleReducer
  onChange?: (state: ToggleState, action: ToggleAction) => void
  on?: boolean
} = {}) {
  const { current: initialState } = useRef<ToggleState>({ on: initialOn })
  const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, initialState)
  const onIsControlled = controlledOn != null
  const on = onIsControlled ? controlledOn : state.on
  // ...
}
Q: If the hook is controlled, does it just stop tracking state at all?
A: No — useReducer keeps running internally either way; the hook just
stops reading its own state.on once controlled (on becomes
controlledOn instead), and gates the actual dispatch call so internal
state updates don’t happen while controlled:
function dispatchWithOnChange(action: ToggleAction) {
  if (!onIsControlled) {
    dispatch(action)
  }
  onChange?.(reducer({ ...state, on }, action), action)
}
Q: Where does the “suggested change” passed to onChange come from?
A: The same reducer the hook already uses internally — called directly,
without dispatching, purely to compute what the next state would be:
reducer({ ...state, on }, action). This is exactly what “suggested
changes” means: the hook computes the state transition as if it owned
state, then hands that computed result to the consumer via onChange
instead of applying it, letting the consumer decide whether (and how) to
adopt it.
Q: Why does the actual visible value only change after the consumer’s own
setState runs?
A: Because while controlled, on is derived straight from the on prop
(controlledOn), not from any internal state. Clicking the toggle calls
dispatchWithOnChange, which (being controlled) skips dispatch entirely
and only calls onChange. Nothing re-renders Toggle from that click
alone — the switch only visibly flips once the consumer’s onChange
handler calls its own setState, causing the consumer to re-render and
pass a new on value back down. Control is a real round-trip, not a
shortcut.
Q: What does this buy you that [[The State Reducer Pattern]] alone
doesn’t?
A: The state reducer pattern lets a consumer intercept what happens in
response to an action the component dispatched — it still can’t trigger a
state change from outside, on its own timeline. Control props adds
exactly that: because the consumer owns the actual state, they can update
on for reasons that have nothing to do with a click at all. The
workshop’s example: two <Toggle>s sharing one bothOn boolean stay
perfectly in sync, and a parent-level rule (“lock after 5 clicks”) can veto
a change simply by not calling setBothOn in handleToggleChange — no
action-type inspection required, because the parent just doesn’t have to
adopt the suggested change:
function handleToggleChange(state: ToggleState, action: ToggleAction) {
  if (action.type === 'toggle' && timesClicked > 4) {
    return // ignore the suggested change — toggle won't visibly move
  }
  setBothOn(state.on)
  setTimesClicked((c) => c + 1)
}
 
<Toggle on={bothOn} onChange={handleToggleChange} />
<Toggle on={bothOn} onChange={handleToggleChange} />
Q: Control props or state reducer — which one do you actually reach for?
A: Per Kent’s blog post: state reducer when a consumer needs to change how
the component responds to its own interactions (intercept/modify/veto
specific action types); control props when the consumer needs to trigger a
change from outside the component’s own interaction handlers entirely
(syncing two instances, driving state from a server response, URL
state, etc.). They compose — a component can accept both an on prop and a
reducer prop at once, and real-world components like downshift do
exactly that.
How control props actually work
The <input> analogy, formalized
Kent’s own framing (from the exercise’s intro README) is that this pattern
isn’t really a React-specific invention — it’s the same contract React’s own
DOM elements already use, generalized to a custom hook/component:
function MyCapitalizedInput() {
  const [capitalizedValue, setCapitalizedValue] = useState('')
  return (
    <input
      value={capitalizedValue}
      onChange={(e) => setCapitalizedValue(e.target.value.toUpperCase())}
    />
  )
}
Here, <input /> is the thing implementing “control props.” Left alone
(no value prop), it manages its own internal text state, the way an
uncontrolled <Toggle onChange={...} /> manages its own on state.
The moment a value prop is supplied, the <input> “takes the back seat” —
it stops trusting its own internal edits and instead treats every keystroke
as a suggestion, surfaced via onChange, that the parent is free to
adopt, transform (as above, forcing uppercase), or ignore outright. useToggle
in this exercise implements exactly that same contract for its own on
boolean, via an on/onChange pair with the identical shape.
That two-input synchronization example from the README is worth sitting
with, because it’s the concrete reason control props exist rather than just
being a fancier way to lift state:
function MyTwoInputs() {
  const [capitalizedValue, setCapitalizedValue] = useState('')
  const [lowerCasedValue, setLowerCasedValue] = useState('')
 
  function handleInputChange(e) {
    setCapitalizedValue(e.target.value.toUpperCase())
    setLowerCasedValue(e.target.value.toLowerCase())
  }
 
  return (
    <>
      <input value={capitalizedValue} onChange={handleInputChange} />
      <input value={lowerCasedValue} onChange={handleInputChange} />
    </>
  )
}
One keystroke in either input drives both — because neither input owns
its own value any more; a single external source of truth does. This is
precisely what the workshop’s App does with its two <Toggle>s sharing
one bothOn boolean.
A full trace through the real solution code
Start from toggleReducer and useToggle in toggle.tsx — the whole
mechanism hinges on one line:
const onIsControlled = controlledOn != null
const on = onIsControlled ? controlledOn : state.on
useReducer(reducer, initialState) is always called, controlled or not —
state/dispatch always exist. What changes is only which value on
resolves to, and whether dispatch is actually allowed to run:
function dispatchWithOnChange(action: ToggleAction) {
  if (!onIsControlled) {
    dispatch(action)
  }
  onChange?.(reducer({ ...state, on }, action), action)
}
Notice reducer({ ...state, on }, action) is called directly as a plain
function, not through dispatch — this is the same toggleReducer used
internally, just invoked once to compute “what would the next state be,”
without committing to it. That computed value becomes the argument to
onChange. Whether or not that suggestion ever becomes real, on-screen
state depends entirely on what the consumer does with it.
Now trace App (app.tsx), which renders two controlled <Toggle>s
sharing one bothOn:
function handleToggleChange(state: ToggleState, action: ToggleAction) {
  if (action.type === 'toggle' && timesClicked > 4) {
    return // the suggestion is simply never adopted
  }
  setBothOn(state.on)
  setTimesClicked((c) => c + 1)
}
 
<Toggle on={bothOn} onChange={handleToggleChange} />
<Toggle on={bothOn} onChange={handleToggleChange} />
Click either switch: dispatchWithOnChange fires, skips dispatch (both
are controlled), computes the suggested { on: true }, and calls
handleToggleChange. If timesClicked <= 4, App calls setBothOn(true)
— its own state changes, App re-renders, both <Toggle>s receive the
new on={true} prop, and both switches flip together, even though only
one was physically clicked. If timesClicked > 4, handleToggleChange
returns immediately — setBothOn never runs, App never re-renders, and
neither switch moves, despite dispatchWithOnChange having run to
completion and called onChange. The component genuinely tried to suggest
a change; the parent genuinely declined it. That’s the whole veto mechanism,
and it requires zero special-casing inside useToggle itself — useToggle
doesn’t know or care that it’s being vetoed.
The same file also renders one uncontrolled <Toggle> for contrast:
<Toggle onChange={(...args) => console.info('Uncontrolled Toggle onChange', ...args)} />
No on prop is passed, so controlledOn is undefined, onIsControlled
is false, and every click runs dispatch(action) for real — useReducer’s
own internal state drives on, onChange still fires (useful for logging,
as here), but nothing external gates or adopts anything. This is the
“back seat” <input> analogy from the other direction: without a value/on
prop, the component reverts to trusting itself.
Control props vs. the state reducer pattern — Kent’s own distinction
Kent’s post When to use Control Props or State Reducers
draws the line this way: The State Reducer Pattern lets a consumer
change how the component responds to its own internally-dispatched
actions (intercept, modify, or veto a specific action type) — but the
component still has to be interacted with directly to trigger anything.
Control props go further: because the consumer owns the actual state value,
they can change it for reasons that have nothing to do with an action the
component dispatched at all — syncing two instances (as App does here),
driving the toggle from a server response, restoring it from a URL, or any
other external trigger. Kent is explicit that control props are “objectively
more powerful,” but that power comes with real cost to the consumer: they
now own the state and must render it back in correctly on every change,
versus a state-reducer consumer who only has to supply a function and can
otherwise leave state management to the hook. This is exactly why
useToggle here accepts both mechanisms rather than picking one — they
solve genuinely different problems, and real components like downshift
support both simultaneously for the same reason.
Rules and caveats

A component doesn’t have to choose one or the other — useToggle
here accepts on (control props) and reducer (state reducer)
simultaneously; they solve different problems and stack cleanly, since
dispatchWithOnChange already routes every state change through both the
reducer and the controlled/uncontrolled check.
onChange firing doesn’t mean the value changed. In the controlled
case it always fires with the “suggested” next state on every
interaction — the parent decides whether to adopt it. Don’t assume
receiving onChange implies your UI must update; that’s the parent’s
call, same as a controlled <input>’s onChange firing doesn’t force you
to call setState with the new value (React docs explicitly note you can
ignore it, e.g. to reject/transform input).
A component can’t tell mid-flight whether it’s controlled if the prop
changes between renders. Switching a real input (or this Toggle)
between controlled and uncontrolled across its lifetime is a known
footgun in React generally — react.dev’s controlled-input docs warn
about exactly this (“switching between controlled and uncontrolled
gives a console warning” for <input>). This workshop step doesn’t
implement that warning for useToggle itself, but it’s worth adding for
a hook meant for real consumers (downshift does).
This is the deepest layer of control in the workshop’s progression.
State Initializers let the consumer set the starting value;
The State Reducer Pattern let the consumer rewrite transitions;
control props let the consumer own the value itself. Each layer is a
strict superset of what the previous one enables.

Sources

EpicWeb Advanced React Patterns workshop, exercise 08.control-props
(step “control”)
Kent C. Dodds — When to use Control Props or State Reducers
react.dev — Controlling an input with a state variable
Real-world usage: downshift,
@radix-ui/react-select

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
The Latest Ref Pattern

Notes from EpicWeb’s Advanced React Patterns
workshop by Kent C. Dodds (exercise 2, “Latest Ref”) plus his posts
How React Uses Closures to Avoid Bugs
and The Latest Ref Pattern in React,
plus outside research on React’s newer useEffectEvent hook. Notes and
clarifications by me are marked with > 💬.

Interview Q&A
Q: What problem does the latest-ref pattern solve?
A: A stale closure — a function created on one render that keeps referring
to that render’s props/state forever, even after newer renders have
happened, because it never gets recreated. In the workshop’s example, a
useDebounce(increment, 3000) hook memoizes its returned debounced function
with useMemo(() => debounce(callback, delay), [callback, delay]). Every
time increment changes identity (which it does on every render, since it’s
declared fresh as () => setCount(c => c + step)), useMemo recomputes and
creates a new debounced wrapper with its own internal timer closure —
so the previous pending timer never gets cancelled, and clicking twice
before the delay fires ends up incrementing twice by whatever step was
active at each click, instead of once by the latest step.
Q: Why not just memoize the callback with useCallback?
A: It doesn’t actually fix the bug — it just relocates when the identity
changes. useCallback(() => setCount(c => c + step), [step]) still produces
a new function every time step changes, and step is exactly the value
the debounced click is supposed to react to. The workshop’s problem
README calls this out directly: swapping increment’s definition between
a plain closure and a useCallback version makes no observable
difference to the bug, because the root issue isn’t “is this memoized,” it’s
“this hook’s public API forces every consumer to hand it a stable
callback just to get correct behavior,” which is a bad API.
Q: How does storing the callback in a ref fix it without a stable callback?
A: By separating two things that were conflated: the debounced function’s
identity (which must stay stable so useMemo doesn’t rebuild it and
lose the pending timer) from the callback’s content (which must always
be the latest one). A ref gives you a mutable box whose .current can be
reassigned on every render without ever changing the ref object’s own
identity:
function useDebounce<Callback extends (...args: Array<unknown>) => unknown>(
  callback: Callback,
  delay: number,
) {
  const callbackRef = useRef(callback)
  useEffect(() => {
    callbackRef.current = callback
  })
  return useMemo(
    () => debounce((...args) => callbackRef.current(...args), delay),
    [delay],
  )
}
Now useMemo’s dependency array only has delay — callback never appears
in it, so the debounced wrapper (and its timer closure) is built exactly
once and kept alive across every re-render. The wrapper still calls the
latest callback, because it reads callbackRef.current at call time
(when the debounce timer fires), not at creation time.
Q: Why write to the ref inside a useEffect, not directly in the
component body?
A: Because a ref write is a side effect, and side effects don’t belong in
the render body — React can call a component’s function multiple times per
commit (Strict Mode’s double-invoke, concurrent rendering retries) and the
render body is supposed to be pure. useEffect runs after the commit is
final, once per actual render, which is the correct place to mutate
anything external to render. > 💬 The workshop’s own comment on this is
worth keeping verbatim: “side-effects run in the function body of your
component can lead to some pretty confusing bugs. Just keep your function
body free of side-effects.”
Q: Why does that useEffect have no dependency array?
A: Because it’s supposed to run after every render — the whole point is
“always sync the ref to whatever the latest render’s callback is.” Giving it
a dependency array ([callback]) would be redundant at best (it would still
run every render, since callback changes every render) and misleading at
worst — it looks like an optimization but changes nothing, so the workshop
solution leaves it bare.
Q: Isn’t this just going back to the class-component this.props/this.state
default that hooks deliberately moved away from?
A: Yes, explicitly — and that’s the tradeoff to understand before reaching
for it. Class components always read the current this.props/this.state
no matter when a method actually runs, which is exactly the bug class of the
workshop’s PetFeeder example (an async feedPet that reads stale
selectedPetFood if state changed while it was awaiting). Hooks’ closures
capture a specific render’s values, which avoids that whole bug class by
default — but it means any code that genuinely needs “the current value at
call time, regardless of when I was created” (a debounce/throttle wrapper,
a subscription callback, react-query’s query/mutation functions) has to
opt back into the old behavior deliberately, with a ref.
Q: Is there a more “official” way to do this now?
A: React added useEffectEvent (stabilizing around React 19.2) as a
first-class primitive for exactly this shape of problem: a function that
always sees the latest props/state but never needs to be a dependency and
never triggers a re-run of the effect that calls it. It formalizes what the
hand-rolled ref-plus-useEffect version does manually — React itself keeps
the wrapped function’s body pointed at the latest render’s closure while
keeping its identity stable. The constraint: an Effect Event may only be
called from inside a useEffect/useLayoutEffect/useInsertionEffect (or,
by extension of this workshop’s shape, from inside something an effect set
up, like the debounced wrapper) — it isn’t meant to be handed to other
components or hooks as a general-purpose stable callback.
Where this pattern comes from: the class-component default
The workshop motivates the whole pattern with a class-component example
worth walking through in full, because it’s the clearest illustration of
what default hooks actually changed. A class component reads
this.props/this.state at the moment a method runs, not at the moment the
method was defined — so it always sees the current values, no matter how
long ago the method reference was created or how long it’s been running:
class PetFeeder extends React.Component {
  state = { selectedPetFood: null }
  feedPet = async () => {
    const canEat = await this.props.pet.canEat(this.state.selectedPetFood)
    if (canEat) {
      this.props.pet.eat(this.state.selectedPetFood)
    }
  }
  render() {
    return (
      <div>
        <PetFoodChooser
          onSelection={selectedPetFood => this.setState({ selectedPetFood })}
        />
        <button onClick={this.feedPet}>Feed {this.props.pet.name}</button>
      </div>
    )
  }
}
This looks harmless until you ask what happens if pet.canEat takes a
couple of seconds to resolve and the user changes selectedPetFood while
it’s pending: this.state.selectedPetFood is read a second time, after
the await, and by then it’s the new selection — so you can check whether
a bird can eat worms, but actually feed it grass, because the two reads of
this.state straddle an async gap and don’t agree with each other. Kent’s
own fix, back in the class-component days, was to snapshot the values into
local variables up front — const { pet } = this.props; const { selectedPetFood } = this.state
— specifically to stop re-reading the live instance mid-function and pin
down what “this call” means.
Hooks flip the default: a function component’s closures capture a
specific render’s props/state permanently, so the equivalent bug is gone
by construction —
function PetFeeder({ pet }) {
  const [selectedPetFood, setSelectedPetFood] = useState(null)
  const feedPet = async () => {
    const canEat = await pet.canEat(selectedPetFood)
    if (canEat) {
      pet.eat(selectedPetFood)
    }
  }
  return (
    <div>
      <PetFoodChooser onSelection={food => setSelectedPetFood(food)} />
      <button onClick={feedPet}>Feed {pet.name}</button>
    </div>
  )
}
feedPet here always uses the selectedPetFood from the render that
created it, even if the user changes the selection while pet.canEat is
still pending — the closure already has its own private copy, there’s no
second read of anything live to go stale. This is a real, deliberate design
decision in hooks, not an accident: closures-by-default fixes an entire
class of async-staleness bugs that class components were prone to, for
free, every time.
The latest-ref pattern is the escape hatch back to the class-component
default, for the (comparatively rare) cases where you actually want it —
useDebounce is exactly such a case, because a debounce wrapper’s entire
job is to be called long after it was created, and it needs to act on
whatever is current then, not whatever was current when the debounce
timer was originally set up.
The debounce bug, traced through both broken attempts
The workshop’s problem step deliberately leaves two “almost-fixes” in place
as commented-out code, specifically so you hit the same bug both ways before
the ref-based fix:
function useDebounce<Callback extends (...args: Array<unknown>) => unknown>(
  callback: Callback,
  delay: number,
) {
  // 🐨 create a latest ref (via useRef and useEffect) here
  return useMemo(() => debounce(callback, delay), [callback, delay])
}
 
function App() {
  const [step, setStep] = useState(1)
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0)
  // 🦉 feel free to swap these two implementations and see they don't make
  // any difference to the user experience
  // const increment = useCallback(() => setCount(c => c + step), [step])
  const increment = () => setCount(c => c + step)
  const debouncedIncrement = useDebounce(increment, 3000)
  // ...
}
Attempt 1 — plain closure (increment above). increment is a new
function every render, so useMemo’s [callback, delay] dependency array
changes every render too, so useMemo recomputes debounce(callback, delay)
fresh every render — a brand-new timer closure every time, with no
memory of the previous debounced call’s pending timeout. Click, change
step, click again before 3000ms: two independent debounced functions each
running their own timer, both eventually firing, each incrementing by
whatever step was current at the click that created that particular
debounced function — the bug is two increments instead of one, using two
different step values.
Attempt 2 — useCallback (commented out above). Swapping to
useCallback(() => setCount(c => c + step), [step]) produces the exact
same bug, just for a subtler reason: increment is now stable only as
long as step doesn’t change, but step changing is precisely the event
this exercise is testing. The moment step changes between the two clicks,
increment gets a new identity anyway, so useMemo rebuilds the debounced
wrapper again, losing the pending timer exactly as before. Memoizing the
callback doesn’t fix anything here — it just makes the bug intermittent
based on whether the dependency happened to change, instead of guaranteed
on every render.
The actual fix decouples the debounced wrapper’s identity from the
callback’s content entirely, so neither attempt’s dependency-array problem
can occur:
function useDebounce<Callback extends (...args: Array<unknown>) => unknown>(
  callback: Callback,
  delay: number,
) {
  const callbackRef = useRef(callback)
  useEffect(() => {
    callbackRef.current = callback
  })
  return useMemo(
    () => debounce((...args) => callbackRef.current(...args), delay),
    [delay],
  )
}
useMemo’s dependency array is now just [delay] — callback is never in
it, so the debounced wrapper (and its one, persistent timer closure) is
built exactly once per delay value and never rebuilt just because a render
happened. The anonymous function actually passed to debounce doesn’t close
over callback at all — it closes over callbackRef, and reads
callbackRef.current only when the debounce timer actually fires, which is
what makes it “latest” rather than “whatever was current when this wrapper
was built.”

💬 The problem step’s own hint is worth calling out directly: “you’ll
need to pass an anonymous function to debounce. Do not simply change this
to debounce(latestCallbackRef.current, delay) as that won’t work.”
That’s because latestCallbackRef.current is read once, at the moment
debounce(...) is called inside useMemo — which only runs once (per
delay) — baking in whatever callback was current then, defeating the
whole point. The extra indirection of wrapping it in (...args) => callbackRef.current(...args)
is what defers the read of .current to call time instead of
construction time.

Rules and caveats

This is an opt-out of hooks’ stale-closure protection, not a bug fix in
the usual sense. Reach for it only when you specifically want “latest
value at call time” semantics — a debounce/throttle wrapper, a
subscription/event-listener callback, a library’s imperative escape hatch
— not as a default habit for silencing exhaustive-deps warnings.
Never read a ref during render. The ref exists to be read from
callbacks that run later (a debounce timer firing, an event handler).
Reading ref.current in the render body reintroduces the exact kind of
impure-render bug the useEffect write was designed to avoid.
Don’t collapse the write into the same effect that uses the ref,
unless they’re genuinely meant to run in the same pass. In the workshop,
the ref-write effect (runs every render, no deps) is intentionally
separate from the debounced function itself (built once via useMemo
with only delay as a dependency) — conflating them would either rebuild
the debounce wrapper too often (losing the pending timer again) or stop
syncing the latest callback.
Prefer useEffectEvent where it’s available and fits. It exists
specifically to replace this hand-rolled pattern; reach for the manual
ref version primarily when you’re on a React version that doesn’t have it
yet, or when you need the ref for something beyond what an Effect Event
covers (e.g. reading the value from outside any effect at all).

Sources

EpicWeb Advanced React Patterns workshop, exercise 02.latest-ref (step
“ref”)
Kent C. Dodds — How React Uses Closures to Avoid Bugs
Kent C. Dodds — The Latest Ref Pattern in React
LogRocket — React useEffectEvent: Goodbye to stale closure headaches
