01 Composition
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
Composition — Render Trace (Exercise 1)

Line-by-line render/execution trace through the 1 solution step of
exercise 1 (“Composition”) of EpicWeb’s
Advanced React Patterns
workshop by Kent C. Dodds. For the concept explanation (not the trace)
see Composition and Layout Components — this note is about
invocation order: when each element is constructed, who owns it, and
why the “before” version re-renders more than the “after” version needs
to.

compose — Composition
Problem: Nav, Main, and Footer all accept raw data props
(user, sportList, selectedSport, setSelectedSport) purely to forward
pieces of them to their own children — none of the three components reads
that data itself.
function App() {
  const [user] = useState<User>({ name: 'Kody', image: '/img/kody.png' })
  const [sportList] = useState<Array<SportData>>(() => Object.values(allSports))
  const [selectedSport, setSelectedSport] = useState<SportData | null>(null)
 
  return (
    <div id="app-root">
      <Nav avatar={<img src={user.image} alt={`${user.name} profile`} />} />
      <Main
        sidebar={
          <List
            listItems={sportList.map((p) => (
              <li key={p.id}>
                <SportListItemButton sport={p} onClick={() => setSelectedSport(p)} />
              </li>
            ))}
          />
        }
        content={<Details selectedSport={selectedSport} />}
      />
      <Footer footerMessage={`Don't have a good day–have a great day, ${user.name}`} />
    </div>
  )
}
Render trace

App() runs. Its three useState calls return the current user,
sportList, and selectedSport (initially null).
Still inside App()’s single function body, the JSX for <Nav avatar={...} />
is evaluated: <img src={user.image} .../> is constructed as a plain
React element right here, where user is in scope — not deferred
into Nav.
Same thing for Main’s two props: sidebar is built by mapping
sportList into <li> elements (each wrapping a
<SportListItemButton> that closes over setSelectedSport directly);
content is built as <Details selectedSport={selectedSport} />. Both
are ordinary element trees, fully constructed, by the time Main is
called.
React calls Nav({ avatar }), Main({ sidebar, content }), and
Footer({ footerMessage }). Each of these function bodies only ever
touches the ReactNode/string prop it was handed — none of them
references user, sportList, selectedSport, or the setter. Their
prop types literally cannot express “give me the whole user object,”
which is the mechanical guarantee this pattern buys.
User clicks a SportListItemButton. Its onClick={() => setSelectedSport(p)}
fires, scheduling a state update on App.
App() re-renders top to bottom (step 1 again). Every child element gets
freshly reconstructed on this pass — <Nav avatar={...}/> is a new
element object even though the <img> inside it is unchanged, because
App’s whole render function reruns. React’s reconciler still diffs
Nav’s previous and new props by value/type and bails out of updating
Nav’s host DOM node for the <img> itself if nothing about it actually
changed — composition doesn’t add a re-render, it only changes who
constructs the element, not how often App (and therefore everything
under it) re-renders.
Details receives the new selectedSport and renders <SportDataView>
instead of Select a Sport.

Why
The “before” version (data drilled through Nav/Main/Footer as raw
props) and the “after” version trigger exactly the same re-render pattern
on a setSelectedSport call — App re-renders, and everything under it
re-evaluates its JSX either way. The pattern isn’t a performance
optimization by itself (that’s what React Re-rendering’s tools —
memo, moving state down — are for); it’s a coupling fix: after the
change, Nav’s function signature is a hard boundary that makes it
impossible for Nav to accidentally read a user field it shouldn’t, and
impossible for a future edit to User to force a change to Nav’s prop
types. The re-render trace looks identical; the dependency graph on paper
does not.
Sources

EpicWeb — Advanced React Patterns workshop, exercise 1 (step + solution)
Kent C. Dodds — Prop Drilling

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: 02 Latest Ref
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
Latest Ref — Render Trace (Exercise 2)

Line-by-line render/execution trace through the 1 solution step of
exercise 2 (“Latest Ref”) of EpicWeb’s
Advanced React Patterns
workshop by Kent C. Dodds. For the concept explanation (not the trace)
see The Latest Ref Pattern — this note is about invocation order:
when the ref gets written vs. read, and exactly why the buggy version’s
useMemo rebuilds while the fixed version’s doesn’t.

ref — Latest Ref
Problem: useDebounce’s useMemo(() => debounce(callback, delay), [callback, delay])
lists callback as a dependency. callback (increment) is a fresh
closure every render, so every render produces a brand-new debounced
wrapper with a brand-new timer closure — the previous pending timer is
abandoned, not cancelled, so rapid clicks each schedule their own timeout
using whatever step was current at click time.
function useDebounce<Callback extends (...args: Array<unknown>) => unknown>(
  callback: Callback,
  delay: number,
) {
  const callbackRef = useRef(callback)
  useEffect(() => {
    callbackRef.current = callback
  })
  return useMemo(
    () => debounce((...args) => callbackRef.current(...args), delay),
    [delay],
  )
}
 
function App() {
  const [step, setStep] = useState(1)
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0)
  const increment = () => setCount((c) => c + step)
  const debouncedIncrement = useDebounce(increment, 3000)
  // ...
}
Render trace

Mount. App() renders with step = 1, count = 0. increment is
created fresh (closes over step = 1, setCount).
useDebounce(increment, 3000) runs. useRef(callback) creates
callbackRef once, seeded with this first increment. useMemo’s
dependency array is [delay] — delay is 3000, unseen before, so it
runs the factory: debounce((...args) => callbackRef.current(...args), 3000)
is built once, capturing callbackRef (the ref object itself, not
its .current) in its closure. This is the wrapper that owns the
timer variable inside debounce.
After commit, React runs the bare useEffect: callbackRef.current = callback
— sets .current to this render’s increment. No-op in practice since
it’s the same value useRef was seeded with.
User clicks the button (step still 1). debouncedIncrement()
(the same function object created in step 2) runs. Inside debounce’s
closure: no existing timer, so it calls setTimeout(() => fn(...args), 3000)
where fn is (...args) => callbackRef.current(...args). Note: nothing
reads callbackRef.current yet — that read is deferred until the
timer actually fires, 3000ms from now.
User changes the step input to 2. setStep(2) fires. App()
re-renders: step = 2, a new increment closure is created (closes
over step = 2 this time). useDebounce(increment, 3000) runs again:
useRef returns the same callbackRef object it always returns after
the first call (refs are stable across renders by design). useMemo
checks its deps — delay is still 3000, unchanged — so it skips
the factory and returns the exact same debounced-wrapper function from
step 2. The pending timer set in step 4 is untouched.
After this render commits, the bare useEffect runs again:
callbackRef.current = increment — now points at the step = 2 closure.
This mutation happens on the ref object, entirely outside any render;
nothing about it triggers a re-render.
User clicks the button again, before the first timer has fired.
debouncedIncrement() — the same function object as steps 4–5 — runs.
Inside debounce: a timer already exists from step 4, so
clearTimeout(timer) cancels it, and a new setTimeout is scheduled.
Only one timer is ever pending at a time now — this is the actual bug
fix, and it only works because steps 5–6 never rebuilt the wrapper.
3000ms later, the surviving timer (from step 7) fires:
fn() runs → callbackRef.current(...args) → reads .current at this
moment, which was last written in step 6 to the step = 2 closure →
calls that increment → setCount(c => c + 2). count becomes 2,
matching the workshop’s stated goal (“count value should be 2”).

Why
The bug and the fix both hinge on the same fact: useMemo’s factory only
reruns when something in its dependency array actually changes by
reference, and object identity, not content, is what useMemo compares.
The buggy version puts callback in that array, so a new closure every
render forces a new wrapper (and a lost timer) every render. The fixed
version removes callback from the array entirely and instead gives the
one, permanently-stable wrapper a way to reach the latest callback
indirectly — through callbackRef.current, which can be freely reassigned
without ever changing callbackRef itself. The useEffect write (steps 3
and 6) and the debounce timer’s read (step 8) are deliberately
decoupled in time — the ref is what lets a value written during one
render be correctly read much later, by code that isn’t part of any render
at all.
Sources

EpicWeb — Advanced React Patterns workshop, exercise 2 (step + solution)
Kent C. Dodds — The Latest Ref Pattern in React

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: 03 Compound Components
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
Compound Components — Render Trace (Exercise 3)

Line-by-line render/execution trace through the 2 solution steps of
exercise 3 (“Compound Components”) of EpicWeb’s
Advanced React Patterns
workshop by Kent C. Dodds. For the concept explanation see
Compound Components — this note is about invocation order: when
the context provider commits relative to its consumers, and exactly where
the error throws when a child is misused.

context — Compound Components
Problem: Toggle, ToggleOn, ToggleOff, and ToggleButton need to
share on/toggle state, but the consumer composing them (App) shouldn’t
have to read or pass that state around itself.
type ToggleValue = { on: boolean; toggle: () => void }
const ToggleContext = createContext<ToggleValue | null>(null)
 
export function Toggle({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const [on, setOn] = useState(false)
  const toggle = () => setOn(!on)
  return <ToggleContext value={{ on, toggle }}>{children}</ToggleContext>
}
 
export function ToggleOn({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const { on } = use(ToggleContext)!
  return <>{on ? children : null}</>
}
 
export function ToggleButton({ ...props }: ToggleButtonProps) {
  const { on, toggle } = use(ToggleContext)!
  return <Switch {...props} on={on} onClick={toggle} />
}
 
export function App() {
  return (
    <Toggle>
      <ToggleOn>The button is on</ToggleOn>
      <ToggleOff>The button is off</ToggleOff>
      <ToggleButton />
    </Toggle>
  )
}
Render trace

App() renders <Toggle> with three JSX children already constructed as
plain elements (<ToggleOn>..., <ToggleOff>..., <ToggleButton/>) —
at this point they’re just element descriptors, not yet invoked as
functions.
React calls Toggle({ children }). useState(false) initializes on.
Toggle returns <ToggleContext value={{ on: false, toggle }}>{children}</ToggleContext> —
note a new { on, toggle } object is created on every render of
Toggle, since object literals aren’t referentially stable across calls.
React commits the provider, making { on: false, toggle } available to
any descendant that reads ToggleContext, then proceeds to render
children — which is exactly the three elements built in step 1.
React calls ToggleOn({ children }). Inside, use(ToggleContext)! reads
the value the provider committed in step 3: { on: false, toggle }. So
on is false, and ToggleOn returns null — its children are not
rendered this pass. Same for ToggleOff, except on: false means it
does render its children this time (opposite condition).
React calls ToggleButton(props). use(ToggleContext)! again returns
{ on: false, toggle }. It renders <Switch on={false} onClick={toggle} />.
User clicks the rendered <Switch>, which calls the onClick it was
given — that’s toggle from step 2, i.e. () => setOn(!on). This
schedules a state update on Toggle, not on ToggleButton — the
state lives where it was declared (useState inside Toggle), even
though the click handler that mutates it fires from deep inside a
different compound child.
Toggle re-renders (step 2 again) with on: true this time, producing a
new context value object { on: true, toggle } (a new toggle
closure too, since it’s redefined every render). React re-commits the
provider with this new value.
Because the context value changed (new object, and on actually
flipped), React re-renders every consumer subscribed to ToggleContext
— ToggleOn, ToggleOff, and ToggleButton all re-run their function
bodies (steps 4–5 again), each reading the fresh { on: true, toggle }.
ToggleOn now renders its children; ToggleOff now returns null;
ToggleButton renders <Switch on={true} .../>.

Why
The context provider has to be the common ancestor of every compound
child for use(ToggleContext) to find it — that’s mechanical, not
optional. What’s worth noticing in the trace is why every child
re-renders on toggle even though only ToggleButton’s on/onClick values
actually change visibly for two of the three consumers: React’s context
subscription is all-or-nothing per value, not per-field. Toggle handing
out a fresh object every render (rather than a stable one) means
consumers can’t bail out via reference equality even if React.memo’d —
this is the tradeoff being made for the convenience of implicit sharing,
and it’s the same class of cost React Re-rendering covers for context
generally.
validation — Compound Components Validation
Problem: rendering <ToggleButton /> outside a <Toggle> (e.g.
export const App = () => <ToggleButton />) crashes with an unhelpful
“Cannot read properties of null” instead of telling the developer what they
did wrong.
function useToggle() {
  const context = use(ToggleContext)
  if (!context) {
    throw new Error(
      'Cannot find ToggleContext. All Toggle components must be rendered within <Toggle />',
    )
  }
  return context
}
 
export function ToggleButton({ ...props }: ToggleButtonProps) {
  const { on, toggle } = useToggle()
  return <Switch {...props} on={on} onClick={toggle} />
}
Render trace

App() renders <ToggleButton /> with no <Toggle> ancestor anywhere
in the tree.
React calls ToggleButton(props), which calls useToggle().
Inside useToggle, use(ToggleContext) looks up the nearest provider —
there is none, so context resolves to ToggleContext’s default
value, which was null (createContext<ToggleValue | null>(null)).
if (!context) is true → useToggle throws a new Error('Cannot find ToggleContext. All Toggle components must be rendered within <Toggle />').
This throw happens synchronously during ToggleButton’s render, same
unconditional try/catch around every component render described in
The use Hook — except here the thrown value is a real Error, not a
Promise, so React routes it to the nearest ErrorBoundary (or, with
none present, surfaces it as an uncaught render error) rather than a
Suspense fallback.
ToggleButton’s return <Switch .../> line never executes this pass —
the function unwound at the throw inside useToggle, one call deeper
than where the use(ToggleContext)! non-null-assertion version used to
fail.

Why
Moving the null-check into a single useToggle hook doesn’t change that
misuse crashes — it changes what the developer sees when it does. Every
compound child funnels through the same throw site with the same message,
so there’s exactly one place to get the error text right, and TypeScript
narrows useToggle()’s return type to non-null automatically from the
early throw — no per-call-site ! assertions needed, and no way to
silently ship a broken narrowing the type checker can’t verify.
Sources

EpicWeb — Advanced React Patterns workshop, exercise 3 (both steps + solutions)
Kent C. Dodds — React Hooks: Compound Components

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: 04 Slots
05 Prop Getters
06 State Initializers
07 State Reducer
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
State Reducer — Render Trace (Exercise 7)

Line-by-line render/execution trace through the 2 solution steps of
exercise 7 (“State Reducer”) of EpicWeb’s
Advanced React Patterns
workshop by Kent C. Dodds. Builds on the same useToggle hook traced in
06 State Initializers. For the concept explanation see
The State Reducer Pattern — this note is about invocation order:
exactly what runs between a click and the next render, and where the
consumer’s reducer sits in that chain.

reducer — State Reducer
Problem: <Toggle /> should stop updating after 4 clicks in a row, but
that’s app-specific policy, not something useToggle itself should know
about. Give the consumer a reducer prop with full control over every state
transition.
// toggle.tsx
function toggleReducer(state: ToggleState, action: ToggleAction) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'toggle': return { on: !state.on }
    case 'reset': return action.initialState
  }
}
 
export function useToggle({ initialOn = false, reducer = toggleReducer } = {}) {
  const { current: initialState } = useRef<ToggleState>({ on: initialOn })
  const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, initialState)
  const { on } = state
  const toggle = () => dispatch({ type: 'toggle' })
  const reset = () => dispatch({ type: 'reset', initialState })
  // getTogglerProps/getResetterProps unchanged from exercise 5
  return { on, reset, toggle, getTogglerProps, getResetterProps }
}
 
// app.tsx
const { on, getTogglerProps, getResetterProps } = useToggle({
  reducer(state, action) {
    switch (action.type) {
      case 'toggle': {
        if (clickedTooMuch) return state
        return { on: !state.on }
      }
      case 'reset': return { on: false }
    }
  },
})
Render trace

App() renders. It calls useToggle({ reducer: <app's inline reducer function> }).
Inside useToggle, the destructured default parameter
reducer = toggleReducer does not apply — a reducer was explicitly
passed, so the app’s function is what gets bound. useReducer(reducer, initialState)
is called with the app’s reducer, not the module’s toggleReducer.
From this point on, toggleReducer (the module-level default) is
completely uninvolved in this render tree — it was never called, only
shadowed by the parameter default mechanism.
User clicks the <Switch>. Two onClick handlers fire in sequence
(composed by callAll inside getTogglerProps, per
State Collections and Prop Getters): the app’s own
() => setTimesClicked((count) => count + 1) and the hook’s internal
toggle.
toggle() runs: dispatch({ type: 'toggle' }). This queues a state
update on the useReducer created in step 2 — the one wired to the
app’s reducer function.
On the next render pass, React invokes useReducer’s reducer:
appReducer(currentState, { type: 'toggle' }). This calls the app’s
switch, not toggleReducer — the hook’s own module-level default
is bypassed entirely whenever a consumer reducer is supplied.
Inside the app’s reducer: if clickedTooMuch is true (this closes over
the app’s own timesClicked state from step 3, captured at the time
this render’s reducer function was created — not a stale value, because
the reducer function itself is recreated fresh every render along with
the rest of App), it returns state unchanged. useReducer sees the
returned value is reference-equal-or-considered-unchanged and skips
the re-render for on — the toggle visually does nothing, even though
dispatch was called and timesClicked still incremented independently.
If clickedTooMuch is false, the app’s reducer returns
{ on: !state.on }, a genuinely new object, and useToggle’s on
updates normally, propagating back into App’s JSX.

Why
The whole mechanism rides entirely on useReducer accepting any function
with the right shape — useToggle never inspects or validates the reducer
it’s given, it just threads it straight into useReducer. That’s what makes
“inversion of control” here a zero-runtime-cost pattern: there’s no
dispatch-interception layer, no wrapping, no extra render — the consumer’s
function is the reducer useReducer calls, full stop. The 4-click cutoff
lives entirely in App, which is exactly the point: useToggle’s own code
never needed to change to support it.
default — Default State Reducer
Problem: the app’s reducer above had to fully reimplement the 'reset'
case even though it never wanted to change that behavior — for a bigger
reducer this becomes real duplicated logic that can drift from the real
default. Export toggleReducer so the app can delegate to it.
// toggle.tsx
export function toggleReducer(state: ToggleState, action: ToggleAction) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'toggle': return { on: !state.on }
    case 'reset': return action.initialState
  }
}
 
// app.tsx
import { toggleReducer, useToggle } from './toggle.tsx'
 
const { on, getTogglerProps, getResetterProps } = useToggle({
  reducer(state, action) {
    if (action.type === 'toggle' && clickedTooMuch) {
      return state
    }
    return toggleReducer(state, action)
  },
})
Render trace

Same dispatch path as steps 3–5 above: click → dispatch({ type: 'toggle' })
→ React calls the app’s reducer function with (state, action).
Inside the app’s reducer: the if checks only the one condition this
consumer actually customizes (action.type === 'toggle' && clickedTooMuch).
If true, return state — same veto as before.
Otherwise — every other case, including every action type this
consumer doesn’t know or care about — it calls
toggleReducer(state, action) directly, a plain function call (not a
dispatch, not a hook) to the module’s real default reducer, and returns
whatever that computes. For 'reset', this is
toggleReducer(state, { type: 'reset', initialState }) →
action.initialState — identical behavior to the hook’s own default,
achieved with zero duplicated switch logic.
useReducer receives the app reducer’s return value either way — it has
no idea (and no way to know) that part of that computation happened
inside a plain function call to toggleReducer rather than inline in the
app’s own switch. From React’s perspective this step changes nothing
about when re-renders happen versus step “reducer” above — only how
the app’s reducer arrives at its answer.

Why
toggleReducer(state, action) being an ordinary exported function — not
tied to useReducer, not a hook itself — is what makes delegation this
cheap: the app calls it exactly like it would call any other pure function,
passing through the very (state, action) pair it already has in scope. If
useToggle’s author later adds a third action type, any consumer using this
delegate-by-default shape picks up the new behavior automatically, for free,
without editing their own reducer at all — only consumers who need to
change that new action’s behavior would need to add a case for it.
Sources

EpicWeb — Advanced React Patterns workshop, exercise 7 (both steps + solutions)
Kent C. Dodds — The State Reducer Pattern with React Hooks

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: 08 Control Props
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
Control Props — Render Trace (Exercise 8)

Line-by-line render/execution trace through the 1 solution step of
exercise 8 (“Control Props”) of EpicWeb’s
Advanced React Patterns
workshop by Kent C. Dodds. For the concept explanation (not the trace)
see Control Props — this note is about invocation order: what
happens inside useToggle on a click when controlled vs. uncontrolled,
and why the switch only visibly flips once the parent’s own setState
runs.

control — Control Props
Problem: <Toggle /> accepts on and onChange props (mirroring
<input value onChange>) but they’re inert — the component still manages
on entirely internally, so passing on from outside has no effect, and
two <Toggle>s can’t be kept in sync.
function App() {
  const [bothOn, setBothOn] = useState(false)
  const [timesClicked, setTimesClicked] = useState(0)
 
  function handleToggleChange(state: ToggleState, action: ToggleAction) {
    if (action.type === 'toggle' && timesClicked > 4) return
    setBothOn(state.on)
    setTimesClicked((c) => c + 1)
  }
 
  return (
    <div>
      <Toggle on={bothOn} onChange={handleToggleChange} />
      <Toggle on={bothOn} onChange={handleToggleChange} />
      <button onClick={() => { setBothOn(false); setTimesClicked(0) }}>Reset</button>
    </div>
  )
}
 
export function useToggle({
  initialOn = false,
  reducer = toggleReducer,
  onChange,
  on: controlledOn,
}: { initialOn?: boolean; reducer?: typeof toggleReducer;
     onChange?: (state: ToggleState, action: ToggleAction) => void;
     on?: boolean } = {}) {
  const { current: initialState } = useRef<ToggleState>({ on: initialOn })
  const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, initialState)
  const onIsControlled = controlledOn != null
  const on = onIsControlled ? controlledOn : state.on
 
  function dispatchWithOnChange(action: ToggleAction) {
    if (!onIsControlled) dispatch(action)
    onChange?.(reducer({ ...state, on }, action), action)
  }
 
  const toggle = () => dispatchWithOnChange({ type: 'toggle' })
  // getTogglerProps wires onClick: callAll(onClick, toggle)
}
 
export function Toggle({ on: controlledOn, onChange }: { on?: boolean; onChange?: (...) => void }) {
  const { on, getTogglerProps } = useToggle({ on: controlledOn, onChange })
  return <Switch {...getTogglerProps({ on })} />
}
Render trace

App() renders. bothOn = false, timesClicked = 0. It renders two
<Toggle on={false} onChange={handleToggleChange} />.
Each Toggle({ on: controlledOn, onChange }) calls
useToggle({ on: controlledOn, onChange }) — controlledOn is false,
which is not null/undefined, so onIsControlled = (false != null)
→ true. Both Toggle instances are controlled from their very first
render.
Inside useToggle, useReducer(reducer, initialState) still runs and
still holds its own internal state.on (false, unused this render),
but const on = onIsControlled ? controlledOn : state.on picks
controlledOn, so the value actually rendered comes from the prop, not
from useReducer’s state.
User clicks the first <Switch>. getTogglerProps’s onClick fires
toggle() → dispatchWithOnChange({ type: 'toggle' }).
Inside dispatchWithOnChange: onIsControlled is true, so
if (!onIsControlled) dispatch(action) is skipped — the internal
useReducer state never changes from this click. React schedules no
re-render of Toggle from this call by itself.
onChange?.(reducer({ ...state, on }, action), action) still runs:
reducer({ on: false }, { type: 'toggle' }) computes { on: true } —
the “suggested” next state — and calls handleToggleChange({ on: true }, { type: 'toggle' })
in App.
handleToggleChange checks timesClicked > 4 (false, so it proceeds),
then calls setBothOn(true) and setTimesClicked((c) => c + 1) — two
state updates on App, batched into one re-render.
App() re-renders with bothOn = true. Both <Toggle on={true} .../>
elements are reconstructed with the new prop.
Each Toggle re-renders, calls useToggle({ on: true, ... }) again.
onIsControlled is still true; on now resolves to true. Both
switches visually flip in this one render pass — not just the one the
user clicked — because both read from the same lifted bothOn.
If timesClicked had already exceeded 4 before this click,
handleToggleChange would return immediately at step 7 — setBothOn
never runs, App never re-renders, and the switch the user clicked
stays visually unchanged, even though dispatchWithOnChange still
ran and still called onChange. This is the mechanism behind “suggested
changes the parent can veto.”

Contrast — the uncontrolled path (the third <Toggle onChange={...} />
in the workshop’s App, with no on prop): at step 2, controlledOn is
undefined → onIsControlled = false. At step 5, dispatch(action) does
run, updating useReducer’s own state.on and triggering Toggle’s own
re-render directly — no round trip through a parent’s setState needed.
onChange still fires (for logging/observation), but nothing depends on the
parent acting on it.
Why
The controlled path deliberately does less work inside useToggle
(skips dispatch) so there’s exactly one source of truth for on — the
prop — instead of two (internal reducer state and the prop) that could
drift out of sync. The trade-off is the round-trip latency this trace makes
visible: a controlled Toggle can never show a new value except by way of
a full re-render triggered by the parent’s own state update. That’s not a
performance concern in practice (it’s one synchronous setState call,
batched), but it is why “the parent didn’t call setState” is a complete,
sufficient explanation for “the controlled toggle didn’t visibly move” —
there’s no other path to a visual update once controlled.
Sources

EpicWeb — Advanced React Patterns workshop, exercise 8 (step + solution)
Kent C. Dodds — When to use Control Props or State Reducers

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: Render Trace
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
Advanced React Patterns — Line-by-Line Render Trace
Index for a companion set of notes to Advanced React Patterns. Where the
notes linked from that MOC explain concepts (what problem a pattern
solves, what the API looks like), these notes trace execution order
through the actual solution code of each exercise of EpicWeb’s
Advanced React Patterns
workshop by Kent C. Dodds — what renders first, when state/context/refs get
read or written, what re-renders and why, and why each pattern needed the
specific React primitive it used.
One note per exercise, each covering every step’s solution code in order,
with real code pulled from the workshop repo
(~/epic-workshops/advanced-react-patterns) and a step-numbered render
trace. Read them in order — later exercises build on patterns established in
earlier ones (compound components build on composition; slots and prop
getters both extend compound components; state reducer and control props
both build on state initializers).
Notes, in order

01 Composition — building elements where the data lives instead of
drilling props through layout components. Step compose.
02 Latest Ref — using a ref (not state) to give a stable callback
identity access to the latest render’s values without becoming a
useEffect/useCallback dependency. Step ref.
03 Compound Components — sharing implicit state between a component
and its children via React.Children/cloneElement, then via context,
plus runtime prop-type validation. Steps context, validation.
04 Slots — a context-based alternative to compound components for
deeply nested or reorderable children, plus a generic hook version and a
render-prop/children-as-function variant. Steps context, generic,
prop.
05 Prop Getters — a reusable-state-logic hook (state collection) and
the prop-getter functions that fix the callback-collision problem
consumers hit when composing their own handlers with the hook’s. Steps
collections, getters.
06 State Initializers — accepting an initial* prop so a custom
hook’s consumer can set the starting state, and keeping that initial
value stable across re-renders with a ref/lazy initializer. Steps
initial, stability.
07 State Reducer — inverting control so the consumer of a hook can
intercept and override every state transition via a reducer they supply,
plus a default-action-types escape hatch. Steps reducer, default.
08 Control Props — fully controlled/uncontrolled dual-mode
components, warnings for mixing the two incorrectly, and the onChange
contract that makes controlling a hook’s state possible. Step control.

See also

Advanced React Patterns — the concept-note MOC these notes complement.
Composition and Layout Components, The Latest Ref Pattern,
Compound Components, The Slots Pattern,
State Collections and Prop Getters, State Initializers,
The State Reducer Pattern, Control Props — the individual concept
deep-dives referenced throughout these trace notes.

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: The Slots Pattern
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
The Slots Pattern

Notes from EpicWeb’s Advanced React Patterns
workshop by Kent C. Dodds (exercise 4, “Slots”) plus
react-aria’s advanced customization docs
(the pattern’s real-world origin) and outside write-ups. Companion to
Compound Components (the cloneElement-based alternative this pattern
replaces for deeply nested children) and
Composition and Layout Components (the “pass elements, not data” idea
this formalizes with context). Notes and clarifications by me are marked
with > 💬.

Interview Q&A
Q: What problem do slots solve that plain compound components (cloneElement)
don’t?
A: `React.Children.map`/`cloneElement` only reaches
direct children — it breaks the moment a consumer wraps a child in a
<div> or their own component, and it can’t hand a specific bundle of props
to a component buried three levels deep. Slots solve this with context
instead of tree-walking: a parent puts a { [slotName]: props } map on
context once, and any descendant — no matter how deeply nested or how the
consumer chose to arrange the tree — can look up “am I filling the label
slot? Here are my props.” In the workshop’s TextField example, Label
and Input need to share a generated id/htmlFor pair, but the consumer
should be free to put other markup between them.
Q: What does the actual mechanism look like?
A: A parent builds a Slots object (a plain Record<string, Record<string, unknown>>
— slot name to the props that slot should receive) and provides it via a
SlotContext. A useSlotProps(props, slotName) hook reads that context and
merges the slot’s props under the ones explicitly passed to the component:
// slots.tsx
type Slots = Record<string, Record<string, unknown>>
export const SlotContext = createContext<Slots>({})
 
function useSlotProps<Props>(props: Props, slot: string): Props {
  const slots = use(SlotContext)
  return { ...slots[slot], slot, ...props } as Props
}
 
export function Label(props: React.ComponentProps<'label'>) {
  props = useSlotProps(props, 'label')
  return <label {...props} />
}
 
export function Input(props: React.ComponentProps<'input'>) {
  props = useSlotProps(props, 'input')
  return <input {...props} />
}
// text-field.tsx — the root component that fills the slots
export function TextField({ id, children }: { id?: string; children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const generatedId = useId()
  id ??= generatedId
  const slots = { label: { htmlFor: id }, input: { id } }
  return <SlotContext value={slots}>{children}</SlotContext>
}
Consumers arrange Label/Input however they like inside <TextField> —
nesting doesn’t matter, because lookup happens through context, not through
walking children.
Q: Slot components need to know which slot they are — how, if a
component like Text can fill more than one role (label vs. description)?
A: Two ways, and the workshop’s step progression covers both:

Hardcoded default slot — a dedicated component like Label always
passes a fixed slot name (useSlotProps(props, 'label')). Simple, but
needs one component per role.
A slot prop the consumer sets explicitly — a single generic
component (like Text) accepts slot and forwards it:
function useSlotProps<Props>(props: Props & { slot?: string }, defaultSlot?: string): Props {
  const slot = props.slot ?? defaultSlot
  if (!slot) return props
  const slots = use(SlotContext)
  return { ...slots[slot], slot, ...props } as Props
}
 
export function Text(props: React.ComponentProps<'span'> & { slot?: string }) {
  props = useSlotProps(props, 'text')
  return <span {...props} />
}
Now one <Text> component can play the onText role in one place and
offText in another, purely by which slot string the consumer passes —
this is exactly how react-aria’s <Text slot="description"> works (see
the workshop README’s CheckboxGroup/ComboBox examples).

Q: How does this let you collapse a compound-component family like
ToggleOn/ToggleOff/ToggleButton into fewer components?
A: Once slot identity comes from a slot prop rather than from which named
component you imported, ToggleOn and ToggleOff (which only differed in
which prop bundle — hidden when off vs. when on — they injected) collapse
into one reusable Text component used twice with different slot values,
and ToggleButton collapses into a generic Switch that reads its id/on/
onClick from the switch slot:
// toggle.tsx — Toggle now defines what each slot receives, nothing else
export function Toggle({ id, children }: { id?: string; children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const [on, setOn] = useState(false)
  const generatedId = useId()
  id ??= generatedId
  const toggle = () => setOn(!on)
 
  return (
    <SlotContext
      value={{
        label: { htmlFor: id },
        onText: { hidden: on ? undefined : true },
        offText: { hidden: on ? true : undefined },
        switch: { id, on, onClick: toggle },
      }}
    >
      {children}
    </SlotContext>
  )
}
// consumer API — no more ToggleOn/ToggleOff/ToggleButton exports needed
<Toggle>
  <Label>Party mode</Label>
  <Switch />
  <Text slot="onText">Let's party 🥳</Text>
  <Text slot="offText">Sad town 😭</Text>
</Toggle>
Q: Can two unrelated compound-component families (Toggle, TextField)
share the same Label component?
A: Yes — that’s the payoff of routing slot props through context instead of
hardcoding them into each family’s own component set. In the workshop, one
Label/Input pair from slots.tsx is reused verbatim by both Toggle
(providing a label slot for its button) and TextField (providing label

input slots) — each root component just provides a different Slots
object down its own subtree.

Q: What’s the actual trade-off versus one-component-per-role compound
components?
A: Flexibility and reuse at the cost of type safety and discoverability.
The workshop’s own solution README calls this out: “there’s not a great way
to have good type safety on these props” — nothing at compile time stops you
from typing slot="labl" or forgetting a slot prop entirely; you only find
out at runtime (or not at all, if the slot silently gets no extra props).
react-aria’s real implementation adds runtime warnings for exactly this
reason (see the source linked in its solution README). Named compound
components (ToggleOn, ToggleOff) don’t have this problem — a typo is a
TypeScript/import error, not a silent no-op — at the cost of one dedicated
component per role.
Why component libraries need this at all
Kent frames the whole exercise around a tension every component-library
author eventually hits: correctness vs. flexibility. A library wants to
stop consumers from breaking accessibility — forgetting an aria-describedby,
mismatching a label’s htmlFor with its input’s id — but it also can’t
hand-author a bespoke component for every layout a consumer might want. Named
compound components (ToggleOn, ToggleOff, ToggleButton) solve
correctness well (the wiring lives inside each component, a consumer can’t
get it wrong) but don’t scale to flexibility: every new role needs a new
component, and React.Children.map/cloneElement-based wiring only reaches
direct children, so a consumer can’t wrap one in a styling <div> without
breaking it.
Slots resolve the tension by separating identity from props: instead of
each role being a distinct, hardcoded component, a root component publishes
a map of { slotName: propsForThatSlot } via context, and any descendant —
arbitrarily deep, arbitrarily wrapped — can ask “do I have props for the
label slot?” This is exactly how react-aria
(the pattern’s real production origin, not just a workshop exercise) builds
its actual component library. Its own CheckboxGroup example, straight from
the workshop’s README:
<CheckboxGroup>
  <Label>Pets</Label>
  <MyCheckbox value="dogs">Dogs</MyCheckbox>
  <MyCheckbox value="cats">Cats</MyCheckbox>
  <MyCheckbox value="dragons">Dragons</MyCheckbox>
  <Text slot="description">Select your pets.</Text>
</CheckboxGroup>
slot="description" tells Text which bucket of props to pull from context
— CheckboxGroup doesn’t need to know Text exists, and Text doesn’t need
to know it’s inside a CheckboxGroup specifically; it only needs to know how
to read SlotContext. The same Text component is reused, unmodified,
inside react-aria’s much more elaborate ComboBox anatomy (also straight
from the workshop):
<ComboBox>
  <Label />
  <Input />
  <Button />
  <Text slot="description" />
  <FieldError />
  <Popover>
    <ListBox>
      <ListBoxItem>
        <Text slot="label" />
        <Text slot="description" />
      </ListBoxItem>
    </ListBox>
  </Popover>
</ComboBox>
Two different roles (label, description) inside the same component
family, filled by the same Text component, purely by which slot string
each instance is given. That’s the flexibility payoff: one generic component
plays many roles, safely, because the actual aria-* attributes, ids, and
event handlers are still assembled centrally by the root component (ComboBox,
Toggle, TextField) — a consumer rearranges where things render, never
what accessibility wiring they get. Confirmed independently outside the
workshop: react-aria’s own production API is described the same way — every
component exposes a matching context so consumers can build custom
compositions, and low-level components like Button and Popover are
genuinely reused, unmodified, across unrelated patterns like NumberField
and Select, which is the same “same Label/Input pair reused by both
Toggle and TextField” reuse this note’s Q&A section demonstrates in
miniature.
How the mechanism assembles, end to end
The workshop’s own “Implementation” writeup collapses the whole pattern into
two halves. First, the root component builds one plain object mapping slot
names to the props each slot should receive, and provides it as context —
here’s its own generic example (NumberField, not Toggle/TextField,
showing the pattern isn’t tied to any one component):
function NumberField({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  // setup state/events/etc
  const slots = {
    label: { htmlFor: inputId },
    decrement: { onClick: decrement },
    increment: { onClick: increment },
    description: { id: descriptionId },
    input: { id: inputId, 'aria-describedby': descriptionId },
  }
  return <SlotContext value={slots}>{children}</SlotContext>
}
Second, every slot-aware component reads that context through one shared
hook and merges what it finds into its own props:
function Input(props) {
  props = useSlotProps(props, 'input')
  return <input {...props} />
}
Walking this through with Toggle (the note’s Q&A section already showed
the code; here’s the sequence): Toggle renders, computes its on state,
and builds a Slots object with one entry per role its children might play
(label, onText, offText, switch) — this happens once per render, at
the top, near the state it depends on. It provides that object via
<SlotContext value={slots}>. Deep inside children (however the consumer
nested them), each Label/Text/Switch calls useSlotProps, which reads
the current SlotContext value and spreads the matching slot’s props
underneath its own explicit props. Nothing about this depends on where in
the tree those consumer components actually sit — React.Children.map never
runs; the connection is purely “whichever SlotContext provider is nearest
above me in the tree, read its value,” the same mechanism [[Compound Components]]’s context step already uses for a single implicit value,
generalized here to a whole map of per-role prop bundles.
Sources for this section

EpicWeb Advanced React Patterns workshop, exercise 04.slots topic
README (“Implementation” section, NumberField example, and the
CheckboxGroup/ComboBox react-aria anatomy examples)
React Aria — Advanced Customization —
confirms useContextProps/slot prop as react-aria’s real, current
mechanism, and that low-level components (Button, Popover) are
genuinely reused across unrelated higher-level patterns the same way this
workshop’s Label/Input are reused across Toggle/TextField

Rules and caveats

Slots are compound components implemented via context instead of
cloneElement. Reach for slots specifically when children may be
deeply nested, conditionally wrapped, or reordered by the consumer — cases
where `React.Children.map` can’t see far enough
into the tree.
Merge order matters. { ...slots[slot], slot, ...props } puts the
slot’s props first and the caller’s explicit props last, so a consumer
can always override what the slot would otherwise inject (e.g. passing
their own id).
Prefer a hardcoded default slot per dedicated component (Label →
always 'label') and only add an overridable slot prop on genuinely
generic, reusable primitives (Text, Switch) that need to play more
than one role across different parents.
This is a real, shipped pattern, not a workshop toy — it’s exactly how
react-aria components wire
up ARIA roles, generated ids, and event handlers across a component
family without forcing one bespoke component per relationship.
It composes with Composition and Layout Components — slots are
still “pass elements, not data” at the JSX level; what’s new is that the
props each element should receive travel via context instead of being
threaded by the parent that renders them.

Sources

EpicWeb Advanced React Patterns workshop, exercise 04.slots (steps
context, generic, prop)
React Aria — Advanced Customization
Sandro Roth — Building Component Slots in React
DeepWiki — Slots Pattern (epicweb-dev/advanced-react-patterns)

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: State Initializers
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
State Initializers

Notes from EpicWeb’s Advanced React Patterns
workshop by Kent C. Dodds (exercise 6, “State Initializer”) plus the
official react.dev useRef
reference. Companion to The State Reducer Pattern (the natural next
step once state is externally initializable) and Control Props (full
external control, of which “set the starting value” is a limited form).
Notes and clarifications by me are marked with > 💬.

Interview Q&A
Q: What does the state initializer pattern add to a custom hook?
A: A way for the consumer of the hook to choose the starting state,
instead of it being hardcoded — and, once you have that, a way to reset
back to that starting state predictably. In our example, useToggle
hardcodes on: false; the pattern makes that an initialOn option instead:
// before — no way to start "on"
export function useToggle() {
  const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(toggleReducer, { on: false })
  // ...
}
 
// after — consumer controls the starting value
export function useToggle({ initialOn = false } = {}) {
  const initialState = { on: initialOn }
  const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(toggleReducer, initialState)
  // ...
}
Q: Why does “reset” need its own reducer action instead of just calling
setState(initialState) (or dispatch({ type: 'toggle' }) twice)?
A: Because “reset” isn’t a transformation of the current state — it’s
“throw away whatever the current state is and go back to a fixed value,”
which the reducer needs to express explicitly rather than derive:
type ToggleAction =
  | { type: 'toggle' }
  | { type: 'reset'; initialState: ToggleState }
 
function toggleReducer(state: ToggleState, action: ToggleAction) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'toggle':
      return { on: !state.on }
    case 'reset':
      return action.initialState
  }
}
 
const reset = () => dispatch({ type: 'reset', initialState })
Q: What’s the bug this pattern’s second half (“stability”) fixes?
A: const initialState = { on: initialOn } is a plain object literal
recomputed on every render of useToggle. useReducer(toggleReducer, initialState)
only uses that value once, on mount — React ignores the second argument on
every render after the first, same as useState’s initial value. But
reset is a closure created fresh every render too, and it captures
that render’s initialState — which holds that render’s initialOn,
not the one from mount. If a consumer’s initialOn prop changes after
mount (their own state toggling it, say) and they later call reset(),
it resets to the current initialOn, not the original one:
// consumer app — initialOn is itself stateful
const [initialOn, setInitialOn] = useState(true)
const { on, reset } = useToggle({ initialOn })
// user flips initialOn to false, then clicks Reset:
// reset() dispatches { type: 'reset', initialState: { on: false } }
// — resets to false, NOT to the true it actually started with.
Q: How does wrapping it in useRef fix it?
A: useRef’s initial value is captured exactly once, on mount, and
ref.current stays whatever was written there regardless of how many times
the component/hook re-renders — unlike a plain const in the function body,
which is a fresh binding every render. Reading initialState off the ref
inside reset always yields the value from the render that first created
it:
export function useToggle({ initialOn = false } = {}) {
  const { current: initialState } = useRef<ToggleState>({ on: initialOn })
  const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(toggleReducer, initialState)
  const { on } = state
 
  const toggle = () => dispatch({ type: 'toggle' })
  const reset = () => dispatch({ type: 'reset', initialState }) // always the mount-time value
  // ...
}
Q: Could useState(() => ({ on: initialOn }))’s lazy initializer do the
same job instead of useRef?
A: For seeding useReducer/useState itself, yes — the lazy-initializer
form is only invoked once, on mount, exactly like useRef’s argument. The
reason this workshop reaches for useRef specifically is that reset needs
a stable value to read back later, not just a one-time seed for
useReducer’s own initial state — useReducer’s initial argument isn’t
something your code can re-read after mount, but ref.current is. useRef
is the general “give me a mutable box that survives re-renders without
changing identity” primitive; a lazy initializer only solves “compute the
first value cheaply.”
Q: Is initialState = { on: initialOn } itself expensive enough to need
the lazy-initializer treatment (i.e., would useRef(computeIt()) waste
work on every render before settling)?
A: In this example, no — it’s a plain object literal, cheap regardless of
how many renders throw the result away. useRef(initialValue) does
technically re-evaluate initialValue on every render (unlike useState’s
lazy form, which skips re-invoking the initializer function after mount) —
it just discards every recomputation after the first. That only matters if
constructing the throwaway value is itself expensive; here it isn’t.
How the pattern builds up, in Kent’s own progression
Kent’s workshop README lays out the state initializer pattern independently
of useToggle’s reducer, using a plainer useCounter hook — worth walking
through on its own because it isolates the pattern from the reducer
machinery the Q&A above is threading through. It builds in three small
steps.
Step 1 — a hook with hardcoded initial state:
function useCounter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0)
  const increment = () => setCount((c) => c + 1)
  return { count, increment }
}
Nothing wrong with this on its own, but every consumer of useCounter is
stuck starting at 0. The first move is to accept the starting value as an
option instead of baking it in:
function useCounter({ initialCount = 0 } = {}) {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(initialCount)
  const increment = () => setCount((c) => c + 1)
  return { count, increment }
}
Step 2 — add a resetter. Once a hook has a concept of “the starting
value,” it’s natural to also expose a way to jump back to it:
function useCounter({ initialCount = 0 } = {}) {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(initialCount)
  const increment = () => setCount((c) => c + 1)
  const reset = () => setCount(initialCount)
  return { count, increment, reset }
}
This looks complete, and for a consumer who never changes initialCount
after mount, it is. The bug only shows up once initialCount itself is
allowed to vary across renders — which is exactly what step stability’s
problem statement sets up: a button that toggles initialOn, followed by a
reset button, so the mismatch between “the value right now” and “the value
this hook actually started with” becomes directly observable rather than
theoretical.
Step 3 — stabilize it with a ref. Kent’s fix, in its simplest form
(before useToggle’s reducer complicates the shape):
function useCounter({ initialCount = 0 } = {}) {
  const initialCountRef = useRef(initialCount)
  const [count, setCount] = useState(initialCountRef.current)
  const increment = () => setCount((c) => c + 1)
  const reset = () => setCount(initialCountRef.current)
  return { count, increment, reset }
}
useRef(initialCount)’s argument is only ever committed to
initialCountRef.current on the render that creates the ref — after that,
.current is a plain mutable field that nothing in this hook writes to
again, so it just keeps holding whatever was there from mount. reset reads
initialCountRef.current, not the initialCount parameter directly, so it’s
immune to whatever initialCount happens to be on the render reset is
called from.
Why a ref specifically, and not something else
The mechanical property this pattern leans on is one of useRef’s two
defining characteristics, per react.dev: a ref returns the same object
across every re-render of the component, and mutating .current does
not trigger a re-render the way setState would (react.dev,
“Referencing Values with Refs”;
useRef reference). Both halves
matter here, for different reasons:

Same object across renders is what makes .current a legitimate place
to stash “the value from a specific earlier render” and read it back
later — a plain const inside the hook body doesn’t have this property at
all; it’s a fresh binding, recomputed from scratch, every single render.
Mutating it doesn’t re-render is why this is safe to do outside of
useState: nothing about capturing initialOn’s mount-time value into a
ref should, by itself, cause useToggle’s consumer to re-render — it’s
bookkeeping for a future reset() call, not a value the UI needs to
reflect right now. (React does still recommend not reading/writing
ref.current during rendering except for this exact one-time
initialization pattern — writing it unconditionally on every render would
reintroduce the same “always follows the latest value” bug this pattern
exists to avoid.)

Contrast this with useToggle’s own state (managed by useReducer):
changing state does need to re-render, because state.on is what
gets rendered on screen. The two live side by side in the same hook
precisely because they answer different questions — “what should the UI
show right now” (state) vs. “what should reset go back to, regardless of
what’s happened since” (the ref) — and conflating them, by reading reset’s
target off a plain closure variable instead of a ref, is exactly the bug
stability fixes.
Rules and caveats

A hook’s initial* option should only ever seed the FIRST render.
Treat it the same way useState’s initial argument behaves: read once,
ignore on every subsequent render, exactly mirroring how <input defaultValue>
behaves vs. a controlled value.
Anything a reset function needs to read back later must be captured in
a ref (or the reducer’s closed-over initial argument), not a plain local
variable. A const inside the hook body is recreated every render; only
useRef’s .current (or state itself) survives with a stable identity
across renders.
Don’t reach for useRef here just out of habit — reach for it because
reset needs a value from a specific past render (mount), not the
current one. If nothing in the hook needs to look backward at the
original value after mount, a lazy useState/useReducer initializer
alone is enough.
This pattern composes with the rest of the workshop. Once a hook
accepts initial*, the natural next questions are “can the consumer
intercept every state transition, not just the starting value?” (see
The State Reducer Pattern) and “can the consumer fully own the state
instead of just seeding it?” (see Control Props).

Sources

EpicWeb Advanced React Patterns workshop, exercise 06.state-initializers
(steps “initial” and “stability”)
react.dev — useRef

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: The State Reducer Pattern
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
The State Reducer Pattern

Notes from EpicWeb’s Advanced React Patterns
workshop by Kent C. Dodds (exercise 7, “State Reducer”) plus his blog post
The State Reducer Pattern with React Hooks
and When to use Control Props or State Reducers.
Builds directly on State Initializers’s useToggle hook. Companion to
Control Props, the next step up in inversion of control. Notes and
clarifications by me are marked with > 💬.

Interview Q&A
Q: What problem does the state reducer pattern solve?
A: A reusable hook/component can’t anticipate every state-transition
customization its consumers will eventually want. Adding a boolean prop per
customization (“don’t close on outside click”, “cap toggles at 4 clicks”)
doesn’t scale — every new request means another prop and another branch
inside the hook’s own reducer. The state reducer pattern sidesteps this by
inverting control: instead of the hook deciding every state transition
itself, it accepts a reducer function from the consumer and calls that
whenever it would normally compute the next state. The consumer now owns the
transition logic; the hook just supplies the mechanism (dispatch,
useReducer) and a sensible default.
Q: What does that look like concretely?
A: The hook’s default reducer becomes a plain, overridable default parameter:
function toggleReducer(state: ToggleState, action: ToggleAction) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'toggle': {
      return { on: !state.on }
    }
    case 'reset': {
      return action.initialState
    }
  }
}
 
export function useToggle({ initialOn = false, reducer = toggleReducer } = {}) {
  const { current: initialState } = useRef<ToggleState>({ on: initialOn })
  const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, initialState)
  const { on } = state
 
  const toggle = () => dispatch({ type: 'toggle' })
  const reset = () => dispatch({ type: 'reset', initialState })
 
  // ...getTogglerProps/getResetterProps as in [[State Collections and Prop Getters]]
  return { on, reset, toggle, getTogglerProps, getResetterProps }
}
Nothing about useReducer(reducer, initialState) cares whether reducer
came from inside this module or from the consumer — useReducer’s whole
API is designed to accept any reducer function. The pattern is really just
“don’t hardcode which reducer function you pass.”
Q: How does a consumer actually use this to add custom behavior?
A: They pass their own reducer to the hook, matching the same
(state, action) => newState shape the hook dispatches internally:
function App() {
  const [timesClicked, setTimesClicked] = useState(0)
  const clickedTooMuch = timesClicked >= 4
 
  const { on, getTogglerProps, getResetterProps } = useToggle({
    reducer(state, action) {
      switch (action.type) {
        case 'toggle': {
          if (clickedTooMuch) return state // veto the transition entirely
          return { on: !state.on }
        }
        case 'reset': {
          return { on: false }
        }
      }
    },
  })
  // ...
}
useToggle still calls toggle() → dispatch({ type: 'toggle' })
internally on every click — the hook’s own code never changed. What changed
is which function useReducer runs to turn that action into a new state:
the consumer’s, not the module’s default. Returning the unchanged state
for the 'toggle' case is how a consumer vetoes a transition entirely —
useReducer treats returning the same reference/an equal value as “nothing
happened,” so on simply doesn’t flip.
Q: Doesn’t this force every consumer to re-implement the whole reducer,
even for a one-line customization?
A: That’s the real cost, and the workshop’s own README calls it out — for a
toggleReducer this small it’s a minor duplication, but a more complex
hook’s default reducer could be substantial, and forcing every consumer to
copy-paste all of it just to override one case is a poor API. The fix:
export the default reducer so consumers can delegate to it for the
cases they don’t want to change:
export function toggleReducer(state: ToggleState, action: ToggleAction) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'toggle': {
      return { on: !state.on }
    }
    case 'reset': {
      return action.initialState
    }
  }
}
import { toggleReducer, useToggle } from './toggle.tsx'
 
const { on, getTogglerProps, getResetterProps } = useToggle({
  reducer(state, action) {
    if (action.type === 'toggle' && clickedTooMuch) {
      return state // the one case this consumer actually customizes
    }
    return toggleReducer(state, action) // delegate everything else
  },
})
Now the consumer’s reducer is a thin wrapper: intercept the one action type
it cares about, delegate the rest to the real default. This is the same
shape downshift’s stateReducer prop uses in production — downshift
exports its own default reducer for exactly this reason.
Q: How is this different from just passing more boolean props?
A: Boolean props are a closed set the hook author has to predict in advance
and grows without bound as requirements grow. A reducer prop is an open
set — the consumer can express any transition logic the (state, action)
shape can represent, including logic the hook’s author never imagined
(click-count limits, logging every action, syncing to localStorage,
combining several vetoes), without the hook’s own source ever changing
again. The tradeoff is that consumers now need to understand the hook’s
internal action shape ({ type: 'toggle' }, { type: 'reset', initialState })
— a state reducer is a more powerful but more leaky abstraction than a prop.
Q: When should I reach for this instead of Control Props?
A: Per Kent’s follow-up post on the two: control props hand the consumer
full ownership of the value (they pass on and onChange and own the
useState entirely) — appropriate when the consumer needs the state to
live in and be driven by their own component tree. State reducer hands the
consumer ownership of the transition logic while the hook still owns
where the state lives — appropriate when consumers just need to customize
how the hook reacts to its own events, not relocate the state itself.
State reducer is the lighter-weight ask of the two; control props is the
escape hatch for when state reducer still isn’t enough (e.g. syncing the
value with another controlled input, or driving it from a URL/router).
Inversion of control, and why this pattern exists at all
The workshop frames this pattern with a specific computer-science term —
inversion of control — and it’s worth taking that framing seriously
rather than treating it as a label. Normally, a reusable hook is the
“author” of every state transition it produces: it decides, in its own
toggleReducer, exactly what { type: 'toggle' } means. Inversion of
control flips that authority: the hook’s author hands the mechanism
(dispatch, useReducer, the shape of its actions) to the consumer and
steps back from deciding what those mechanisms actually do. The hook still
drives when a transition happens (a click still calls toggle(), which
still dispatches { type: 'toggle' }) — what moves is who decides what
that dispatch results in.
The workshop’s own motivating example makes the alternative’s failure mode
concrete: a combobox that closes its menu whenever the user clicks outside
it. That’s the right default for most consumers, but not all of them — and
the fix isn’t “add a closeOnClickOutside boolean prop,” because the next
consumer wants something the hook author didn’t anticipate either. Kent’s
blog post on this pattern (linked above) gives the real production instance
this generalizes from: downshift’s isOpen state normally flips to
false the instant a user selects an item, which is correct for a typical
single-select dropdown — until someone building a multi-select combobox
with downshift needed the menu to stay open after a selection, so the
user could keep picking more items without reopening it each time. Rather
than adding a keepOpenOnSelect prop (and the next one, and the one after
that), downshift exposes a stateReducer prop with exactly the shape this
exercise’s useToggle ends up with — the multi-select consumer’s own
reducer intercepts the 'selection'-type action and overrides just that one
transition, while every other action still goes through unchanged.
The mechanism, traced through real code
The trick that makes this pattern almost free to implement, once you’re
already using useReducer, is that useReducer(reducer, initialState)
never cared where reducer came from — it’s just a function reference.
Exercise 6 ([[State Initializers]]) already had useToggle calling
useReducer(toggleReducer, initialState) with a hardcoded reducer; this
exercise’s entire change is turning that hardcoded reference into a
default parameter:
// Before this exercise: reducer is hardcoded
const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(toggleReducer, initialState)
 
// After: reducer is a parameter, toggleReducer only supplies the default
export function useToggle({ initialOn = false, reducer = toggleReducer } = {}) {
  const { current: initialState } = useRef<ToggleState>({ on: initialOn })
  const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, initialState)
  // ...
}
Nothing else in useToggle changes. toggle() still calls
dispatch({ type: 'toggle' }) exactly as before — the hook’s own click
handling is completely unaware of whether reducer is its own default or
something a consumer supplied. All the new behavior lives entirely in
which function useReducer happens to be holding onto, which is precisely
why the workshop’s aside calls this “WAY better” with hooks than the
pre-hooks class-component equivalent: useReducer already has an
extensibility point (its first argument) built into its design, so there’s
no new API surface to invent — just a default parameter.
Once a consumer supplies their own reducer, the trace of an actual click
looks like this: the user clicks the toggle → useToggle’s own toggle()
runs, calling dispatch({ type: 'toggle' }), exactly as it always did →
useReducer calls the consumer’s reducer(state, { type: 'toggle' }),
not toggleReducer → the consumer’s function runs its own logic (check
clickedTooMuch, then either return state unchanged or
return { on: !state.on }) → whatever it returns becomes the new state.
useReducer’s own “did this actually change?” check (structurally the same
one useState’s setter uses) is what turns return state into a real
veto — React sees the returned value is reference-equal to the current
state and skips scheduling a re-render, so nothing about the toggle
visually moves, with no special “cancel this action” API needed anywhere.
Making the pattern practical: exporting the default
The second half of this exercise addresses a real cost the workshop names
directly: forcing every consumer to hand-write a full replacement reducer
is fine for a two-case toggleReducer, but becomes a burden the moment a
hook’s default reducer is genuinely complex — a consumer who only wants to
change one case shouldn’t have to correctly reimplement every other case
too (and keep that copy in sync if the hook’s own default reducer ever
changes). The fix the workshop walks through is mechanically small but
practically important: export the default reducer function itself, so a
consumer’s custom reducer can call it directly for anything it doesn’t want
to change:
// toggle.tsx — the default reducer is now a named export, not just an
// internal default parameter value
export function toggleReducer(state: ToggleState, action: ToggleAction) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'toggle': return { on: !state.on }
    case 'reset': return action.initialState
  }
}
// app.tsx — the consumer's own reducer delegates instead of duplicating
import { toggleReducer, useToggle } from './toggle.tsx'
 
function toggleStateReducer(state: ToggleState, action: ToggleAction) {
  if (action.type === 'toggle' && clickedTooMuch) {
    return state // the ONE case this consumer actually cares about
  }
  return toggleReducer(state, action) // everything else: use the real default
}
 
const { on, getTogglerProps, getResetterProps } = useToggle({
  reducer: toggleStateReducer,
})
This is the exact shape downshift ships in production for the same
reason: its own default reducer handles many action types (item
highlighted, item selected, menu opened/closed, blur, escape key…), and a
consumer customizing one of them needs a way to fall through to “everything
else, handle it the normal way” without vendoring the whole switch
statement. Exporting the default reducer is what turns “you have complete
control” from a burden into a genuinely additive customization.
Rules and caveats

Match the action shape exactly. The consumer’s reducer receives the
exact action objects the hook dispatches internally ({ type: 'toggle' },
{ type: 'reset', initialState }) — this is effectively a public API
contract even though it looks like an implementation detail. Renaming an
action’s type or its payload shape is a breaking change for every
consumer with a custom reducer, so treat ToggleAction’s shape (and the
exported action-type strings, if you formalize them further) as part of
the hook’s public surface.
Export the default reducer, not just use it internally. Without an
exported toggleReducer, every customization forces a full
reimplementation — the “default” step in this pattern isn’t optional
polish, it’s what makes the pattern practical for anything more complex
than a two-case toggle.
Returning the same state vetoes the transition. useReducer doesn’t
re-render for a reducer call that returns a value React considers
unchanged — this is how “ignore this action” is expressed, not a special
API. A consumer’s reducer that wants to no-op an action should return state
(the exact same reference), not construct a new object with the same
values.
This composes with State Collections and Prop Getters and
State Initializers. The reducer default parameter, the
initialOn/useRef-captured initial state, and the getTogglerProps/
getResetterProps prop getters all live in the same useToggle hook —
each pattern in this workshop is a layer added on top of the same running
example, not a separate hook.

Sources

EpicWeb Advanced React Patterns workshop, exercise 07.state-reducer
(steps “reducer” and “default”)
Kent C. Dodds — The State Reducer Pattern with React Hooks
Kent C. Dodds — When to use Control Props or State Reducers
downshift — the real-world
library this pattern is drawn from (stateReducer prop)

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
Hello World in JS

Notes from the EpicReact “React Fundamentals” workshop by Kent C. Dodds. Notes and clarifications by me are marked with > 💬.

Before touching React, this exercise builds “Hello World” using nothing but the raw DOM APIs — the same primitives React itself is built on top of.
Interview Q&A
Q: Why doesn’t document.createElement alone put anything on the page?
A: This is a general fact about the DOM API, independent of any framework: createElement only builds a node in memory — it isn’t attached to the visible document tree until it’s explicitly append-ed (or insertBefored, etc.) to a node that’s already on the page. That imperative create → mutate → append sequence is exactly the tedium that any declarative UI library, React included, exists to hide behind a simpler API. In our example, element only becomes visible after the final rootElement.append(element) call — the two lines before it just built it in memory.
const element = document.createElement('div') // built in memory only
element.textContent = 'Hello World'            // still not visible
rootElement.append(element)                    // now it's on the page
Q: Why use textContent instead of innerHTML when setting text?
A: This is a security-relevant DOM API distinction that applies anywhere user or dynamic content is rendered: textContent never parses its input as HTML, so a malicious string like <img src=x onerror=alert(1)> is inserted as inert, literal visible text rather than becoming a live, executable element — while innerHTML would parse and run it, opening the door to XSS. This is the same underlying distinction behind why React escapes every string it renders by default and gates raw HTML injection behind the deliberately alarming dangerouslySetInnerHTML name. In our example, element.textContent = 'Hello World' is what keeps this safe by default, with no framework involved yet.
Q: Is there anything special about a “root” DOM node?
A: No, and this holds for any UI framework mounted into the DOM: a “root” is just a regular DOM node, created and appended exactly like any other element — frameworks don’t have privileged access to some special container, they’re just consistently automating the same createElement/append calls you’d otherwise write by hand. In our example, the “Generate the Root Node” step creates <div id="root"> itself and appends it to document.body, proving there’s nothing pre-existing or magical about it.
Hello World in JS

Lesson

const rootElement = document.getElementById('root')
const element = document.createElement('div')
element.className = 'container'
element.textContent = 'Hello World'
rootElement.append(element)

💬 Creating an element with document.createElement only builds it in memory — it isn’t on the page until you explicitly append it to something that already is on the page. This imperative, step-by-step nature (create → mutate → append) is exactly the tedium React’s declarative API exists to hide.


💬 Notice this uses textContent, not innerHTML. textContent never parses its input as HTML — a string like <img src=x onerror=alert(1)> just becomes literal visible text, not a live element. That’s the same reason React escapes every string it renders by default, and why injecting raw HTML requires the deliberately alarming-looking dangerouslySetInnerHTML escape hatch. The safety isn’t a React invention — it’s this same DOM-level distinction, just made the default.

Generate the Root Node

Lesson

Rather than relying on a <div id="root"> already in the HTML, create the root itself and append it to document.body:
const rootElement = document.createElement('div')
rootElement.id = 'root'
document.body.append(rootElement)
 
const element = document.createElement('div')
element.textContent = 'Hello World'
rootElement.append(element)

💬 This is purely to drive home that there’s nothing magic about a “root” element — it’s just another DOM node created and appended like any other. Libraries like React aren’t doing anything you couldn’t do by hand; they’re just doing a lot of it, consistently, for you.
