Raw React APIs
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
Raw React APIs

Notes from the EpicReact “React Fundamentals” workshop by Kent C. Dodds. Notes and clarifications by me are marked with > 💬.

React ships as two packages for the web: React (creates React elements — components, hooks, the declarative API) and ReactDOM (renders those elements to the actual DOM — the web-specific renderer; React also has renderers for native, VR, and even the terminal). This exercise uses both directly, with no JSX yet, to see what a “React element” actually is before the syntactic sugar is added.
Interview Q&A
Q: What does createElement actually return, and why does that matter?
A: In general, React’s rendering model is built on “virtual DOM” — every createElement(type, props, ...children) call returns a lightweight plain JS object describing what should be on screen, not an actual DOM node. This is what lets React diff two renders cheaply (comparing objects) before touching the real, expensive-to-mutate DOM. In our example, createElement('div', { className: 'container', children: 'Hello World' }) returns a descriptor like { type: 'div', props: { className: 'container', children: 'Hello World' } } — nothing is on screen yet until it’s passed to a renderer.
const element = createElement('div', { className: 'container' }, 'Hello World')
// element is roughly: { type: 'div', props: { className: 'container', children: 'Hello World' } }
Q: What’s the difference between React and ReactDOM, and why are they separate packages?
A: React is split into a renderer-agnostic core (creating elements, managing components/hooks/reconciliation) and one or more platform-specific renderers, so the same component model can target different environments — ReactDOM for the browser, React Native for mobile, react-three-fiber for WebGL, even terminal renderers exist. This separation is what makes “learn React once, write anywhere” possible. In our example, react.js provides createElement while react-dom/client.js provides createRoot(...).render(...), the step that actually turns element objects into real DOM nodes.
Q: Are React elements mutable?
A: No, generally React elements are meant to be treated as immutable snapshots — a component re-renders by creating brand-new element objects rather than mutating old ones, which is central to how React’s diffing/reconciliation can trust that a previous render’s objects won’t change out from under it. In our example specifically, TypeScript and a dev-mode Object.freeze both guard against reassigning element.props after creation.
Q: Why are key and ref handled specially in createElement/JSX?
A: Generally, key and ref are reserved props React itself needs to read (for list reconciliation and imperative DOM/instance access, respectively) — if they were passed through like any other prop, a component could never define its own key/ref-named prop without ambiguity, and libraries wrapping components could accidentally leak them. React solves this by stripping them out of props before a component ever sees them. In our example, that means createElement('li', { key: 'a' }, ...) never has a key in the resulting element.props — key only shows up in React’s internal bookkeeping.
const el = createElement('li', { key: 'a', className: 'item' }, 'Ham')
// el.props is { className: 'item' } — no `key` in there
Q: What is JSX’s relationship to createElement?
A: JSX in general is purely syntactic sugar — a build step (Babel/TypeScript/etc.) compiles JSX tags into nested createElement (or the newer jsx/jsxs runtime) calls; there’s no special JSX runtime behavior beyond that transformation. In our example, hand-writing the nested createElement calls in “Deep Nesting Elements” below is exactly what a JSX compiler automates — see Using JSX for the same UI written with the sugar.
// This JSX...
<div className="container"><span>Hello</span></div>
// ...compiles to this:
createElement('div', { className: 'container' }, createElement('span', null, 'Hello'))
Create React Elements

Lesson

import { createElement } from '/react.js'
import { createRoot } from '/react-dom/client.js'
 
const element = createElement('div', { className: 'container', children: 'Hello World' })
createRoot(rootElement).render(element)

💬 createElement(type, props, ...children) doesn’t create a DOM node — it creates a plain JS object (a React element), essentially a UI descriptor: { type: 'div', props: { className: 'container', children: 'Hello World' } }. createRoot(...).render(...) is the step that actually turns that description into DOM nodes. children is just a prop — you can pass it in the props object, as extra arguments to createElement, or as an array.


💬 Two more things worth knowing about that descriptor object: it’s immutable — React elements are meant to be created fresh on every render, not mutated in place, and TypeScript (plus a dev-mode Object.freeze) will stop you from reassigning element.props after the fact. And key and ref, if you pass them, are not part of props — React strips them out before your component ever sees them, specifically so they can’t collide with a key/ref a component might otherwise want to define itself as a regular prop. key gets its own dedicated exercise later in Rendering Arrays.

Nesting Elements

Lesson

const element = createElement(
  'div',
  { className: 'container' },
  createElement('span', null, 'Hello'),
  ' ',
  createElement('span', null, 'World'),
)

💬 Arguments after the props object all become children. A plain string doesn’t need createElement — React turns it into a text node automatically. The explicit ' ' string between the two spans matters because, unlike raw HTML source, there’s no whitespace between these createElement calls for the browser to collapse.

Deep Nesting Elements

Lesson

const element = createElement(
  'div',
  { className: 'container' },
  createElement('p', null, "Here's Sam's favorite food:"),
  createElement(
    'ul',
    { className: 'sams-food' },
    createElement('li', null, 'Green eggs'),
    createElement('li', null, 'Ham'),
  ),
)

💬 createElement calls compose arbitrarily deep — this is the exact mechanism JSX compiles down to. Once nesting gets a few levels deep, hand-written createElement calls become hard to read, which is precisely the motivation for Using JSX.

React Fundamentals
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
React Fundamentals
Notes from Kent C. Dodds’ EpicReact “React Fundamentals” workshop. It builds React up from first principles — starting at the raw DOM and raw createElement calls, through JSX, custom components, TypeScript, styling, forms, error boundaries, and the key prop — so that by the end, nothing about React’s core API feels like magic.
Exercises

Hello World in JS — DOM basics before any React: creating and appending nodes by hand.
Raw React APIs — createElement and createRoot, with no JSX: what a React element actually is.
Using JSX — JSX as sugar over createElement; interpolation, spread props, nesting, fragments.
Custom Components — the real definition of a component, built up in four small steps.
TypeScript with React — typing props, narrowing, deriving types, defaults, satisfies.
Styling — className vs style, and wrapping a native element in a styled Box component.
Forms — action, method, encType, FormData, and React’s function-valued action prop.
Inputs — checkboxes, selects, radios, hidden inputs, and the value/defaultValue distinction.
Error Boundaries — catching render errors declaratively with react-error-boundary.
Rendering Arrays — why arrays of elements need a key, and what goes wrong without one.


My Additional Angles
The whole workshop is really one long “de-sugaring” exercise
Every exercise strips away one more layer of convenience to show what’s underneath it: the DOM under createElement, createElement under JSX, plain functions under components, native input behavior under React’s defaultValue. Understanding React deeply mostly means being able to mentally compile forward and backward between each of these layers — especially JSX ↔ createElement, which pays off constantly when debugging.
key and Error Boundaries are the same kind of “leak”
Both the key prop and Error Boundaries exist because React’s declarative model has a genuine gap it can’t paper over: React can’t infer array diffs without help (Rendering Arrays), and it can’t try/catch around code that hasn’t run yet at JSX-authoring time (Error Boundaries). Both are places where you have to hand React explicit information (a key, a boundary component) that it structurally cannot derive on its own.
TypeScript’s role here mirrors “props are just an object”
Because a component actually is just a function, there’s no special “React way” to type one — TypeScript with React is just ordinary TypeScript (union types, typeof/keyof, Record, satisfies) applied to a function’s parameter. The one genuinely React-specific type that shows up repeatedly is React.ComponentProps<'div'> (used in Styling) for borrowing a native element’s full prop type when wrapping it.
This workshop deliberately stops short of state
useState shows up exactly once, unexplained, as scaffolding in Rendering Arrays — every other exercise renders purely from props, with nothing remembered between renders (see the aside in Custom Components about components being re-invoked from scratch every render). That’s not an oversight; it’s the boundary of this workshop. The natural next step is EpicReact’s “React Hooks” workshop, where components stop being purely a function of their props and start holding on to values across renders.

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
TypeScript with React

Notes from the EpicReact “React Fundamentals” workshop by Kent C. Dodds. Notes and clarifications by me are marked with > 💬.


“TypeScript is not making your life terrible. It’s just showing you how terrible your life already is.” — Kent C. Dodds

Since a React component is just a function, typing one is no different from typing any other function — the challenge is really (1) getting better at TypeScript generally and (2) learning React’s specific types (like React.ReactNode).
This exercise progressively types a Calculator component through six steps.
Interview Q&A
Q: Should you type React function components with React.FC?
A: As a general modern TypeScript+React recommendation, no — React.FC implicitly adds an optional children prop even to components that never accept one, and makes generic components (function List<T>(...)) awkward to express, since React.FC isn’t itself generic-friendly. Typing the props parameter directly covers every case React.FC does, with none of the downsides. In our example, Calculator is typed as function Calculator({ left, operator, right }: CalculatorProps) rather than const Calculator: React.FC<CalculatorProps> = (...) => ....
Q: Why use a union of string literals instead of string for a prop like operator?
A: This is a general TypeScript narrowing technique, not React-specific: a plain string type accepts any string, including invalid values that compile fine but blow up at runtime because nothing handles them; a literal union narrows the type to exactly the valid set and gives editor autocomplete for free. In our example, operator: '+' | '-' | '*' | '/' rejects a typo like '**' at compile time instead of only failing when Calculator actually runs.
type CalculatorProps = { left: number; operator: '+' | '-' | '*' | '/'; right: number }
Q: What’s the difference between typeof and keyof when deriving a type from an object?
A: Generally, typeof pulls a type out of a runtime value (turning a JS object into its TS shape), and keyof then extracts a union of that type’s own key names — chaining them (keyof typeof obj) is a common way to avoid hand-duplicating a union that already exists as an object’s keys. In our example, keyof typeof operations derives Operator ('+' | '-' | '*' | '/') straight from the operations object, so adding a new operator to that object is the only change needed instead of also updating a separately hand-written union.
const operations = { '+': (l: number, r: number) => l + r, /* ... */ }
type Operator = keyof typeof operations // '+' | '-' | ...
Q: What does satisfies give you that a type annotation doesn’t?
A: As a general TypeScript rule, annotating a value with a type (const x: T = value) widens its inferred type to exactly T, discarding narrower literal information the value actually had; satisfies instead checks that the value is compatible with a wider type while leaving its own inferred type untouched (still narrow). In our example, operations satisfies Record<string, OperationFn> validates every function matches OperationFn while operations keeps its narrow, literal keys ('+' | '-' | '*' | '/') so keyof typeof operations still works — combining the safety of Reduce Duplication with the narrow-key derivation of Derive Types.
Q: What’s the difference between React.ComponentProps<'div'> and ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'div'>?
A: More generally, ComponentProps<T> gives you the full prop type of a JSX element or component (including ref), which is convenient for typing a wrapper component — but a plain function component can’t actually receive a ref without forwardRef (or React 19’s ref-as-prop support), so including it can be misleading. ComponentPropsWithoutRef<T> is the same shape minus ref, and is the safer default when a component wraps a native element without specifically handling ref forwarding. In our example (see Styling), Box is typed with React.ComponentProps<'div'> since it doesn’t forward a ref at all — ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'div'> would be the more precise choice there.
Props

Lesson

type CalculatorProps = { left: number; operator: string; right: number }
 
function Calculator({ left, operator, right }: CalculatorProps) {
  /* ... */
}

💬 Without this, someone could pass left={"2"} and the compiler wouldn’t catch it — only a runtime bug would reveal it. Naming the props type (CalculatorProps) vs. inlining it ({ left, operator, right }: { left: number; ... }) is purely a style choice; both work identically.


💬 You’ll often see React.FC<CalculatorProps> (or React.FunctionComponent) used for the component’s type instead of typing the parameter directly, especially in older code and tutorials. It’s generally discouraged today: it implicitly adds an optional children prop even to components that never accept one, and it makes generic components (function List<T>(...)) awkward to express. Typing the props parameter directly — the way every example in this note does — is the currently recommended approach and works for every case React.FC does.

Narrow Types

Lesson

type CalculatorProps = {
  left: number
  operator: '+' | '-' | '*' | '/'
  right: number
}

💬 A plain string type for operator allows any string — including '**', which would compile fine but blow up at runtime because there’s no handler for it. A union of literal strings narrows the type to exactly the valid values, which also unlocks editor autocomplete for free.

Derive Types

Lesson

const operations = {
  '+': (left: number, right: number) => left + right,
  '-': (left: number, right: number) => left - right,
  '*': (left: number, right: number) => left * right,
  '/': (left: number, right: number) => left / right,
}
 
type Operations = typeof operations
type Operator = keyof Operations // '+' | '-' | '*' | '/'

💬 Hand-listing '+' | '-' | '*' | '/' separately from the operations object duplicates the same information in two places — add a new operator to one and forget the other, and you get either a silent runtime gap or a spurious type error. typeof pulls a type out of a runtime value; keyof then extracts a union of that type’s keys. Deriving Operator from operations this way means adding an operator to the object is the only change needed.

Default Props

Lesson

type CalculatorProps = { left?: number; operator?: Operator; right?: number }
 
function Calculator({ left = 0, operator = '+', right = 0 }: CalculatorProps) {
  /* ... */
}

💬 ? on a type property makes it optional (allows undefined); the destructuring default (= 0) supplies the runtime fallback when the caller omits it. Both pieces are needed — the ? alone would leave left typed as number | undefined inside the function body.

Reduce Duplication

Lesson

type OperationFn = (left: number, right: number) => number
type Operator = '+' | '-' | '*' | '/'
 
const operations: Record<Operator, OperationFn> = {
  '+': (left, right) => left + right,
  '-': (left, right) => left - right,
  '*': (left, right) => left * right,
  '/': (left, right) => left / right,
}

💬 Every operation function has the identical shape (number, number) => number — repeating that signature on each one is its own duplication. Record<Operator, OperationFn> types the whole object as a map instead. The catch: this reintroduces the earlier problem — Operator now has to be listed by hand again, because you can’t derive a key union from a value you’re still in the middle of typing (a circular dependency). Deriving from a Record-typed object also loses per-key literal narrowing.

Satisfies

Lesson

const operations = {
  '+': (left: number, right: number) => left + right,
  '-': (left: number, right: number) => left - right,
  '*': (left: number, right: number) => left * right,
  '/': (left: number, right: number) => left / right,
} satisfies Record<string, OperationFn>
 
type Operator = keyof typeof operations

💬 Casting a value to a type (const x: T = value) widens the value’s type to exactly T, losing narrower literal information. satisfies checks that the value is compatible with a wider type, without widening the value’s own inferred type. So operations still has its narrow, literal keys ('+' | '-' | '*' | '/' inferred directly from the object), while TypeScript still verifies every value matches OperationFn — the best of both the Derive Types and Reduce Duplication approaches, without either one’s downside.


💬 One more React-specific type worth knowing, used in Styling: React.ComponentProps<'div'> includes a ref in its type, but a plain function component can’t actually receive one without extra work (forwardRef, or React 19’s ref-as-prop support). React.ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'div'> is the same prop set minus ref — the safer default to reach for when wrapping a native element in a component that doesn’t specifically handle forwarding a ref.

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: DOM Refs and Effect Dependencies
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
DOM Refs and Effect Dependencies

Notes from EpicWeb’s React Hooks
workshop by Kent C. Dodds (exercise 4, “DOM Side-Effects”) plus react.dev’s
useRef and
useEffect references.
Companion to Side Effects (the general useEffect/cleanup mechanics
this note assumes). Notes and clarifications by me are marked with > 💬.

Interview Q&A
Q: Why can’t you just grab a DOM node the normal JS way inside a
component?
A: Because <div>hi</div> compiles to React.createElement(...) — it
describes an element, it doesn’t create a DOM node. Real DOM nodes don’t
exist until React’s own reconciler creates them during commit, which
happens after your component function has already returned. The only way
to get a reference to the actual node is to ask React for it via the
special ref prop.
Q: What’s the simplest way to do that (step ref)?
A: A ref callback — a function passed directly to ref that React calls
with the DOM node once it exists (and calls again, with null in older
React, or via its own cleanup return in React 19+, when the node is
removed):
function Tilt({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <div
      className="tilt-root"
      ref={(tiltNode: HTMLVanillaTiltElement) => {
        if (!tiltNode) return
        VanillaTilt.init(tiltNode, vanillaTiltOptions)
        return () => tiltNode.vanillaTilt()
      }}
    >
      <div className="tilt-child">{children}</div>
    </div>
  )
}
vanilla-tilt is a plain DOM library — it wants a real node to attach
listeners to, has nothing to do with React elements. The callback ref is
React’s hand-off point: “here’s the node, do what you need, and here’s your
chance to clean up when it’s gone.”
Q: Why does the tilt effect reset every time the count button is clicked
(step deps), even though nothing about the tilt options changed?
A: Because ref={(tiltNode) => {...}} is a new function literal every
render. React treats a changed ref-callback identity as “this ref is
different now” — it runs the old callback’s cleanup (destroying the tilt
instance) and then calls the new callback (recreating it), even though the
function’s actual behavior is identical. Any state update anywhere in
Tilt (or its parent) re-runs Tilt, creates a fresh callback, and resets
the effect — clicking the unrelated count button is exactly that.
Q: How does moving the setup into useEffect fix that?
A: It doesn’t, by itself — the fix is really the dependency array.
useEffect(fn, deps) only re-runs fn (and its returned cleanup) when
something in deps has actually changed between renders, as judged by
Object.is. Moving to useEffect plus a stable ref={tiltRef} (a
useRef object, not a new callback each render) means the ref itself no
longer triggers a reset on every render — only the effect’s own dependency
comparison decides that now:
const tiltRef = useRef<HTMLVanillaTiltElement>(null)
useEffect(() => {
  const { current: tiltNode } = tiltRef
  if (!tiltNode) return
  VanillaTilt.init(tiltNode, vanillaTiltOptions)
  return () => tiltNode.vanillaTilt()
}, [vanillaTiltOptions])
Q: The workshop README warns this still doesn’t fully fix it — why?
A: vanillaTiltOptions is rebuilt as a new object literal every render
({ max, speed, glare, 'max-glare': maxGlare }), even when max/speed/
glare/maxGlare themselves haven’t changed. useEffect’s comparison uses
Object.is, which for objects is reference equality:
const options1 = { glare: true, max: 25, 'max-glare': 0.5, speed: 400 }
const options2 = { glare: true, max: 25, 'max-glare': 0.5, speed: 400 }
Object.is(options1, options2) // false — different objects, same contents
Every render produces a structurally identical but referentially
different vanillaTiltOptions, so the dependency array “changes” on every
render regardless of whether the actual numbers changed — the count
button’s click still resets the tilt effect.
Q: What’s the actual fix (step primitives)?
A: List the individual primitive values in the dependency array instead of
the object that wraps them:
useEffect(() => {
  const { current: tiltNode } = tiltRef
  if (!tiltNode) return
  const vanillaTiltOptions = { max, speed, glare, 'max-glare': maxGlare }
  VanillaTilt.init(tiltNode, vanillaTiltOptions)
  return () => tiltNode.vanillaTilt()
}, [glare, max, maxGlare, speed])
max, speed, glare, maxGlare are numbers/booleans — primitives
compare by value under Object.is, so 25 === 25 is true regardless of
which render produced each 25. The options object is still rebuilt fresh
every render (that part didn’t need to change), but it’s now only
constructed inside the effect callback, which only runs when a primitive
dependency actually changed.
How refs and the dependency array actually work
Why DOM nodes don’t exist during render
The workshop’s own README opens with the fact this whole exercise hinges
on: <div>hi</div> isn’t a DOM node, it’s sugar for
React.createElement('div', null, 'hi') — a plain JS object describing
what should exist, not a reference to anything real. As Kent puts it,
“your component’s render method is really just responsible for creating and
returning React Elements and has nothing to do with the DOM in particular.”
Actual DOM nodes come into being only when React’s reconciler commits —
which happens strictly after your component function has already
finished running and returned. There is no point during render where a
document.createElement-style real node is reachable from your own code;
ref exists specifically to hand you that node once it’s real, on React’s
own schedule, not yours.
Two hand-off mechanisms, not one API
React actually gives you two distinct ways to receive that node, and the
workshop is explicit that the callback form is the preferred default:
// Ref callback — React calls this directly with the node (and, since
// React 19, can call whatever function *this* callback returns, as its
// own cleanup, when the node is removed)
<div ref={(myDiv) => {
  console.log(`here's my div!`, myDiv)
  return function cleanup() {
    console.log(`my div is getting removed from the page!`, myDiv)
  }
}}>
  Hey, this is my div!
</div>
 
// Ref object — useRef gives you a stable box; React writes into its
// .current when the node mounts, and you read it back out later, usually
// inside an effect or an event handler
function MyDiv() {
  const myDivRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null)
  useEffect(() => {
    const myDiv = myDivRef.current // the actual DOM node
    console.log(myDiv)
  }, [])
  return <div ref={myDivRef}>hi</div>
}
The object form exists for the case the callback form can’t cover cleanly:
needing to reach the node again later, from a different effect or an event
handler, rather than only at the moment it’s attached/detached. Both are
really the same underlying mechanism — React handing you a live reference —
packaged two different ways for two different access patterns.

💬 Worth knowing, per Kent’s own aside in the README: “a ref is basically
state that’s associated to a React component that will not trigger a
rerender when changed.” That’s the general definition — refs aren’t only
for DOM nodes, they’re a general mutable-storage-without-re-render
primitive; this exercise happens to use that primitive specifically to
hold a DOM node.

The Tilt component’s actual bug progression
This exercise’s three steps are one continuous bug fix, and the trace only
makes sense read together:
Step ref wires up vanilla-tilt — a library that “works directly
with DOM nodes to setup event handlers,” per the step’s own README — via an
inline ref callback that both initializes the library and returns its own
cleanup:
<div
  ref={(tiltNode: HTMLVanillaTiltElement) => {
    if (!tiltNode) return
    VanillaTilt.init(tiltNode, vanillaTiltOptions)
    return () => tiltNode.vanillaTilt()
  }}
>
This works, but introduces a hidden cost: the callback is a brand-new
function object on every single render of Tilt, for any reason at all —
including a state update in a totally unrelated sibling like the count
button. React’s rule for callback refs is that a changed callback
identity means “detach the old ref, attach the new one” — so every
unrelated re-render tears down and rebuilds the tilt instance.
Step deps tries to fix this by moving the setup into useEffect with
vanillaTiltOptions in the dependency array, reasoning (correctly, as far
as it goes) that useEffect only re-runs when a dependency actually
changes. But the step’s own README flags that this doesn’t fix the bug —
clicking the count button still resets the tilt effect, because
vanillaTiltOptions (an object built fresh every render via
{ ...spread }) is never Object.is-equal to the previous render’s
version even when every field inside it is identical:
const options1 = { glare: true, max: 25, 'max-glare': 0.5, speed: 400 }
const options2 = { glare: true, max: 25, 'max-glare': 0.5, speed: 400 }
Object.is(options1, options2) // false — same content, different object
Step primitives is the actual fix: depend on the individual
primitives (glare, max, maxGlare, speed) instead of the object that
wraps them, and build the options object inside the effect body where its
freshness no longer matters:
const tiltRef = useRef<HTMLVanillaTiltElement>(null)
useEffect(() => {
  const { current: tiltNode } = tiltRef
  if (!tiltNode) return
  const vanillaTiltOptions = { max, speed, glare, 'max-glare': maxGlare }
  VanillaTilt.init(tiltNode, vanillaTiltOptions)
  return () => tiltNode.vanillaTilt()
}, [glare, max, maxGlare, speed])
Numbers and booleans compare by value under Object.is — 25 === 25 is
true no matter which render produced either 25 — so now the effect only
re-runs when one of those four values genuinely changes, not on every
render of the component.
A modern counterpoint worth knowing about
The workshop teaches “move DOM setup out of the ref callback and into
useEffect with a correct dependency array” as the fix — and for this
specific bug (an unstable callback identity), it is the fix. But it’s
worth knowing this isn’t universally considered the best pattern for DOM
synchronization work specifically. TanStack Query maintainer TkDodo’s post
“Avoiding useEffect with callback refs”
argues that for DOM-interaction code like this, a stable ref callback
(one that doesn’t change identity every render, achieved by not closing
over changing values directly and instead reading fresh values from inside
it) can be simpler and more correct than routing through useEffect at
all — because a ref callback fires exactly when the node is actually
attached/detached, which is precisely the event a useEffect with a
dependency array is only approximating by comparing dependencies on every
render. The workshop’s fix (step primitives) is a completely valid way to
solve this particular bug; TkDodo’s broader point is that the root cause
(step ref’s literal problem) was an unstable callback, and a stabilized
callback ref can sometimes be a more direct fix than reaching for
useEffect in the first place. Both approaches are legitimate — which one
reads more clearly depends on whether the DOM interaction is naturally
framed as “respond to this node appearing/disappearing” (favors a ref
callback) or “keep this in sync with these specific values” (favors
useEffect with a dependency array, as this exercise settles on).
Rules and caveats

A ref callback’s identity matters as much as a dependency array
entry’s. An inline ref={(node) => {...}} is a fresh function every
render — fine for something truly one-shot, a footgun for anything with
setup/cleanup that shouldn’t re-run on unrelated state changes. Prefer a
useRef object + useEffect once the ref needs cleanup tied to specific
dependencies rather than “every render.”
useEffect’s dependency comparison is Object.is, not a deep
equality check. Objects, arrays, and functions built fresh inside the
render body are never Object.is-equal to the previous render’s version,
even with identical contents — this is the single most common cause of
“my effect re-runs when it shouldn’t.”
Prefer primitive dependencies over object dependencies when you can.
Passing [glare, max, maxGlare, speed] instead of [vanillaTiltOptions]
sidesteps the reference-identity problem entirely, rather than requiring
the object to be memoized (useMemo) to fix the same issue a different
way.
Never disable react-hooks/exhaustive-deps to silence a dependency
warning — the workshop’s own problem-step code has this rule turned off
as scaffolding, with an explicit comment warning against doing that in
real code. An incomplete dependency array is usually a real bug (stale
closures), not just lint noise.

Sources

EpicWeb React Hooks workshop, exercise 04.dom (steps ref, deps,
primitives)
react.dev — useRef
react.dev — useEffect

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: Managing UI State
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
Managing UI State

Notes from EpicWeb’s React Hooks
workshop by Kent C. Dodds (exercise 1, “Managing UI State”) plus Shawn
Wang’s Getting Closure on Hooks
and react.dev’s useState
reference. Notes and clarifications by me are marked with > 💬.

Interview Q&A
Q: What does useState actually give you?
A: A pair — the current value, and a function to request a new one — backed
by React’s own per-component storage rather than a plain JS variable. A
plain variable is reset to its initial expression on every call of the
component function; useState is what survives across those calls and
triggers React to re-run the function when it changes:
function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0)
  const increment = () => setCount(count + 1)
  return <button onClick={increment}>{count}</button>
}
Q: Why does typing into the search box (step use-state) not make the
checkboxes reflect what’s typed, or vice versa?
A: Because nothing yet ties the <input> element’s own DOM value to React
state — onChange writes into query, but nothing reads query back into
the input’s value attribute. The DOM node still owns its own value
independently; React is only being told about changes, not driving them.
This is the step-use-state version:
<input
  id="searchInput"
  name="query"
  type="search"
  onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.currentTarget.value)}
/>
Q: What turns this into a “controlled” input (step control)?
A: Adding value={query} alongside the existing onChange. Now the
rendered DOM value is forced to match React state on every render — typing
only visibly works because onChange fires, updates query, triggers a
re-render, and that re-render’s value={query} re-asserts the new value
back onto the DOM node. Same wiring applies to the checkboxes:
checked={dogChecked} alongside their own onChange. Once controlled,
React — not the browser — is the single source of truth for what’s on
screen; this is the same “controlled” concept covered from the other
direction in [[Control Props]], applied here to a plain DOM element
instead of a custom hook.
Q: Where do dogChecked/catChecked/caterpillarChecked come from in
step control, and why does step derive change that?
A: In control, they don’t exist yet — only query (a string) and
handleCheck, which mutates query by splitting/joining it as a
space-separated word list, but nothing renders the checkboxes’ checked
state at all yet. Step derive fixes the gap not by adding three more
useState calls, but by computing the three booleans from query itself,
every render:
const words = query.split(' ')
const dogChecked = words.includes('dog')
const catChecked = words.includes('cat')
const caterpillarChecked = words.includes('caterpillar')
Q: Why derive instead of adding three more useStates?
A: Because query already contains this information — it’s the search
string, and the tags are just words within it. A second, independently-owned
useState for each checkbox would let them drift out of sync with query
(check “dog” via the checkbox, but never see it reflected if query was set
some other way, or vice versa). Deriving means there is exactly one
source of truth (query); everything else is a pure computation from it,
recomputed fresh every render — the general principle Kent calls “derived
state” and treats as the default over redundant state that has to be kept
in sync by hand.
Q: What does step init add, and why doesn’t useState('') cover it?
A: Reading the initial query from the URL (?query=cat+dog) so a shared
link pre-fills the search:
const params = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search)
const [query, setQuery] = useState(params.get('query') ?? '')
useState('') can’t do this because its argument has to be a plain value
known at the call site — this replaces that hardcoded '' with a value
computed from window.location.search instead. It works, but re-runs
new URLSearchParams(window.location.search) on every render, not just
the first — wasted work, since useState’s argument is provably only used
once (see next question).
Q: What’s the “one more thing” step cb adds, and why does it matter?
A: useState accepts either a value or a function that computes the
value — the function form is called only on the render that actually
mounts the component, never again:
// ❌ getQueryParam() is called on every render — its result is thrown away
// every time except the first
const [query, setQuery] = useState(getQueryParam())
 
// ✅ getQueryParam itself is passed — React calls it once, on mount, and
// never again
const [query, setQuery] = useState(getQueryParam)
This matters more as the initializer gets more expensive (parsing a large
URL, JSON.parse-ing a big blob from localStorage, etc.) — useState(fn())
does that work on every single re-render of the component and discards the
result on all but the first, while useState(fn) hands React the function
itself so React can choose to call it only when it’s actually needed. React
itself doesn’t reach for the JS engine’s laziness here — it’s an explicit
API surface (useState checks “is this argument a function?” and calls it
itself if so) — the caller has to opt in by passing the bare function.
How useState actually works: hooks as a persistent array
The Q&A above treats useState as a black box that “just remembers” a
value across renders. It’s worth being precise about how, because the
mechanism explains several things the API surface alone doesn’t: why hooks
can’t be called conditionally, why two useState calls in one component
don’t collide, and why the value really does survive the function being
called again from scratch.
A component function is just a function — every render, React calls it
again, and every local const/let inside it is recreated from nothing.
useState’s value has to live somewhere else for it to survive that.
Shawn Wang’s Getting Closure on Hooks
(linked from this exercise’s own README) builds a minimal hand-rolled
useState that makes this concrete: React keeps, per component instance,
an array of “hook cells” plus a cursor (currentHook) that starts at 0
on every render and increments by one every time a hook is called. Each
useState call reads/writes the cell at its own position in that array —
not a fresh variable, the same array slot, render after render:
// simplified shape of the idea (not React's literal internals)
let hooks = []
let currentHook = 0
 
function useState(initialValue) {
  const hookIndex = currentHook
  hooks[hookIndex] = hooks[hookIndex] ?? initialValue
  function setState(newValue) {
    hooks[hookIndex] = newValue
    rerender()
  }
  currentHook++
  return [hooks[hookIndex], setState]
}
The returned setState closes over hookIndex — this is the actual
“closure” the post’s title refers to. It’s not that query itself is
magically preserved; it’s that the updater function permanently remembers
which slot to write into, and the array those slots live in is kept
outside the component function entirely, so calling the component function
again doesn’t wipe it. This is also exactly why hooks can’t be called
conditionally: currentHook only makes sense as an index if every render
calls hooks in the same order — skip a useState call on one render but
not another, and every hook after it reads/writes the wrong slot.
In our App, this is why useState('') for query and (once you get to
step derive) any other useState calls in the same component each get
their own stable slot, independent of each other, and independent of
App’s own local variables like words, which are recomputed fresh every
call and never touch the hooks array at all.
Controlled inputs and the single source of truth
The workshop’s own README frames this exercise around one idea: “there’s a
cycle of user interaction, state changes, and re-rendering.” Steps
use-state and control are really about where in that cycle the DOM
sits. An uncontrolled <input onChange={...}> participates in the cycle
only on the way in — the browser owns the visible value, and React just
gets told about changes after the fact. Making it controlled
(value={query} alongside onChange) inserts the DOM node into the
output side of the cycle too: every render, React doesn’t just read from
the input, it writes to it, asserting query’s current value back onto the
node whether or not that value actually changed since last render. Once
that’s true for every stateful visual element (the search box and all
three checkboxes’ checked props), query becomes the single place
that determines everything on screen — there’s no longer a second,
DOM-native copy of any of it that could quietly drift out of sync.
Deriving state vs. storing it
Step derive’s real lesson generalizes past this one exercise: any value
that can be computed from state you already have should be computed, not
stored. dogChecked, catChecked, and caterpillarChecked are genuinely
just query.split(' ').includes(tag) — nothing about them needs to be
remembered independently across renders, because they can be recomputed,
correctly, from query alone, every single time. Kent’s broader framing
(the workshop links to his blog post on this, and it comes up again in
Lifting State’s colocate step) is that every useState call is a
commitment to keep a value in sync by hand — a second source of truth
that only stays correct as long as every code path that changes query
also remembers to update it. Deriving removes that obligation entirely by
making the “redundant” state structurally impossible to represent: there’s
no dogChecked variable sitting in the hooks array waiting to disagree
with query, so it can’t.
The two forms of useState’s initializer
React’s own useState reference
states this plainly: pass a function instead of a value, and “React will
call your initializer function when initializing the component, and store
its return value as the initial state” — called exactly once, ever, for
that component instance. One detail worth knowing that neither this
exercise’s README nor the Q&A above covers: in Strict Mode, React
deliberately calls the initializer function twice on mount (development
only) specifically to help surface accidental impurities — a reason
getQueryParam (and any lazy initializer) needs to be a pure, side-effect-free
read, not something that mutates external state each time it runs.
The full progression across this exercise’s five steps, side by side:
// step use-state — reactive, not controlled
const [query, setQuery] = useState('')
<input onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.currentTarget.value)} />
 
// step control — DOM is now driven BY state, not just informing it
const [query, setQuery] = useState('')
<input value={query} onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.currentTarget.value)} />
 
// step derive — checkboxes computed FROM query, never stored separately
const words = query.split(' ')
const dogChecked = words.includes('dog')
 
// step init — initial value computed from the URL, but recomputed every render
const params = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search)
const [query, setQuery] = useState(params.get('query') ?? '')
 
// step cb — the same computation, but handed to React as a function,
// so it only actually runs once
function getQueryParam() {
  const params = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search)
  return params.get('query') ?? ''
}
const [query, setQuery] = useState(getQueryParam)
Each step is a strict refinement of the one before it — nothing about
what query means changes across these five steps, only how faithfully
the code expresses “the DOM reflects state,” “state doesn’t duplicate
itself,” and “expensive work only happens when it needs to.”
Rules and caveats

useState’s initial-value argument is only read on the mount render.
Passing a fresh value every render (useState(someExpression)) is
harmless but wasteful if someExpression is at all expensive to compute —
reach for the lazy-initializer form (useState(() => someExpression) or
useState(fn)) once it is.
Controlled inputs need both halves. value/checked without
onChange freezes the input (React repaints the DOM value back every
render, so nothing the user types ever sticks); onChange without
value/checked leaves the DOM element’s own internal value as the
actual source of truth, with React state just shadowing it — neither half
alone is “controlled.”
Prefer deriving state over storing a second copy of it. If a value can
be computed from state you already have (as dogChecked can be computed
from query), computing it fresh every render is simpler and can’t drift
out of sync — a second useState is only justified when the value can’t
be reconstructed from existing state and props.
The lazy-initializer form isn’t free performance — it’s a targeted
fix. For a cheap initial value (useState(''), useState(0)), passing
a function adds a call indirection for no benefit; it’s specifically for
initializers expensive enough that recomputing them on every render (and
discarding the result) would actually be noticeable.

Sources

EpicWeb React Hooks workshop, exercise 01.managing-ui-state (steps
use-state, control, derive, init, cb)
Shawn Wang — Getting Closure on Hooks
react.dev — useState

React Hooks Workshop
Notes on React’s built-in hooks — useState, useEffect, useRef, useId
— and the everyday component-design habits they enable (controlled inputs,
derived state, lifting/colocating state, effect cleanup, avoiding stale
closures), from EpicWeb’s React Hooks
workshop by Kent C. Dodds, plus outside research.
The exercises build toward each other more than they’re independent
topics: useState basics → making inputs actually controlled by state →
deriving values instead of duplicating state → lazy state initialization →
synchronizing with the outside world (useEffect) and cleaning that up →
sharing state between components (lifting) and pulling it back down once
it’s no longer shared (colocating) → useRef for direct DOM access →
getting the effect dependency array right → stable unique IDs for
SSR-safe markup → and finally a capstone (tic-tac-toe) that uses nearly all
of the above together, plus the state-updater-function form for avoiding
stale-closure bugs.
Notes

Managing UI State — useState basics, what makes an input actually
“controlled,” deriving state instead of duplicating it, and the two forms
of useState’s initial-value argument (plain value vs. lazy function).
Side Effects — useEffect for synchronizing React state with
something outside React, and the cleanup function’s exact timing (before
the next effect run, and on unmount).
Lifting State — moving useState up to a common parent so siblings
can share it, extending that to arrays/lists of items, and moving state
back down (colocation) once it’s no longer actually shared.
DOM Refs and Effect Dependencies — useRef for direct DOM access
outside React’s own render cycle, and getting the useEffect dependency
array right — including why object/array/function dependencies recreated
every render defeat React’s comparison.
The useId Hook — generating a stable, unique-per-instance ID that’s
also safe across server/client hydration, for wiring <label htmlFor> to
<input id> correctly even when a component renders more than once on a
page.
Building Tic-Tac-Toe — a capstone combining state updater functions
(avoiding stale-closure bugs when the next state depends on the
previous), localStorage persistence via lazy useState init +
useEffect, and a history/time-travel feature built on an array of past
states.

Line-by-line render trace
The notes above explain concepts. Render Trace is a companion set of
notes that instead trace execution order through the actual solution code
of all 6 exercises of the workshop — when state actually gets read or
written, which components re-render and why, and exactly when an effect or
its cleanup function runs relative to render and commit.

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: 01 Managing UI State
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
Managing UI State — Render Trace (Exercise 1)

Line-by-line render/execution trace through the 5 solution steps of
exercise 1 (“Managing UI State”) of EpicWeb’s
React Hooks workshop by
Kent C. Dodds. For the concept explanation (not the trace) see
Managing UI State — this note is about invocation order: when
state actually gets read vs. written, and exactly which render an
expensive initializer runs on.

use-state — useState Basics
Problem: typing into the search box doesn’t filter the post list on
screen, because nothing renders the current query value back into
anything other than <MatchingPosts>.
function App() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('')
  return (
    <div className="app">
      <form>
        <input id="searchInput" name="query" type="search"
          onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.currentTarget.value)} />
        {/* checkboxes not yet wired to state */}
      </form>
      <MatchingPosts query={query} />
    </div>
  )
}
Render trace

App() runs for the first time (mount). useState('') registers a new
piece of state for this component instance, seeded with '', and
returns ['', setQuery].
App renders <input onChange={...}/> and <MatchingPosts query="" />.
MatchingPosts calls getMatchingPosts(''), gets every post back
(empty query matches all), and renders the full list.
User types “c”. The <input>’s own DOM onChange fires (a real browser
event, nothing React-specific yet), calling setQuery('c').
React schedules a re-render of App. App() runs again from the top:
useState('') this time returns the current state — 'c', not ''
— because React, not the function body, owns this value across calls.
App renders <MatchingPosts query="c" />. getMatchingPosts('c')
filters down the list. The <input> itself keeps showing “c” — but
that’s the browser’s own memory of what was typed, not anything React
asserted; nothing in this step’s code reads query back into the
input’s value.

Why
This step establishes the base loop (state → re-render → new UI) without
yet making the input “controlled” — the DOM element’s visible value and
React’s query state happen to agree here only because the user’s typing
and setQuery are triggered by the same event, not because React is
enforcing it. Step control (next) is what makes React actually own it.
control — Controlled Inputs
Problem: the checkboxes don’t reflect query, and there’s no
value={query} on the text input, so React never actually asserts what
should be on screen — it’s only reacting to it.
<input
  id="searchInput" name="query" type="search"
  value={query}
  onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.currentTarget.value)}
/>
<input type="checkbox"
  onChange={(e) => handleCheck('dog', e.currentTarget.checked)} />
Render trace

Mount: query = ''. <input value="" onChange={...}/> renders — React
sets the DOM node’s value property to '' as part of this commit, not
just reads it.
User types “c” in the search box. Browser fires onChange →
setQuery('c') → re-render → App() runs → <input value="c" .../> is
rendered again → React’s commit phase writes "c" onto the DOM node’s
value property (even though it already visually shows “c” from the
user’s own keystroke — this write is what makes it controlled, not
incidental).
User checks the “dog” checkbox. Its onChange fires
handleCheck('dog', true), which splits query into words, appends
'dog', and calls setQuery(newQuery).
Re-render: App() runs with the new query. But nothing in this
step’s code computes dogChecked/catChecked/caterpillarChecked —
the checkbox checked attributes aren’t wired up yet in this exact
solution step’s shown excerpt, so the checkbox’s own DOM-native checked
state is still what’s visually shown, exactly the same “not fully
controlled yet” gap the search input had in step use-state. (Step
derive, next, is what supplies those booleans.)

Why
A controlled element needs the round-trip to actually be enforced every
render, not just triggered once on the change event — that’s the difference
between “React reacts to this” and “React owns this.” Committing value/
checked on every render is what closes the loop.
derive — Derived State
Problem: the checkboxes still have no checked prop wired to state.
function App() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('')
  const words = query.split(' ')
  const dogChecked = words.includes('dog')
  const catChecked = words.includes('cat')
  const caterpillarChecked = words.includes('caterpillar')
  // ...
  return (
    <input type="checkbox" checked={dogChecked}
      onChange={(e) => handleCheck('dog', e.currentTarget.checked)} />
  )
}
Render trace

Every render of App (not just mount) recomputes words,
dogChecked, catChecked, caterpillarChecked fresh from whatever
query currently is — these are plain consts, not useState, so
there’s no “stale” version of them to worry about; they simply don’t
exist independently between renders.
User checks “cat”. handleCheck('cat', true) computes newWords from
the current words (closed over from this render), calls
setQuery(newWords.join(' ')).
Re-render: query is now "cat" (say). words, catChecked (now
true), dogChecked (still false) are all recomputed in this same
pass — no separate re-render or effect needed for the checkboxes to
catch up, because they were never separately stored to begin with.

Why
Because dogChecked etc. are recomputed every render rather than stored,
there is no possible render where query says one thing and a checkbox’s
checked prop says another — the trace has no branch where they could
diverge, which is the mechanical guarantee “derive, don’t duplicate” buys.
init — Initialize State
Problem: visiting ?query=cat+dog doesn’t pre-fill the search box —
useState('') always starts empty regardless of the URL.
function App() {
  const params = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search)
  const [query, setQuery] = useState(params.get('query') ?? '')
  // ...
}
Render trace

Mount, URL is ?query=cat+dog. App() runs: line 1 constructs
new URLSearchParams(window.location.search) — real work, parsing the
query string. Line 2 reads params.get('query') → "cat dog", passes it
to useState. React uses this only for this mount — query is now
"cat dog".
User types an extra character. setQuery(...) → re-render → App()
runs from the top again, which means line 1
(new URLSearchParams(window.location.search)) runs again too —
even though its result (params) is only used to compute useState’s
argument, and that argument is provably discarded by React on every
render after the first. This parse is wasted work on every keystroke
from here on.

Why
This step is deliberately left “working but wasteful” so step cb’s fix is
motivated by something the trace itself just demonstrated — new URLSearchParams
running on every render for a value that’s read exactly once.
cb — Init Callback
Problem: step init’s URL parsing re-runs on every render for no
benefit.
function getQueryParam() {
  const params = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search)
  return params.get('query') ?? ''
}
 
function App() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState(getQueryParam)
  // ...
}
Render trace

Mount: useState(getQueryParam) is called with the function itself,
not its result. Internally, React checks whether its argument is a
function; here it is, so React calls getQueryParam() itself, once,
uses the return value ("cat dog") as the initial state, and remembers
internally that this state is already initialized.
User types. setQuery(...) → re-render → App() runs again →
useState(getQueryParam) is called again, passing the same function
reference (a new one, actually — getQueryParam is a stable top-level
declaration, not recreated per render, but even if it were, this doesn’t
matter). Crucially: React does not call it this time — it already
has state for this hook slot from mount, so the function argument is
read and then ignored.
window.location.search is never touched again for the rest of this
component’s lifetime (barring unmount/remount).

Why
The only difference between this step and init is whether React calls
the initializer or your own code does — useState(fn()) calls it in your
code, every render, unconditionally; useState(fn) hands the call itself to
React, which only makes it once. Same eventual state value, very different
number of times the expensive part actually runs — a trace is what makes
that difference visible, since reading the two code snippets side by side
without tracing invocation count looks almost identical.
Sources

EpicWeb — React Hooks workshop, exercise 1 (all 5 steps + solutions)
react.dev — useState

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
Side Effects — Render Trace (Exercise 2)

Line-by-line render/execution trace through the 2 solution steps of
exercise 2 (“Side-Effects”) of EpicWeb’s
React Hooks workshop by
Kent C. Dodds. For the concept explanation (not the trace) see
Side Effects — this note is about invocation order: exactly when
React runs an effect relative to the commit, and exactly when it runs the
cleanup relative to the next effect run and to unmount.

effects — useEffect
Problem: clicking the browser’s back button after a search doesn’t
restore the previous search box value — nothing is listening for
popstate.
function App() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState(getQueryParam)
  // ...
  useEffect(() => {
    window.addEventListener('popstate', () => setQuery(getQueryParam()))
  }, [])
  // ...
}
Render trace

Mount. App() runs top to bottom: useState(getQueryParam) initializes
query, the derived dogChecked/etc. are computed, and the JSX is
built. The useEffect call itself just registers the effect with
React during this render — the callback passed to it is not called
yet.
React commits: the returned JSX is turned into real DOM nodes and
inserted into the page. The browser paints.
After the paint, React calls the registered effect callback for the
first time: window.addEventListener('popstate', ...) actually runs
now, not during step 1. This ordering — effect runs after commit and
paint, not during render — is why effects are safe for things that would
otherwise block or fight with rendering (subscribing to something,
reading real DOM layout, etc.).
Because the dependency array is [], React records that this effect
has no dependencies to watch, so it will not run this callback again on
any future re-render of App — only on a fresh mount.
User submits a search, then clicks the browser’s back button. The
browser fires a real popstate event. The listener registered in step 3
fires: setQuery(getQueryParam()) re-reads the URL and updates state.
React re-renders App in response. Because of the empty dependency
array, the useEffect call on this render is skipped (not re-invoked) —
the listener from step 3 is still the one attached; it never gets
replaced.

Why
Running the effect after commit/paint (not during render) is what makes
useEffect safe to use for anything that has to talk to something outside
React’s own tree without risking tearing the DOM update or delaying the
visible paint. But that same “only runs once, on mount” behavior, combined
with never removing the listener, is exactly the setup for the leak step
cleanup fixes next — this step’s trace has no step 7 where the old
listener gets removed, because nothing in this code does that yet.
cleanup — Effect Cleanup
Problem: every mount of App (e.g. toggling a “show form” checkbox on
and off) adds another popstate listener that’s never removed, leaking
memory (hugeData, closed over by the listener) a little more each cycle.
useEffect(() => {
  const hugeData = new Array(1_000_000).fill(new Array(1_000_000).fill('🐶🐱🐛'))
  function updateQuery() {
    console.log(hugeData)
    setQuery(getQueryParam())
  }
  window.addEventListener('popstate', updateQuery)
  return () => {
    window.removeEventListener('popstate', updateQuery)
  }
}, [])
Render trace

DemoApp renders with showForm = true, so <App /> mounts. App’s
effect runs after commit (same as trace step 3 above): hugeData is
allocated, updateQuery is defined (closing over hugeData and
setQuery), addEventListener('popstate', updateQuery) runs. React
also stores the returned cleanup function from this call, associated
with this exact effect instance — it does not call it yet.
User unchecks “show form”. DemoApp re-renders with showForm = false;
<App /> is no longer in the returned JSX, so React unmounts it.
Before finishing the unmount, React calls the cleanup function it
stored in step 1: window.removeEventListener('popstate', updateQuery)
runs. Because updateQuery is the exact same function reference that
was passed to addEventListener, the browser successfully finds and
removes that specific listener.
With no listener referencing updateQuery anymore, and App itself
unmounted, nothing keeps updateQuery’s closure (and therefore
hugeData) reachable — it becomes eligible for garbage collection on
the JS engine’s own schedule.
User re-checks “show form”. <App /> mounts fresh — a new effect
run, a new hugeData array, a new updateQuery closure, a
new addEventListener call. Because step 3 actually removed the
previous listener, there is exactly one live popstate listener at any
given time, not an accumulating stack of them.

Contrast — the effects-step (pre-cleanup) version: step 2 above (React
unmounting <App/>) is identical, but step 3 never happens — there is no
stored cleanup function to call, because the effect callback in step
effects doesn’t return one. updateQuery’s closure (and hugeData) stays
reachable via the still-attached popstate listener on window,
indefinitely, even though the component that created it is long gone from
the tree. Each mount/unmount cycle adds one more such listener, permanently.
Why
React ties a cleanup function’s execution to two specific moments — right
before the next run of that same effect (not relevant here, since []
means there is no next run while mounted) and right before unmount — because
those are exactly the two moments something registered “for as long as this
effect’s dependencies hold” needs to be torn down: either it’s about to be
replaced by a fresh run, or the component that wanted it no longer exists at
all. The trace makes visible why “leak” is the right word for the
effects-step bug: it’s not that the app breaks visibly, it’s that step 3
above — the one call that would sever the reference chain keeping
hugeData alive — simply never happens.
Sources

EpicWeb — React Hooks workshop, exercise 2 (both steps + solutions)
react.dev — useEffect

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: 03 Lifting State
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
Lifting State — Render Trace (Exercise 3)

Line-by-line render/execution trace through the 3 solution steps of
exercise 3 (“Lifting State”) of EpicWeb’s
React Hooks workshop by
Kent C. Dodds. For the concept explanation (not the trace) see
Lifting State — this note is about invocation order: exactly which
components re-render when the lifted (or colocated) state changes, and
why that scope shrinks once state moves back down.

lift — Lift State
Problem: after a refactor split the app into Form and MatchingPosts
components, query’s state and its popstate-listening effect ended up in
the wrong place to be shared between them.
function App() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState(getQueryParam)
  useEffect(() => {
    const updateQuery = () => setQuery(getQueryParam())
    window.addEventListener('popstate', updateQuery)
    return () => window.removeEventListener('popstate', updateQuery)
  }, [])
  return (
    <div className="app">
      <Form query={query} setQuery={setQuery} />
      <MatchingPosts query={query} />
    </div>
  )
}
Render trace

Mount. App() runs: useState(getQueryParam) initializes query once
(lazy initializer, see [[Managing UI State]]). useEffect(..., [])
is registered with an empty dependency array — React will run its setup
function once, after this first commit, and never again on its own.
React commits Form and MatchingPosts to the DOM, then runs the
effect’s setup: window.addEventListener('popstate', updateQuery).
User types in the search box (inside Form). Form’s own onChange
calls setQuery — the same setQuery function App passed down as
a prop, not a local copy.
React re-renders starting from App (the component that owns the
changed state) — App() runs again, then both Form and
MatchingPosts re-render as its children, because both receive query
as a prop and React re-renders a parent’s subtree by default. Form
re-renders with the new query value even though the user’s own
typing is what changed it — that round-trip through React state is what
keeps it a controlled input (see [[Managing UI State]]’s control
step).
User clicks the browser’s back button. The browser fires a native
popstate event — updateQuery (registered in step 2, still the same
closure) runs, calls setQuery(getQueryParam()) with whatever the URL
now says. Same re-render path as step 4: App → Form + MatchingPosts.
If App unmounts (it won’t in this app, but in general): React runs the
effect’s cleanup (removeEventListener) before the component is torn
down, preventing a listener leak.

Why
Both consumers of query (Form displays/edits it, MatchingPosts filters
by it) have to re-render whenever it changes, no matter where the state
lives — lifting doesn’t reduce how many components re-render on a query
change, it’s what makes both consumers able to see the same value at all.
The popstate effect had to move with query because it’s the thing that
calls setQuery — an effect and the state it updates can’t be split across
components without either prop-drilling a setter back down (defeating the
point) or duplicating state (breaking single-source-of-truth).
lift-array — Lift More State
Problem: a per-card “favorite” heart button works fine with local state
in Card, but sorting the whole post list by favorited-first requires
comparing every card against every other — no single Card has that view.
function MatchingPosts({ query }: { query: string }) {
  const matchingPosts = getMatchingPosts(query)
  const [favorites, setFavorites] = useState<Array<string>>([])
  return (
    <ul className="post-list">
      {matchingPosts
        .sort((a, b) => { /* favorited-first */ })
        .map((post) => (
          <Card key={post.id} post={post} isFavorited={favorites.includes(post.id)}
            onFavoriteClick={(fav) => { /* update favorites array */ }} />
        ))}
    </ul>
  )
}
Render trace

MatchingPosts mounts owning favorites: []. It maps matchingPosts
into <Card> elements, computing each one’s isFavorited by checking
array membership — every Card gets a plain boolean + callback prop,
nothing stateful of its own.
User clicks post B’s heart. Card’s onClick calls the
onFavoriteClick prop it was handed, which is a closure created fresh,
inline, on every MatchingPosts render — this specific closure calls
setFavorites([...favorites, post.id]) for post B’s post.id.
React re-renders MatchingPosts (the owner of favorites). Its render
function runs again: .sort() re-runs over the entire matchingPosts
array (now with B’s favorited status flipped, changing its sort
position), and every <Card> element is reconstructed — one prop
object per card, all of them new objects this render, even for cards
whose isFavorited/onFavoriteClick value is unchanged.
React’s reconciler diffs each Card’s new props against its previous
ones by value. A card whose isFavorited boolean and computed
onFavoriteClick behavior is unchanged still gets a new prop object
(the inline arrow function is a new reference every render), so without
memo on Card, every card’s component function re-runs even though
only one card’s actual data changed — this is the re-render cost the
workshop’s own solution notes call out as the reason to colocate once
sorting is removed.

Why
Lifting favorites to MatchingPosts is necessary for the sort feature —
there’s no way around a common-ancestor render pass touching every card when
the list order itself depends on their combined state. But it’s also
expensive in exactly the way state colocation warns about: one card’s
click re-renders the whole list’s render function, not just that card.
colocate — Colocate State
Problem: the sort-by-favorite feature is removed, but favorites is
still living in MatchingPosts — no longer earning its lifted position.
function MatchingPosts({ query }: { query: string }) {
  const matchingPosts = getMatchingPosts(query)
  return <ul className="post-list">{matchingPosts.map((post) => <Card key={post.id} post={post} />)}</ul>
}
 
function Card({ post }: { post: BlogPost }) {
  const [isFavorited, setIsFavorited] = useState(false)
  return (
    <li>
      {isFavorited
        ? <button onClick={() => setIsFavorited(false)}>❤️</button>
        : <button onClick={() => setIsFavorited(true)}>🤍</button>}
      {/* ... */}
    </li>
  )
}
Render trace

MatchingPosts mounts owning nothing but matchingPosts (derived from
query, not stateful itself). It renders N <Card post={post} />
elements — no isFavorited/onFavoriteClick props at all now.
Each Card mounts its own useState(false) — N independent pieces
of state, one per card instance, each living inside that card’s own
fiber.
User clicks post B’s heart. Card’s own onClick calls its own
setIsFavorited(true) — a state update scoped to that one Card
instance.
React re-renders starting from that Card — not from
MatchingPosts, not from App. MatchingPosts’s render function does
not run again; the other N-1 <Card> elements it previously rendered are
untouched, because nothing about MatchingPosts’s own state or props
changed.

Why
Contrast with lift-array’s trace, step 3: there, every card
re-rendered on any card’s click, because the click’s state update happened
in their shared parent. Here, the exact same user action (clicking a heart)
triggers a re-render scoped to a single component. This is the concrete,
traceable version of the workshop’s own claim — “React only needs to
re-render that card rather than the entire MatchingPosts component” — and
it’s a direct, mechanical consequence of where the useState call lives,
nothing more exotic than that.
Sources

EpicWeb — React Hooks workshop, exercise 3 (all 3 steps + solutions)
Kent C. Dodds — State Colocation will make your React app faster

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: 04 DOM
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
DOM — Render Trace (Exercise 4)

Line-by-line render/execution trace through the 3 solution steps of
exercise 4 (“DOM Side-Effects”) of EpicWeb’s
React Hooks workshop by
Kent C. Dodds. For the concept explanation (not the trace) see
DOM Refs and Effect Dependencies — this note is about invocation
order: exactly when React decides a ref or effect needs to re-run, and
what Object.is actually compares on each render.

ref — Refs
Problem: vanilla-tilt needs a real DOM node to attach its own event
handlers to, but a component’s render function only produces React elements
— no DOM node exists yet at that point.
function Tilt({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <div
      className="tilt-root"
      ref={(tiltNode: HTMLVanillaTiltElement) => {
        if (!tiltNode) return
        VanillaTilt.init(tiltNode, vanillaTiltOptions)
        return () => tiltNode.vanillaTilt()
      }}
    >
      <div className="tilt-child">{children}</div>
    </div>
  )
}
Render trace

Tilt() runs, returns a <div ref={callbackFn}> element tree. No DOM
node exists yet — callbackFn is just a function value sitting in the
returned element’s ref field.
React commits this element tree to the real DOM: it creates the actual
<div> node, inserts it into the page, then calls callbackFn(theRealDivNode)
— refs are populated strictly after the DOM mutation that creates the
node, never before.
Inside the callback, VanillaTilt.init(tiltNode, options) runs
synchronously, attaching real DOM event listeners (mouse move, etc.)
directly to the node.
User clicks “Toggle Visibility.” showTilt flips to false. React
re-renders App, and Tilt’s <div> is removed from the tree entirely.
Before removing the DOM node, React calls the cleanup function the
callback returned in step 3 — () => tiltNode.vanillaTilt()
— releasing vanilla-tilt’s listeners before the node itself is torn down.

Why
The two-phase handoff (call the callback with the node after it exists;
call its returned cleanup before the node is removed) is what makes ref
callbacks safe for imperative libraries that need to both attach and detach
themselves — there’s no window where vanilla-tilt could be initialized
against a node that isn’t in the document yet, or leaked against one that’s
already gone.
deps — Dependencies
Problem: clicking the unrelated “increment count” button resets the
tilt effect, because the inline ref callback is reconstructed every render.
const tiltRef = useRef<HTMLVanillaTiltElement>(null)
const vanillaTiltOptions = { max, speed, glare, 'max-glare': maxGlare }
useEffect(() => {
  const { current: tiltNode } = tiltRef
  if (!tiltNode) return
  VanillaTilt.init(tiltNode, vanillaTiltOptions)
  return () => tiltNode.vanillaTilt()
}, [vanillaTiltOptions])
Render trace

Mount: tiltRef (a stable object across renders — useRef guarantees
this) gets attached to the <div ref={tiltRef}>. After commit,
tiltRef.current holds the real DOM node.
React runs the effect (mount always runs every effect once).
vanillaTiltOptions — this render’s freshly-built object — is captured
in the closure. VanillaTilt.init runs.
User clicks the count button. setCount fires, App (and Tilt)
re-render. tiltRef itself is unchanged (same object across renders —
useRef never creates a new one), so the ref={tiltRef} prop causes
no ref-callback churn this time — that part of the bug from step
ref’s trace is gone.
But vanillaTiltOptions is rebuilt fresh this render — a new object,
even though max/speed/glare/maxGlare are literally the same
numbers/booleans as before. React’s effect-scheduling code compares this
render’s vanillaTiltOptions against the previous render’s via
Object.is(prev, next) — two different object references are never
Object.is-equal, so this comparison returns false.
Because the comparison says “changed,” React runs the previous effect’s
cleanup (tiltNode.vanillaTilt()) and then runs the effect
again (VanillaTilt.init(...) again) — on every render, including
the click that had nothing to do with tilt options. The visible reset
persists, for a different underlying reason than step ref’s.

Why
Moving the ref to useRef fixed one source of unwanted churn (the
ref-callback identity) but exposed a second one hiding behind it (the
options-object identity) — the dependency array only ever compares whatever
you hand it, and an object literal built inline in the render body is never
stable across renders no matter what’s inside it.
primitives — Primitive Dependencies
Problem: step deps’s fix still resets on every render, because the
options object’s reference changes even when its contents don’t.
useEffect(() => {
  const { current: tiltNode } = tiltRef
  if (!tiltNode) return
  const vanillaTiltOptions = { max, speed, glare, 'max-glare': maxGlare }
  VanillaTilt.init(tiltNode, vanillaTiltOptions)
  return () => tiltNode.vanillaTilt()
}, [glare, max, maxGlare, speed])
Render trace

Mount: max=25, speed=400, glare=true, maxGlare=0.5. Effect runs,
builds vanillaTiltOptions inside the callback this time (not
captured from the render body), initializes vanilla-tilt.
User clicks the count button. setCount fires, App/Tilt re-render.
This render’s max, speed, glare, maxGlare are the exact same
primitive values as last render — 25, 400, true, 0.5.
React compares each entry of the new dependency array
[glare, max, maxGlare, speed] against the previous render’s, entry by
entry, via Object.is. For primitives, Object.is(25, 25) is true —
primitive values compare by value, not by the storage location they
happen to live in this render. Every entry matches.
Because nothing in the dependency array changed, React skips running
the cleanup and skips re-running the effect entirely this render — the
tilt instance from mount is left alone. The vanillaTiltOptions object
inside the (unexecuted) callback is never even reconstructed this
render.
User adjusts the “Speed” input. setOptions (or equivalent state
update) changes speed to a new number. Now
Object.is(400, 500) is false for that one entry — the array counts as
“changed” overall (any single differing entry is enough), so cleanup runs,
then the effect re-runs with the new options.

Why
This is the same Object.is comparison mechanism as step deps — nothing
about how React compares dependencies changed between these two steps.
What changed is what gets compared: primitives that are equal by value
survive the comparison regardless of which render produced them, while an
object that’s equal by content but not by reference never does. The fix
is entirely about picking dependency values that behave the way Object.is
needs them to, not about changing React’s comparison itself.
Sources

EpicWeb — React Hooks workshop, exercise 4 (all 3 steps + solutions)
react.dev — useRef
react.dev — useEffect

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: 05 Unique IDs
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
Unique IDs — Render Trace (Exercise 5)

Line-by-line render/execution trace through the 1 solution step of
exercise 5 (“Unique IDs”) of EpicWeb’s
React Hooks workshop by
Kent C. Dodds. For the concept explanation (not the trace) see
The useId Hook — this note is about invocation order: what happens
when the same component is rendered more than once on one page, and why
a hardcoded id would collide where useId doesn’t.

use-id — useId
Problem: clicking a Field’s <label> doesn’t focus its <input>,
because Field renders no id/htmlFor pair at all — and the fix can’t be
a single hardcoded id, since Field is rendered four separate times on
this page (Max, Speed, Max Glare, plus whichever others exist in the
form).
function Field({ label, ...inputProps }: { label: string } & React.ComponentProps<'input'>) {
  const generatedId = useId()
  const id = inputProps.id ?? generatedId
  return (
    <div>
      <label htmlFor={id}>{label}</label>
      <input {...inputProps} id={id} />
    </div>
  )
}
 
function App() {
  return (
    <form>
      <Field label="Max" name="max" type="number" defaultValue={25} />
      <Field label="Speed" name="speed" type="number" defaultValue={400} />
      <Field label="Max Glare" name="maxGlare" type="number" defaultValue={0.5} />
    </form>
  )
}
Render trace

App() renders three <Field> elements as siblings in the tree —
Field (Max), Field (Speed), Field (Max Glare) — three separate
fiber instances, each with its own component state.
React renders the first Field instance. Inside it, useId() is
called. React’s internal id generator produces a string encoding this
fiber’s position in the tree (something like :r0: — an opaque,
tree-position-derived value, not a counter your code manages). Because no
id prop was passed for “Max”, inputProps.id ?? generatedId resolves
to the generated value. Both the <label htmlFor> and <input id> in
this instance’s output use that same string.
React renders the second Field instance (“Speed”). useId() is
called again — this is a separate call, on a separate fiber, so it
returns a different string (say :r1:), reflecting this instance’s
own distinct position in the tree. This Field’s <label>/<input>
pair uses :r1:, never colliding with the first instance’s :r0:.
Same for the third Field instance (“Max Glare”) — a third distinct id
(:r2:).
Commit: the DOM now has three <label htmlFor>/<input id> pairs, each
internally consistent and each unique across the whole document. Clicking
any label now correctly focuses its own input, because the browser’s
native label-click-focuses-input behavior only needs htmlFor/id to
match within that pair — which they do, regardless of what the other
two pairs’ ids happen to be.
Contrast — what a hardcoded id="field-input" would do instead: all
three Field instances would render <input id="field-input">. The
browser only honors the first element with a given id for
document.getElementById/label-association purposes — clicking the
“Speed” or “Max Glare” labels would incorrectly focus the “Max” input (or
behave unpredictably depending on the browser), and the HTML itself would
be invalid (duplicate id values are non-conforming).
A later re-render (e.g. typing in one field triggers App’s own
setOptions state update) re-renders all three Field instances again.
useId() is called again on each — and returns the same value as
