before for each instance, because it’s derived from the fiber’s stable
identity/position, not recomputed from anything that changes between
renders.

Why
The trace makes the actual mechanism concrete: useId isn’t “a random
string generator called once” — it’s a value derived from where this
component instance sits in the tree, which is exactly why multiple
instances of the same component automatically get different, stable values
without any coordination between them, and why (per react.dev) the same
tree position produces the same id on both the server’s render and the
client’s hydration render, since the tree shape itself is what’s shared
between the two environments — not a counter that could drift out of sync.
Sources

EpicWeb — React Hooks workshop, exercise 5 (step + solution)
react.dev — useId

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.filePath: 40 Resources/Engineering/JavaScript/React/React Hooks Workshop/Render Trace/06 Tic Tac Toe.md
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: 06 Tic Tac Toe
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
Tic Tac Toe — Render Trace (Exercise 6)

Line-by-line render/execution trace through the 3 solution steps of
exercise 6 (“Tic Tac Toe”) of EpicWeb’s
React Hooks workshop by
Kent C. Dodds. For the concept explanation (not the trace) see
Building Tic-Tac-Toe — this note is about invocation order:
exactly when a closure captures a stale squares vs. when the updater
function sees the real current value, and when localStorage gets read
vs. written.

set-state-callback — setState Callback
Problem: clicking a square needs to write into the current board, not
whatever squares happened to be when the click handler function was
created.
function Board() {
  const [squares, setSquares] = useState<Squares>(defaultState)
  const nextValue = calculateNextValue(squares)
 
  function selectSquare(index: number) {
    if (winner || squares[index]) return
    setSquares((previousSquares) => previousSquares.with(index, nextValue))
  }
  // ...
}
Render trace

Board() renders. squares is the current array (say, all null).
selectSquare is created fresh this render — it’s a new function
object closing over this render’s squares and nextValue (‘X’).
User clicks square 0. The click handler captured in step 1 runs:
setSquares((previousSquares) => previousSquares.with(0, 'X')). React
queues this updater function — not a computed value — for the
squares state slot.
React re-renders Board. Right before running the component function
again, React applies the queued update: it calls the updater function
with whatever squares actually is right now (still all null at
this point, since this is the first update) → returns a new array with
index 0 set to 'X'. This becomes the new squares.
Board() runs again with the new squares. nextValue recomputes to
'O'. A new selectSquare closes over this render’s squares
(one X placed) and nextValue ('O').

Contrast — what a non-callback version would risk: if selectSquare
instead did setSquares(squares.with(index, nextValue)), step 3 would use
the squares value captured back in step 1’s closure, not whatever
squares is at the moment the update actually applies. For a single click
with nothing else queued, this happens to produce the same result — the
divergence only shows up once multiple queued updates for the same state
exist before a render flushes (e.g. a handler that calls setSquares twice
in a row, or two updates scheduled from different sources before React gets
a chance to re-render): each non-callback call would compute its “new”
value from the same stale snapshot, so only the last call’s effect
would actually stick — the callback form instead threads each update
through the one before it, so all of them apply.
Why
The updater-function form isn’t “more correct” for every single call in
this exercise — a single, isolated click behaves identically either way.
It’s correct unconditionally, including in the cases where multiple
updates could be queued before React re-renders, which is why the workshop
teaches it as the default rule for “new state computed from old state,”
rather than something to add only after hitting the bug.
local-storage — Preserve State in localStorage
Problem: the game state resets if the tab is closed and reopened.
const [squares, setSquares] = useState<Squares>(() => {
  let localStorageValue
  try {
    localStorageValue = JSON.parse(window.localStorage.getItem(localStorageKey) ?? 'null')
  } catch { /* ignore */ }
  return localStorageValue && Array.isArray(localStorageValue) ? localStorageValue : defaultState
})
 
useEffect(() => {
  window.localStorage.setItem(localStorageKey, JSON.stringify(squares))
}, [squares])
Render trace

Mount. useState(fn) — the lazy-initializer form — means React calls
this function once: it reads localStorage, JSON.parses it, and
either returns the parsed array or falls back to defaultState. This is
the only time window.localStorage.getItem runs for initialization,
exactly per [[Managing UI State]]’s cb step’s mechanism.
Still during mount, after Board’s render commits, React runs the
useEffect. squares is whatever came out of step 1 — the effect
JSON.stringifys it and writes it straight back to localStorage
(a no-op in content, but it does run).
User clicks a square. selectSquare → setSquares(prev => ...) (per the
set-state-callback trace above) → re-render → Board() runs with the
new squares.
After this render commits, React compares this render’s effect
dependency array ([squares]) against the previous render’s — the
array reference changed (a new array was returned by .with(...), never
mutated in place), so the effect re-runs: writes the updated
squares to localStorage.
Every subsequent squares change repeats steps 3–4: state update →
re-render → dependency check → effect re-run → localStorage write.
localStorage is never read again after step 1 for the lifetime of this
mounted component.

Why
Reading is a one-time lazy-init concern (mount only); writing is an
ongoing sync concern (every change) — that’s why they use two different
mechanisms (useState’s lazy initializer vs. useEffect with a dependency
array) rather than one. Using the non-lazy form here
(useState(JSON.parse(...))) would re-parse localStorage on every render
for no reason, exactly the wasted-work trap [[Managing UI State]]#init
already demonstrated with URLSearchParams.
history — Add Game History Feature
Problem: there’s no way to go back to an earlier move; squares only
ever holds the current board.
function selectSquare(index: number) {
  if (winner || currentSquares[index]) return
  setState((previousState) => {
    const { currentStep, history } = previousState
    const newHistory = history.slice(0, currentStep + 1)
    const squares = history[currentStep].with(index, nextValue)
    return { history: [...newHistory, squares], currentStep: newHistory.length }
  })
}
Render trace

Mount: state = { history: [Array(9).fill(null)], currentStep: 0 }.
currentSquares = state.history[0] — the empty board.
User plays move 1 (square 0). selectSquare fires the updater: reads
currentStep (0) and history (length 1) from whatever previousState
actually is at apply-time (the updater-function form again, same
reasoning as set-state-callback). newHistory = history.slice(0, 1) —
unchanged, since currentStep + 1 === history.length already. Appends
the new board: history becomes length 2, currentStep becomes 1.
User clicks “Go to game start” in the moves list. That button’s own
handler: setState(prev => ({ ...prev, currentStep: 0 })) — note this
does not touch history at all, it only moves which entry
currentStep points at.
Re-render: currentSquares = state.history[0] again — the empty board
is shown, but state.history still has both boards in it; nothing was
discarded.
User now plays a different move from this earlier point. selectSquare
runs again: currentStep is 0, history.length is 2.
newHistory = history.slice(0, 1) — this time it does truncate,
dropping the old move-1 entry, since currentStep + 1 (1) is less than
history.length (2). The new move is appended at index 1, and
currentStep becomes 1 again — but now pointing at a different
board than the one that used to be there.

Why
Step 5 is the moment this data structure actually earns its shape: without
the history.slice(0, currentStep + 1) truncation, the old “future” move
from before the time-jump would still be sitting in the array, making the
“go to move” list show moves that no longer make sense once a different
move was chosen from an earlier point. Tracing through “jump back, then
play differently” is what makes that truncation’s necessity concrete rather
than an abstract rule.
Sources

EpicWeb — React Hooks workshop, exercise 6 (all 3 steps + solutions)
react.dev — Updating state based on the previous state

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: Render Trace
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
React Hooks Workshop — Line-by-Line Render Trace
Index for a companion set of notes to React Hooks Workshop. Where the
notes linked from that MOC explain concepts, these notes trace execution
order through the actual solution code of each exercise of EpicWeb’s
React Hooks workshop by
Kent C. Dodds — when state actually gets read or written, which components
re-render and why, and exactly when an effect or its cleanup function runs
relative to render and commit.
One note per exercise, each covering every step’s solution code in order,
with real code pulled from the workshop repo (~/epic-workshops/react-hooks)
and a step-numbered render trace. Read them in order — later exercises reuse
mechanisms established earlier (the tic-tac-toe capstone’s localStorage
persistence reuses Managing UI State’s lazy-initializer trick).
Notes, in order

01 Managing UI State — useState basics, what makes an input
actually controlled, deriving state, and the two forms of useState’s
initial value. Steps use-state, control, derive, init, cb.
02 Side Effects — when useEffect runs relative to render/commit,
and exactly when its cleanup function runs relative to the next effect
and to unmount. Steps effects, cleanup.
03 Lifting State — which components re-render when lifted state
changes, extended to arrays of items, and the re-render-scope payoff of
moving state back down (colocation). Steps lift, lift-array,
colocate.
04 DOM — direct DOM access via useRef, and exactly how React’s
dependency-array comparison does or doesn’t consider two renders’ values
“the same.” Steps ref, deps, primitives.
05 Unique IDs — how useId gives each component instance its own
stable, hydration-safe ID even when the same component renders more than
once on a page. Step use-id.
06 Tic Tac Toe — a stale-closure bug scenario contrasting the
updater-function form of setState with the plain form, localStorage
persistence, and history/time-travel. Steps set-state-callback,
local-storage, history.

See also

React Hooks Workshop — the concept-note MOC these notes complement.
Managing UI State, Side Effects, Lifting State,
DOM Refs and Effect Dependencies, The useId Hook,
Building Tic-Tac-Toe — the individual concept deep-dives referenced
throughout these trace notes.

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: Side Effects
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
Side Effects

Notes from EpicWeb’s React Hooks
workshop by Kent C. Dodds (exercise 2, “Side-Effects”) plus react.dev’s
useEffect reference and
Synchronizing with Effects.
Builds on Managing UI State — same search app, now synchronizing with
something outside React (the browser’s own back/forward history).
Notes and clarifications by me are marked with > 💬.

Interview Q&A
Q: What’s a “side effect,” and why does it need its own hook instead of
just running code in the component body?
A: A side effect is anything that reaches outside React’s own
render-and-diff model to touch the wider world — a browser API, a
third-party library, a subscription, a timer. Code in the component body
runs on every render, synchronously, as part of computing what to display;
useEffect is specifically for work that should run after React has
committed the DOM update, and — critically — only when you’ve actually asked
it to run again (via the dependency array), not on every single render:
useEffect(() => {
  doSomeThing()               // the effect itself
  return function cleanup() {
    doSomeCleanup()           // optional — see cleanup section below
  }
}, [dep1, dep2])              // when to re-run: only if these change
Q: What problem does step effects actually fix?
A: The search app can already update the URL (via setGlobalSearchParams)
when the user submits, but clicking the browser’s back button doesn’t
update the search box — nothing is listening for that. The fix is a
popstate event listener (the only way to observe back/forward navigation)
that re-reads the URL and calls setQuery:
useEffect(() => {
  window.addEventListener('popstate', () => setQuery(getQueryParam()))
}, [])
Q: Why does this have to be inside useEffect instead of just being
called directly in App’s body?
A: addEventListener is exactly the kind of side effect useEffect exists
for — it reaches outside React (the global window object) and, unlike
reading a prop or computing derived state, it has an ongoing lifetime that
outlives a single render. Calling it directly in the component body would
re-subscribe a new listener on every single render (since the whole
function body reruns every time), stacking up duplicate listeners forever.
The empty dependency array ([]) tells React “only run this effect once,
after the first render” — exactly matching “subscribe once, for the whole
time this component exists.”
Q: The workshop calls out that step effects still has a bug — what is
it, and why doesn’t the fix show up until step cleanup?
A: The listener registered in effects is never removed. Every time the
App component using this effect unmounts (e.g. toggling a “show form”
checkbox that conditionally renders it) and remounts, a new popstate
listener gets added on top of the old one — the old one is never told to go
away, because nothing calls removeEventListener. The bug is invisible from
just looking at the search box working correctly; it only shows up as a
slow memory/listener leak over repeated mount/unmount cycles, which is
exactly why the workshop adds a DemoApp wrapper with a toggle checkbox
specifically to make it observable.
Q: How does the cleanup function actually fix it?
A: By returning a function from the effect — React treats whatever a
useEffect callback returns as its dedicated cleanup, and calls it
automatically right before the next time this same effect would run
again, and once more when the component unmounts for good:
useEffect(() => {
  const hugeData = new Array(1_000_000).fill(new Array(1_000_000).fill('🐶🐱🐛'))
  function updateQuery() {
    console.log(hugeData) // keeps hugeData reachable as long as the listener exists
    setQuery(getQueryParam())
  }
  window.addEventListener('popstate', updateQuery)
  return () => {
    window.removeEventListener('popstate', updateQuery)
  }
}, [])
Q: Why does the handler have to be extracted into a named updateQuery
function instead of staying inline?
A: removeEventListener only removes a listener if you pass it the exact
same function reference that was used to add it — two separate inline
arrow functions (() => setQuery(...)), even with identical bodies, are two
different objects as far as removeEventListener is concerned and won’t
match each other. Naming the function once and referencing it in both the
addEventListener and the removeEventListener call is what makes removal
actually work.
Q: What does the hugeData array and its console.log actually
demonstrate?
A: It’s a deliberately memory-heavy value captured in updateQuery’s
closure purely to make the leak measurable — as long as updateQuery is
still referenced by a live event listener, hugeData can’t be
garbage-collected, since JS closures keep every variable they reference
alive for as long as the closure itself is reachable. Once the cleanup
actually calls removeEventListener, nothing references updateQuery
anymore, so hugeData becomes eligible for garbage collection too. It’s a
stand-in for any real closed-over state a subscription might be keeping
alive — a network connection, a large fetched dataset, DOM references.
What useEffect is actually for
useState manages state inside React’s own model; useEffect is the
escape hatch for everything React doesn’t otherwise touch — “things that
happen outside our React components,” in the workshop’s own words: browser
APIs (local storage, geolocation, media devices, window events),
third-party library integrations (D3, Chart.js), timers, subscriptions,
network requests. The dividing line isn’t “does this run after render” —
plenty of derived-state computation also conceptually happens “after” a
state change — it’s “does this reach past React’s virtual-DOM diffing to
touch something that has its own lifetime, independent of any single
render.” An event listener, once added, keeps existing whether or not the
component re-renders again; that persistence is exactly what needs its own
hook rather than a plain line in the component body.
The hook-flow lifecycle: where effects actually sit
The workshop’s own README leans on Donavon West’s “hook flow” diagram
to place useEffect precisely in React’s mount/update/unmount timeline,
and it’s worth internalizing this order rather than treating useEffect as
a vague “runs sometime after render” hook:
Mount:

Lazy initializers run (any function passed to useState/useReducer —
see [[Managing UI State]]’s cb step for why this matters).
Render — the component function body runs, producing what to show.
React updates the DOM to match.
Any useLayoutEffects run, synchronously, blocking paint — this
matters for effects that need to measure/mutate the DOM before the user
sees anything (not what this exercise uses, but worth knowing why it
exists as a sibling hook).
The browser paints the screen.
useEffect callbacks run — scheduled after paint specifically so
they never block the user from seeing the updated UI. This is the core
design reason useEffect exists as a separate hook from
useLayoutEffect: most side effects (a fetch, a subscription, logging)
have no reason to delay what the user sees.

Update (a parent re-rendering, a state change, or a context change):
same sequence as mount, except step 4/6 become “cleanup the previous
layout effect / effect, then run the new one” — not skipped, not merged,
a genuine cleanup-then-run pair, and only for effects whose dependency
array actually changed.
Unmount: React runs the cleanup for every currently-active useEffect
and useLayoutEffect one final time — this is the only place effects
(the buggy first step) is missing anything, and exactly what cleanup
(the fixed step) adds.

💬 In development, React (in Strict Mode) deliberately runs an extra
mount → effect → cleanup → effect cycle immediately after the real mount,
purely to surface exactly this class of bug earlier — an effect that
isn’t idempotent, or a cleanup that doesn’t fully undo its effect, breaks
visibly in dev under this double-invoke instead of silently leaking in
production. This doesn’t happen in a production build.

The bug, traced through both steps
Step effects (the workshop’s own solution) wires up the popstate
listener but never removes it:
useEffect(() => {
  window.addEventListener('popstate', () => setQuery(getQueryParam()))
}, [])
The workshop’s README is explicit about why this leaks, in terms of
closures rather than just “you forgot a line”: the inline arrow function
passed to addEventListener closes over everything in scope at the time
it’s created — including, in the real exercise, a large fake dataset
(hugeData) deliberately added to make the leak measurable in the
browser’s memory profiler. As long as window’s popstate listener list
still holds a reference to that function, everything it closes over stays
reachable and un-garbage-collectible — even after the component that
created it has fully unmounted and has nothing else pointing to it. A
DemoApp wrapper with a “show form” checkbox exists in the exercise purely
to mount/unmount the component repeatedly and make the leak visible, since
a single mount alone wouldn’t show anything wrong.
Step cleanup fixes it by giving the same function a name and
returning a matching teardown:
useEffect(() => {
  const hugeData = new Array(1_000_000).fill(new Array(1_000_000).fill('🐶🐱🐛'))
  function updateQuery() {
    console.log(hugeData)
    setQuery(getQueryParam())
  }
  window.addEventListener('popstate', updateQuery)
  return () => {
    window.removeEventListener('popstate', updateQuery)
  }
}, [])
Walking the mount → unmount → remount cycle against the hook-flow order
above: mount runs the effect, registering updateQuery and its closure
over hugeData. Unmount (unchecking “show form”) runs the returned cleanup
— removeEventListener('popstate', updateQuery) — which drops the
window-held reference to updateQuery, at which point hugeData becomes
eligible for garbage collection since nothing else in the app holds it.
Remount (re-checking the box) runs the effect fresh, creating a new
hugeData and a new updateQuery closure, registered exactly once.
Repeat this indefinitely and memory usage stays flat, instead of climbing
with every toggle the way effects’ version does.
Sources for this section

react.dev — useEffect
Max Rozen — Demystifying useEffect’s clean-up function
Donavon West — hook-flow diagram (linked from the workshop’s own README)

Rules and caveats

Any subscription/listener registered in an effect needs a matching
cleanup, or every unmount leaves a dangling reference — this is true of
addEventListener, third-party library subscriptions (D3, Chart.js
instances), timers (setInterval/setTimeout), and network connections
(AbortController) alike, not just popstate.
removeEventListener needs the exact same function reference passed to
addEventListener. An inline arrow function can’t be removed later —
extract a named function if you’ll need to remove the listener.
The empty dependency array ([]) means “run once, on mount, cleanup
once, on unmount” — this workshop step doesn’t yet cover a non-empty
dependency array, where cleanup instead runs before every re-run of the
effect (any time a dependency changes), not just at the very end. That’s
the general rule per react.dev: cleanup for run N fires right before
run N+1 starts, and one final time on unmount.
A side effect belongs in useEffect, not the render body, specifically
because render can happen many times for reasons that have nothing to do
with “should I resubscribe” (a parent re-rendering, unrelated state
changing) — useEffect’s dependency array is what decouples “did this
specific dependency change” from “did anything cause a re-render.”

Sources

EpicWeb React Hooks workshop, exercise 02.side-effects (steps effects,
cleanup)
react.dev — useEffect
react.dev — Synchronizing with Effects
Bharathi Kannan — React Hooks Flow (linked from the workshop’s own README)

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: Building Tic-Tac-Toe
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
Building Tic-Tac-Toe

Notes from EpicWeb’s React Hooks
workshop by Kent C. Dodds (exercise 6, “Tic Tac Toe”) plus his blog post
useState lazy initialization and function updates
and react.dev’s Updating state based on the previous state.
A capstone exercise — mostly review of useState/useEffect from earlier
exercises (see Managing UI State for the lazy-initializer mechanism
this one reuses directly), plus the one useState form not covered yet:
the updater-function form. Notes and clarifications by me are marked with
> 💬.

Interview Q&A
Q: What’s “managed” vs. “derived” state in this exercise, concretely?
A: squares — the 9-cell board array — is the one piece of managed state;
everything else is computed fresh from it every render:
const [squares, setSquares] = useState<Squares>(defaultState)
const nextValue = calculateNextValue(squares) // derived: 'X' or 'O', whoever's turn
const winner = calculateWinner(squares)        // derived: 'X', 'O', or null
const status = calculateStatus(winner, squares, nextValue) // derived: a message
Same principle as [[Managing UI State]]’s derive step — nextValue,
winner, and status could each be stored in their own useState, but
they don’t need to be, since all three are pure functions of squares
alone; storing them separately would just create three more ways for the UI
to get out of sync with the board.
Q: Why does selectSquare use setSquares((previousSquares) => ...)
instead of setSquares(squares.with(index, nextValue))?
A: Because the new board depends on the current board, and squares
inside selectSquare is a value captured in a closure from whichever render
created this particular selectSquare function — it’s guaranteed correct
only if no other state update for squares has happened between that
render and when the click handler actually runs. The updater-function form
sidesteps that entirely: React calls it with whatever the actual current
state is at the moment the update is applied, not whatever squares
happened to close over:
function selectSquare(index: number) {
  if (winner || squares[index]) return
  setSquares((previousSquares) => previousSquares.with(index, nextValue))
}
Q: When does the closure-captured value actually go stale — isn’t one
click always based on the board state at the time of that click?
A: Not always — anywhere multiple state updates for the same piece of state
can be queued up before a re-render actually happens (rapid double-clicks,
multiple setSquares calls inside one event handler or one effect, an
update inside a setTimeout/promise callback scheduled from an earlier
render), the non-callback form risks each update overwriting the others’
work because they all captured the same pre-update squares. The
callback form composes correctly no matter how many updates get queued,
because each one is handed the result of the one before it, not a
snapshot from render time. Kent’s rule of thumb (from the workshop’s topic
README): if the new value is calculated from the previous value, use
the function form; otherwise either form is fine.
Q: Why squares.with(index, nextValue) instead of squares[index] = nextValue?
A: React decides whether to re-render by comparing whether setSquares was
called with a new value, and for objects/arrays that comparison is by
reference, not by deep equality — mutating the existing array in place
(squares[index] = ...) leaves the same array reference, so setSquares(squares)
would look like “no change” to React even though the data changed.
Array.prototype.with
returns a new array with one element replaced, leaving the original
untouched — the general “don’t mutate state” rule any React app needs,
here satisfied by a built-in immutable-update method instead of manual
spreading.
Q: How does step local-storage combine what this workshop already
taught in [[Managing UI State]]?
A: Exactly the lazy-initializer form from that exercise’s cb step, applied
to reading from localStorage instead of URLSearchParams — and a new
useEffect to write back out on every change:
const [squares, setSquares] = useState<Squares>(() => {
  let localStorageValue
  try {
    localStorageValue = JSON.parse(
      window.localStorage.getItem(localStorageKey) ?? 'null',
    )
  } catch {
    // something is wrong in localStorage, so don't use it
  }
  return localStorageValue && Array.isArray(localStorageValue)
    ? localStorageValue
    : defaultState
})
 
useEffect(() => {
  window.localStorage.setItem(localStorageKey, JSON.stringify(squares))
}, [squares])
Same reasoning as [[Managing UI State]]#cb: JSON.parse-ing whatever’s in
localStorage is work that should happen once, on mount, not on every
re-render — passing a function to useState is what limits it to exactly
that. The try/catch guards against corrupted or hand-edited storage
content that isn’t valid JSON.
Q: What does step history change structurally, and why?
A: squares (one array) becomes state.history (an array of squares
arrays) plus state.currentStep (which entry in that history is currently
shown) — because “go back and change a move” needs every past board state
kept around, not just the latest one:
const defaultState: GameState = {
  history: [Array(9).fill(null)],
  currentStep: 0,
}
const currentSquares = state.history[state.currentStep]
 
function selectSquare(index: number) {
  if (winner || currentSquares[index]) return
  setState((previousState) => {
    const { currentStep, history } = previousState
    const newHistory = history.slice(0, currentStep + 1) // drop any "future" moves
    const squares = history[currentStep].with(index, nextValue)
    return { history: [...newHistory, squares], currentStep: newHistory.length }
  })
}
history.slice(0, currentStep + 1) is the key line: if the player jumped
back to an earlier move and then makes a new move from there, every move
that happened after that point in the old timeline is discarded — the same
behavior a real time-travel UI needs (you can’t both “go back to move 3”
and “keep the moves that happened after move 3” once you make a different
move 4).
Why the callback form exists: the classic double-increment bug
The workshop’s own topic README states the rule plainly: “If your new
value for state is calculated based on the previous value of state, use the
function form. Otherwise, either works fine.” The Q&A above shows the fix;
it’s worth seeing the bug the rule is protecting against in its simplest
possible form, stripped of the tic-tac-toe board entirely, because it’s the
same failure mode any setState(currentValue + something) call is exposed
to:
function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0)
 
  function handleClick() {
    setCount(count + 1)
    setCount(count + 1) // two calls, same event handler
  }
 
  return <button onClick={handleClick}>{count}</button>
}
Clicking this button increments count by one, not two — surprising if
you haven’t internalized why. React batches both setCount calls from this
one event handler into a single re-render rather than re-rendering twice,
but batching isn’t actually the root cause; it just makes the bug visible in
one click instead of requiring two separate renders to observe. The real
cause is that count inside handleClick is a value captured once, when
this render’s Counter() call created this particular handleClick
function — both setCount(count + 1) calls read that same captured 0 and
both compute 1, so the second call doesn’t build on the first, it just
overwrites it with the identical result. Swapping to the function form fixes
it because each callback is handed whatever the actual current value is
at the moment React applies it, not a value frozen at render time:
function handleClick() {
  setCount((previousCount) => previousCount + 1)
  setCount((previousCount) => previousCount + 1) // now chains onto the first
}
Now the second call receives 1 (the first call’s result) as
previousCount, and count correctly ends up 2. This is exactly the
shape of bug selectSquare’s setSquares((previousSquares) => ...) avoids
in the real exercise — the board version just makes the “queued updates
before a re-render” scenario a double-click or a rapid-fire event instead of
two calls in one handler, but the underlying mechanics (a closure captures
one render’s value; the function form doesn’t) are identical. React’s own
docs describe this as “queueing a series of state updates” — each updater
function in the queue receives the pending state from the update before
it, not the state at render time, which is precisely what makes them
composable no matter how many get queued.
Full code walkthrough: one board, then persistence, then time-travel
Step set-state-callback — the whole game as one component, all state
in a single flat array:
const defaultState = Array(9).fill(null)
 
function Board() {
  const [squares, setSquares] = useState<Squares>(defaultState)
  const nextValue = calculateNextValue(squares)
  const winner = calculateWinner(squares)
  const status = calculateStatus(winner, squares, nextValue)
 
  function selectSquare(index: number) {
    if (winner || squares[index]) return
    setSquares((previousSquares) => previousSquares.with(index, nextValue))
  }
 
  function restart() {
    setSquares(defaultState) // no previous-state dependency — plain form is fine
  }
 
  function renderSquare(i: number) {
    return (
      <button className="square" onClick={() => selectSquare(i)}>
        {squares[i]}
      </button>
    )
  }
  // ...renders a 3x3 grid of renderSquare(0..8) plus a restart button
}
Every piece of the UI — nextValue, winner, status, and what each
square shows — is a pure function of the one managed array, squares.
restart() uses the plain form deliberately: it isn’t computing anything
from the current state, it’s replacing it outright with a constant, so
there’s no stale-closure risk to guard against — matching the workshop’s own
rule of thumb exactly.
Step local-storage layers persistence onto the same squares state
without changing how the board itself works — it only changes how squares
gets its initial value and adds one new effect:
const [squares, setSquares] = useState<Squares>(() => {
  let localStorageValue
  try {
    localStorageValue = JSON.parse(window.localStorage.getItem(localStorageKey) ?? 'null')
  } catch {
    // something is wrong in localStorage, so don't use it
  }
  return localStorageValue && Array.isArray(localStorageValue) ? localStorageValue : defaultState
})
 
useEffect(() => {
  window.localStorage.setItem(localStorageKey, JSON.stringify(squares))
}, [squares])
Reading and writing use two genuinely different mechanisms for a reason:
reading only ever needs to happen once, at mount — exactly what
useState’s lazy-initializer form guarantees, reusing the identical trick
[[Managing UI State]]#cb establishes for URLSearchParams. Writing needs
to happen on every change, which is what an effect with [squares] in its
dependency array does — it re-runs each time squares becomes a new array
reference (which, per the “don’t mutate state” rule below, it always does
on a real move).
Step history is the biggest structural jump: squares (one array)
becomes state.history (an array of squares arrays) plus
state.currentStep, and the component that owns state moves from Board
up to App, with Board turned into a plain presentational component that
just renders whatever squares/onClick it’s given:
const defaultState: GameState = { history: [Array(9).fill(null)], currentStep: 0 }
 
function App() {
  const [state, setState] = useState<GameState>(() => { /* same localStorage lazy-init, now for the whole GameState object */ })
  const currentSquares = state.history[state.currentStep]
  // nextValue/winner/status are now derived from currentSquares, not squares directly
 
  useEffect(() => {
    window.localStorage.setItem(localStorageKey, JSON.stringify(state))
  }, [state])
 
  function selectSquare(index: number) {
    if (winner || currentSquares[index]) return
    setState((previousState) => {
      const { currentStep, history } = previousState
      const newHistory = history.slice(0, currentStep + 1)
      const squares = history[currentStep].with(index, nextValue)
      return { history: [...newHistory, squares], currentStep: newHistory.length }
    })
  }
 
  const moves = state.history.map((_stepSquares, step) => (
    <li key={step}>
      <button
        onClick={() => setState((previousState) => ({ ...previousState, currentStep: step }))}
        disabled={step === state.currentStep}
      >
        {step ? `Go to move number ${step}` : 'Go to game start'}
      </button>
    </li>
  ))
  // renders <Board onClick={selectSquare} squares={currentSquares} /> plus the moves list
}
Two things worth tracing explicitly here. First, currentSquares is
always derived from state.history[state.currentStep], never stored on
its own — exactly the derived-state discipline from [[Managing UI State]],
now applied to a nested structure instead of a flat one. Second, the “go to
move” buttons’ own setState call doesn’t touch history at all — it
only moves currentStep, which is why time-traveling backward doesn’t lose
any of the later moves by itself; those only get discarded once the player
actually plays a new move from that earlier point, via the
history.slice(0, currentStep + 1) truncation inside selectSquare — the
branch-on-write behavior any real “undo, then diverge” history needs.
Rules and caveats

Reach for the updater-function form whenever the new state depends on
the old state, especially inside a handler that might fire multiple
times before a re-render happens (rapid clicks, multiple calls in one
handler). For state that doesn’t depend on its own previous value
(setSquares(defaultState) in restart()), either form works —
restart doesn’t need the callback form because it’s not computing
anything from current state.
Never mutate state in place. Whether it’s a single array
(squares.with(...)) or nested history ([...newHistory, squares]),
every update in this exercise produces a new array/object rather than
editing the existing one, so React’s reference-based change detection
actually sees the update.
Lazy useState initializers and localStorage reads compose directly
— this exercise doesn’t introduce a new mechanism for that, it’s the exact
same useState(fn) pattern from [[Managing UI State]], just with a
different (and this time genuinely worth avoiding-on-every-render)
initializer.
A history array needs an explicit truncation step on branch. Forgetting
history.slice(0, currentStep + 1) and just appending
([...history, squares]) would silently keep “future” moves around after
the player changes the past, corrupting the “go to move N” list.

Sources

EpicWeb React Hooks workshop, exercise 06.tic-tac-toe (steps
set-state-callback, local-storage, history)
Kent C. Dodds — useState lazy initialization and function updates
react.dev — Updating state based on the previous state
MDN — Array.prototype.with

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: The useId Hook
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
The useId Hook

Notes from EpicWeb’s React Hooks
workshop by Kent C. Dodds (exercise 5, “Unique IDs”) plus react.dev’s
useId reference. Notes and
clarifications by me are marked with > 💬.

Interview Q&A
Q: What problem does useId solve?
A: Wiring a <label htmlFor> to its <input id> correctly inside a
reusable component that might render more than once on the same page.
Clicking a label only focuses its input if the two share a matching, page-
unique id/htmlFor pair — but a reusable Field component can’t hardcode
that id, because rendering <Field name="max" /> and <Field name="speed" />
twice on one page would either collide (same hardcoded id) or require every
caller to pass a unique id manually:
// ❌ before: no id at all, so htmlFor has nothing to point at
function Field({ label, ...inputProps }: { label: string } & React.ComponentProps<'input'>) {
  return (
    <div>
      <label>{label}</label>
      <input {...inputProps} />
    </div>
  )
}
Q: Why not just use name as the id?
A: Because name isn’t guaranteed unique either — the workshop’s own
Field is rendered multiple times with different names in this
particular form, but nothing stops two Fields from sharing a name
(radio groups routinely do), and HTML requires id to be unique across the
entire document, not just within one component instance.
Q: Why not Math.random() or a module-level incrementing counter?
A: Both produce a value that isn’t guaranteed to match between the server’s
render and the client’s hydration render. React’s hydration expects the
first client render to produce identical output to what the server already
sent down as HTML; a random or run-order-dependent ID diverges between the
two environments (the server’s counter and the client’s counter don’t
necessarily start or advance in lockstep, and Math.random() obviously
never matches by definition), which surfaces as a hydration mismatch error.
useId is specifically built to avoid this — react.dev is explicit that
it’s designed for SSR and produces the same string on server and client.
Q: How is the actual fix wired up?
A: useId() generates a stable string once per component instance; the
component prefers a caller-supplied id if one was given, falling back to
the generated one only when the caller didn’t provide one — so useId
never overrides an explicit choice:
function Field({ label, ...inputProps }: { label: string } & React.ComponentProps<'input'>) {
  const generatedId = useId()
  const id = inputProps.id ?? generatedId
  return (
    <div>
      <label htmlFor={id}>{label}</label>
      <input {...inputProps} id={id} />
    </div>
  )
}
Q: Why does useId take no arguments and return no setter, unlike
useState?
A: Because the value it produces isn’t meant to change — it’s an identity
for this component instance, established once and stable for the instance’s
whole lifetime, not state that responds to events. A setter would imply the
ID is meant to be reassigned, which would defeat its one job (staying
constant so htmlFor/id never drift apart while the component is
mounted).
Q: Is useId appropriate for list keys?
A: No — the workshop’s own README calls this out directly. useId
generates an identity tied to where a component sits in the render tree,
not to a specific piece of data. React’s key prop needs to track a data
item’s identity across reorders/insertions/deletions so React can match up
the right DOM node to the right data — that has to come from the data
itself (a database id, a stable field), not from useId, which would just
describe the component’s position, not the item it happens to be rendering
this time.
Why a counter can’t do this, and what useId does instead
The workshop’s own README lays out the constraint plainly: to build an
accessible form, every input needs a globally unique id, its label needs a
matching htmlFor, you can’t hardcode that id in a reusable component
(multiple instances would collide), and you don’t want to force every
caller to pass one in by hand either. useId exists to fill exactly that
gap — but why it’s a hook, rather than a plain utility function you could
write yourself, only becomes clear once you look at what a naive
implementation actually breaks.
The obvious first attempt is a module-level counter:
let count = 0
function useMyId() {
  const [id] = useState(() => `id-${count++}`)
  return id
}
This works fine for a purely client-rendered app: every mount increments
the counter, every instance gets a distinct string, done. It falls apart
the moment server rendering enters the picture, and the failure mode is
worth tracing through concretely, because it’s the exact bug useId
exists to make impossible.
React’s server renderer produces a string of HTML by rendering the
component tree once, top to bottom, on the server. That HTML is sent to the
browser and painted immediately — before any JavaScript has run. Then
React “hydrates”: it walks the same component tree again, this time on
the client, attaching event handlers to the DOM nodes that are already
there, and it expects each element’s attributes (including id) to match
what the server already emitted, node for node. If the client’s first
render produces a different id for the same element than the server
did, React can’t just accept the DOM as-is — that mismatch is exactly what
raises a hydration error.
A module-level counter has no way to guarantee this, for a structural
reason, not an implementation bug: the server and the client are two
independent JS runtimes, each starting their own count at 0 — and per
React’s own docs, when a page uses streaming SSR, the order components
hydrate on the client isn’t guaranteed to match the order they were
rendered on the server. So even if both environments happened to run the
exact same components, an ordering difference alone is enough to hand two
different Field instances swapped IDs between server and client — a bug
that wouldn’t show up in a client-only app at all, since there’s only ever
one runtime’s counter to worry about.
useId sidesteps the whole problem by not counting at all. Per react.dev’s
reference: the ID React generates is derived from the calling component’s
position in the tree — its “parent path” through the component
hierarchy — rather than from when it happened to render relative to
anything else. Server and client walk the same tree structure (that’s the
whole premise of hydration), so a given component occupies the same
position in both, and therefore gets the same generated ID in both, with no
dependency on render order, timing, or how many other components happened
to call useId first. That’s the actual mechanism behind “stable across
server and client” — not that React is somehow synchronizing two counters,
but that it never needed a counter’s ordering guarantee in the first place.
Applied to this exercise: Field’s two lines —
const generatedId = useId()
const id = inputProps.id ?? generatedId
— mean every <Field label="Max" name="max" .../>, <Field label="Speed" .../>,
and <Field label="Max Glare" .../> rendered in App’s form gets its own
generatedId, derived from that specific <Field> element’s own position
in the tree, not from a shared counter any of them could race or collide
on. Render the exact same tree again — another pass client-side after SSR,
or just a normal re-render — and each Field instance recomputes to the
same string it had before, because its position in the tree hasn’t
changed. Swap two Fields’ order in the JSX, though, and their generated
IDs would legitimately change too, since their tree position changed — which
is fine, because nothing outside the component ever depends on the literal
string, only on id and htmlFor matching each other within the same
instance.
One more piece the README flags but the exercise doesn’t exercise:
identifierPrefix. If a single page mounts more than one independent React
tree (e.g. two separate createRoot/hydrateRoot calls, common in
gradually-adopted or micro-frontend setups), each tree’s useId calls could
otherwise generate colliding strings, since each root has no visibility into
the others’ component positions. identifierPrefix, passed to
createRoot/hydrateRoot, prefixes every ID that root’s useId calls
generate — and if the app is server-rendered too, the same prefix has to
be passed to the matching server API (e.g. renderToPipeableStream) so the
client and server strings still agree. It’s a narrow case — most apps have
exactly one root — but it’s the same underlying idea as the rest of this
note: useId’s guarantees hold only as long as server and client are
walking comparably-structured trees with comparable inputs.
Rules and caveats

Never use useId for list keys or any non-DOM-element identity.
It’s specifically for linking DOM elements together for accessibility
(htmlFor/id, aria-describedby, etc.), not as a general-purpose
unique-value generator.
Respect a caller-supplied id over the generated one. A reusable
field-style component should still allow a caller who genuinely needs a
specific id (e.g. to target it from CSS or an external script) to
override the generated value, as the workshop’s inputProps.id ?? generatedId
does.
The generated string is stable for the component instance’s lifetime
— it doesn’t change across re-renders, and doesn’t need to be memoized or
stored separately; calling useId() again on the same instance on a later
render returns the same value.
This is an SSR-safety mechanism first, a convenience second. In a
client-only app you technically could get away with a random or
counter-based ID scheme, but useId is the one approach that also works
correctly the moment server rendering enters the picture — reaching for it
by default avoids having to revisit the decision later.

Sources

EpicWeb React Hooks workshop, exercise 05.unique-ids (step use-id)
react.dev — useId
react.dev — hydrateRoot (the identifierPrefix option)

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: useState vs useReducer
React Lifecycle
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
React Lifecycle

Summary of the YouTube video “The React Lifecycle: Simply Explained!” by Darius Cosden.


Interview Q&A
Q: What are the three stages of a React component’s lifecycle?
A: Mount (the initial render, happens exactly once when the component first appears), Update (a re-render triggered by a state change, new props, or a context change — can repeat any number of times), and Unmount (the component is removed from the tree and React frees the memory it was holding). Every class-component “lifecycle method” you may have seen (componentDidMount, componentDidUpdate, componentWillUnmount) and every hook-based equivalent (useEffect with different dependency arrays) maps onto one of these three stages. In our example, the note’s “Full Client-Side Flow” diagram walks through exactly these three stages end to end, from function call through paint.
useEffect(() => {
  // runs after MOUNT and after every UPDATE where deps changed
  return () => {
    // cleanup: runs before the next UPDATE's effect, and once on UNMOUNT
  }
}, [dep])
Q: Does React re-run the whole component function on every render, or just the changed parts?
A: The entire function body re-executes top to bottom on every single render, mount or update alike — this is true of all function components in React, not just this example; React never partially executes a component or skips lines based on what changed. What is selective is purely on the output side: React diffs the newly-returned JSX (via the Virtual DOM) against the previous snapshot and only writes the minimal set of changes to the real DOM, which is why re-running the whole function is cheap in practice even though it sounds wasteful. In our example, the “Initialize vs. Update” table makes this explicit: const/let values are “evaluated fresh” on every render regardless of stage, while only useState (preserved) and useMemo (conditionally recomputed) get special treatment from React’s internal state store.
Q: Why does useEffect run after the browser paints, and when would you use useLayoutEffect instead?
A: useEffect is deliberately scheduled to run after the browser has painted the committed DOM changes, which is what makes it a “side effect” rather than part of rendering — this keeps expensive or non-visual work (fetching data, logging, subscribing to something) from blocking the user from seeing the UI update. useLayoutEffect runs synchronously before the browser paints instead, which matters when the effect needs to read or mutate the DOM in a way the user must never see flicker (e.g. measuring an element’s size and repositioning something based on it) — the tradeoff is that it can delay the paint since the browser waits for it to finish. In our example, the sequence diagram under “The useEffect timing distinction” shows the exact ordering: function runs → JSX evaluated → Virtual DOM → DOM → browser paint → useEffect fires.
useLayoutEffect(() => {
  const { height } = ref.current.getBoundingClientRect() // read before paint, no flicker
}, [])
Q: When does a useEffect cleanup function run, and what values does it see?
A: Generally, a cleanup function returned from useEffect runs in exactly two situations: right before the next time that effect re-runs (so React can tear down whatever the previous run set up before setting up the new one), and one final time when the component unmounts. Because the cleanup function was created during a specific render, it’s a closure over that render’s values — so it always operates on the state/props from when the effect was originally scheduled, not whatever the values are by the time it actually runs; this is the same closure behavior that causes stale-closure bugs elsewhere in React (see React Re-rendering). In our example, the “Between Renders: Cleanup Timing” section diagrams this as Render N effect fires → Render N+1 triggered → Render N cleanup runs (with Render N's values) → Render N+1 runs → Render N+1 effect fires.
useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(tick, 1000)
  return () => clearInterval(id) // uses this render's `id`, not a later one
}, [])
Q: How is a Server Component’s lifecycle different from a Client Component’s?
A: A Server Component executes exactly once, on the server, has no access to hooks or state, and its output is plain HTML rather than something that participates in a Virtual DOM diff — so there is no mount/update/unmount cycle in the traditional sense at all. Instead of re-rendering in response to state changes, “updates” happen through revalidation: some server action or framework API tells React to re-run the server component function and produce new HTML, which the framework then patches into the page — the component itself has no concept of re-rendering. In our example, the “Server Components — A Different Model” comparison table lays out these differences point by point (hooks, lifecycle, output, Virtual DOM, data fetching), and the “How updates work on the server” section walks through the concrete revalidation flow (revalidatePath('/') in Next.js, then a fresh HTML response).
Core Concept: Components Are JavaScript Functions
Every React component is just a plain JavaScript function. React takes that function and does several things to it behind the scenes:

Adds lifecycle tracking
Enforces hook rules
Runs the function at the right time in each lifecycle stage

This wrapping is why hooks work. useState, useEffect, useMemo, and custom hooks all depend on React executing the function — they aren’t available in plain JS functions because React is the one managing the context around them.
Components can return JSX or null. Returning null is a valid render that tells React to remove that component’s output from the screen.

Only components that are currently active on screen enter the lifecycle. Components on other pages or hidden by conditions are not tracked — they don’t exist in the lifecycle at all.


The Three Lifecycle Stages
Mount → Update (repeats) → Unmount

At every stage, React re-executes the entire function body from top to bottom. The output feeds into the Virtual DOM → real DOM → browser paint pipeline.

Stage 1 — Initial Render (Mount)
Happens once, when the component appears on screen for the first time.
Step-by-step

Run all code in the function body — every line executes top to bottom
Initialize all values

useState(defaultValue) — default value is set and stored in React’s memory
useMemo(fn, deps) — computed immediately and cached
const, let, inline functions — evaluated and held in memory for use in JSX or other functions


Evaluate and return JSX — the returned markup is handed to React
Virtual DOM — React builds an in-memory representation of the component tree; this is React’s working copy used for diffing
DOM update — React compares the Virtual DOM against the real DOM and applies only the necessary changes
Browser paints — the user sees the component on screen
Effects are scheduled — useEffect callbacks are queued to run after the browser has painted

The useEffect timing distinction
useEffect is called a side effect because it runs after the render is committed to the screen, not during it. The sequence is:
function runs → JSX evaluated → Virtual DOM → DOM → browser paint → useEffect fires

If you need code to run before the browser paints (e.g. measuring DOM layout), use useLayoutEffect instead — it blocks the paint until it completes. This can cause visible delays, so it should only be used when strictly necessary.

Stage 2 — Update (Re-render)
Triggered whenever something affecting the component changes: state update, new props from a parent, context change, or an external store update.
Step-by-step

Run cleanup functions — any useEffect that returned a cleanup function runs now, with the values from the previous render (not the new ones). This cleans up subscriptions, timers, or listeners set up in the last effect.
Run all code in the function body again — the entire function re-executes from top to bottom
Update all values

useState — holds its current (updated) value; does not re-initialize from the default
useMemo — recomputes only if its dependencies have changed; otherwise returns the cached value
const, let, inline functions — re-evaluated fresh on every render


Evaluate and return new JSX
Virtual DOM diff — React compares the new Virtual DOM snapshot against the previous one and calculates the minimal set of DOM changes needed
DOM update — only the changed parts are written to the real DOM
Browser repaints — the user sees the updated UI
Effects are scheduled — useEffect callbacks whose dependency arrays include changed values are queued to run after paint

Initialize vs. Update























StageuseStateuseMemoconst/letMountSet to default valueComputed and cachedEvaluated freshUpdateHolds current valueRecomputed only if deps changedEvaluated fresh
The function always re-runs completely — React does not skip lines. The difference is that React’s internal state store preserves useState values across renders; only useMemo and derived values are recomputed conditionally.

Between Renders: Cleanup Timing
The cleanup function returned from useEffect runs in two situations:

Before the next update — right before the component re-renders, React runs the cleanup from the previous render’s effect (using that render’s closed-over values), then runs the new effect after the new paint
On unmount — runs one final time when the component leaves the screen

This means cleanup always runs with stale values (the values from when the effect was set up), which is why closures matter in React. The flow looks like:
Render N effect fires
  → Render N+1 triggered
  → Render N cleanup runs (with Render N's values)
  → Render N+1 runs
  → Render N+1 effect fires


Stage 3 — Exit (Unmount)
Happens when the component is no longer needed — the user navigates away, a condition removes it from the tree, or a parent stops rendering it.
Step-by-step

Run cleanup functions — all useEffect cleanup functions fire one last time
Release all values from memory — useState, useMemo, const/let, and everything else held in the component’s memory is freed
Virtual DOM update — React removes the component from its in-memory tree
DOM update — the corresponding DOM nodes are removed
Browser repaints — the user sees the component disappear


Full Client-Side Flow (Visual Summary)
Your function component
        ↓
   React wraps it
        ↓
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  LIFECYCLE                      │
│                                                 │
│  MOUNT          UPDATE           UNMOUNT        │
│  ─────          ──────           ───────        │
│  Run code  →    Cleanup prev  →  Cleanup        │
│  Init vals      Run code         Release mem    │
│  JSX →          Update vals                     │
│  VirtualDOM     JSX →                           │
│  DOM            VirtualDOM                      │
│  Paint          DOM                             │
│  useEffect      Paint                           │
│                 useEffect                       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        ↓
   Browser (what the user sees)


Server Components — A Different Model
Server components are still JavaScript functions, but they never reach the client and have no lifecycle in the traditional sense.













































AspectClient ComponentServer ComponentHooksSupportedNot supportedLifecycleMount → Update → UnmountRuns once on server, doneOutput to clientJavaScript bundle + JSXPure HTMLVirtual DOMYesNo — HTML goes directly to DOMAsync/awaitNot at top level (use useEffect)Supported nativelyData fetchingVia useEffect after paintDirectly in the function bodyRe-rendersTriggered by state/propsNo concept — revalidation instead
Why server components are faster (and more limited)

No JavaScript is shipped to the client for these components — only HTML
No round-trips: fetch data, render, send HTML in one pass
Trade-off: no interactivity, no hooks, no state

How “updates” work on the server
Since there is no state or re-render concept, updating server-rendered content requires revalidation:

A server action (a function running on the server) runs — triggered by user interaction on a client component, a timer, a webhook, etc.
That function calls something like revalidatePath('/') (Next.js) or an equivalent framework API
React re-executes the server component function, generates new HTML
The new HTML is delivered to the browser via an HTTP response
The framework patches the DOM with the new HTML — the user sees the update

The framework handles all of this automatically once you call the revalidation function. You don’t manage a lifecycle; you just trigger a re-run.

Key Takeaways

The entire function runs on every render — React doesn’t partially execute components; the whole function body re-executes each time
Only active components are in the lifecycle — components not currently on screen don’t exist in React’s memory
useEffect is always post-paint — if you need pre-paint behavior, use useLayoutEffect, but expect potential jank
Cleanup runs with stale values — the cleanup function closes over the values from the render that created the effect, not the new render
useMemo is not free — it recomputes when dependencies change; the cache is per-render, not global
Server components have no lifecycle — they run once, produce HTML, and are done; updates come through framework revalidation
Mix both — use server components for data-heavy, non-interactive UI (better performance); use client components for anything stateful or interactive

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: Concurrent Rendering
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
Concurrent Rendering

Notes from EpicWeb’s React Performance
workshop by Kent C. Dodds (exercise 3, “Concurrent Rendering”), plus the
React v18 release post
and the react.dev useDeferredValue
reference. This is the overview note for the exercise. The single
workshop step is covered in useDeferredValue + memo. It builds on
Memoize Components (memo is a hard requirement here) and is a
sibling of useTransition and Avoiding Loading Flicker from the React
Suspense module. My own notes and clarifications are marked with > 💬.

Interview Q&A
Q: What is concurrent rendering?
A: It’s React’s ability to make rendering interruptible. Before React
18, an update rendered in one synchronous, uninterrupted pass. Now React
can start rendering, pause to let the browser handle input or paint, then
resume, or throw the work away if a newer update arrives. The DOM is only
changed once a whole tree is finished, so the user never sees a
half-rendered UI. In our example, this is what lets the search checkbox
respond instantly while a slow list of cards re-renders in the background.
Q: What’s the difference between urgent and non-urgent updates?
A: Urgent updates reflect direct interaction (typing, clicking, pressing)
and must feel instant. Non-urgent updates move the UI from one view to
another (filtered results, a new tab’s content) and can lag a little.
React can’t tell them apart on its own, so you mark the non-urgent part
with useTransition/startTransition or useDeferredValue. In our
example, the search input is urgent and the matching cards are
non-urgent.
Q: useDeferredValue vs useTransition: when do you use which?
A: Both create low-priority, interruptible renders.

useTransition wraps the state update (startTransition(() => setQuery(q))), so you need access to the setter.
useDeferredValue wraps a value you receive, which is useful when
the state lives elsewhere (a context, a URL, a library hook).

In our example the query comes from a URL-params context, so deferring
the value is the natural fit:
const deferredQuery = useDeferredValue(query)
Q: Does concurrent rendering make slow components faster?
A: No. The same work still happens, but it no longer blocks the main
thread. The initial render is still slow, because there’s no previous UI to
show while React works. The workshop is explicit: “it’s better to just
‘make it faster’ if you can.”
The problem: 16 milliseconds per frame
The workshop frames the constraint concretely: “The human eye perceives
things at around 60 frames per second. That means a single frame is around
16 milliseconds. So if your JavaScript is taking longer than 16ms to
render, the browser won’t be able to keep up and your users will have a
janky experience.”
With a synchronous renderer, a single keystroke that triggers 200ms of
component rendering freezes the page for 200ms. Nothing else runs on the
main thread in that time: no paint, no next keystroke, no hover. The input
the user is typing into can’t even show the character they just typed.
Sometimes “you really just do have enough work to do that you can’t keep
within that budget.”
The fix: let React split the work and yield
The workshop’s summary of the idea: “instead of rendering everything all at
once, React can break up the work into smaller chunks. When the rendering
is taking longer than a threshold React manages, it will pause its work and
let the browser do whatever work it needs to do. Then when React gets a
turn, it’ll continue the work it was doing … before finally updating the
DOM with the updates of all that work.”
The React 18 release post calls concurrent React “a behind-the-scenes
mechanism that enables React to prepare multiple versions of your UI at the
same time”, and lists its key properties:

Interruptible: “React may start rendering an update, pause in the
middle, then continue later. It may even abandon an in-progress render
altogether.”
Consistent: React waits “to perform DOM mutations until the end, once
the entire tree has been evaluated”, so an interrupted render never leaks
a partial UI.

Only some renders are allowed to be interrupted. That’s why React needs
priorities, and why it needs you to supply them: “a user drag-and-drop
interaction should be prioritized over rendering a list of items. React
can’t know what’s a priority and what’s not, so it needs you to tell it.”
Why it works: one input, two renders with different priorities
useDeferredValue(value) splits one state change into two renders:
keystroke → setQuery('cat')
│
├─ RENDER 1 (urgent, synchronous, can't be interrupted)
│    query = 'cat'          deferredQuery = ''   ← still the OLD value
│    input shows 'cat' right away; the slow list gets the same props it had → skipped (needs memo)
│    commit → browser paints
│
└─ RENDER 2 (background, low priority, interruptible)
     query = 'cat'          deferredQuery = 'cat'
     slow list re-renders with the new value, in chunks, yielding to the browser
     ├─ new keystroke arrives? → abandon RENDER 2, start over from RENDER 1
     └─ finished → commit the whole new list at once

react.dev on the background render: “If a user provides new input while a
background render is in progress, React abandons the current attempt and
restarts with the latest value. This ensures the UI always prioritizes the
most recent user input.”
The catch is RENDER 1. The component that calls useDeferredValue
re-renders with the old value, so its children re-render too, unless they
are memoized and their props are unchanged. The workshop’s warning: “You
must memo-ize the slow component … if you don’t use memo on the
component, React is forced to rerender the entire component with the old
value anyway which defeats the purpose.” The equality rules behind that
skip are the ones from Element Optimization. See
useDeferredValue + memo for this app’s object identities.
Deferring vs debouncing and throttling
A common alternative is to debounce the input (render only after the user
stops typing for N ms) or throttle it (render at most every N ms).
react.dev lists why useDeferredValue is usually better for rendering
work:






























Debounce / throttleuseDeferredValueDelayfixed N ms, chosen by younone. React starts the background render right after the urgent one paintsAdapts to deviceno. The same delay on a fast laptop and a slow phoneyes. It “lag[s] proportionally” on slow devicesWhile it rendersa long render still blocks the main threadinterruptible. It yields to input and is abandoned when staleBest forlimiting network requestslimiting rendering cost

💬 These combine well. Debounce the fetch you send to a server, and
defer the rendering of the results. useDeferredValue reduces rendering
work. It doesn’t reduce how many requests you make.

Where concurrent rendering fits in this workshop
The FINISHED note points out how much this took: “React managed to provide
this feature to developers by re-writing the internals of React while
avoiding huge breaking changes.” For you, it takes two lines: memo the
slow component, and pass it a deferred value. It’s the tool for when the
earlier exercises (render less often, Element Optimization; memoize,
Memoize Components) aren’t enough, because the render left over is
simply expensive. The Suspense workshop used the same hook for a different
job, showing stale results while new ones load. See
useTransition and Avoiding Loading Flicker.
Rules and caveats

Memoize the component that receives the deferred value. Without
memo, the urgent render repeats all the slow work with the old value,
and nothing gets faster.
The first render isn’t deferred. On mount, deferredValue equals
value, so there’s nothing old to show. React 19 accepts an
initialValue second argument if you want a cheap first render.
Pass primitives or stable objects. If you defer a newly created
object each render, React sees a “new” value every time and schedules a
background render every time.
It isn’t a replacement for making the component faster. Concurrent
rendering hides latency. It doesn’t remove work.
Measure. The workshop’s test asserts the checkbox responds in under
50ms while the list is still busy.

Sources

EpicWeb React Performance workshop, exercise 03.concurrent-rendering (README, FINISHED, step deferred)
React v18 release post: What is Concurrent React?
react.dev: useDeferredValue (how it works under the hood, vs debouncing, the memo pitfall)
Dan Abramov: JSConf Iceland 2018 talk (linked from the workshop README)

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: useDeferredValue + memo
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
useDeferredValue + memo

Notes from EpicWeb’s React Performance
workshop by Kent C. Dodds (exercise 3, “Concurrent Rendering”, step
deferred), plus the react.dev useDeferredValue
reference. Part of Concurrent Rendering, which covers the background
concepts (the 16ms frame budget, interruptible rendering). The memo
mechanics come from Memoize Components. My own notes and
clarifications are marked with > 💬.

Interview Q&A
Q: What does useDeferredValue do?
A: It gives you a lagging copy of a value. When the value changes,
React first renders with the old copy (fast, so the UI stays
responsive), then re-renders in the background with the new copy. That
background render can be interrupted if the value changes again. In our
example, the input uses query and the slow card list uses
deferredQuery.
Q: Why must the slow component be wrapped in memo?
A: In the first, fast render, the component that holds the deferred value
still runs, with the old value. Without memo, all its children re-render
too, doing the slow work for nothing, and the fast render isn’t fast
anymore. With memo, the children see the same props as last time and
skip. In our example, Card is wrapped in memo.
Q: Why isn’t memo enough on its own?
A: memo only skips renders when nothing changed. When the search really
changes, the list really changes, and without deferring that slow render
happens right away, blocking the input. The workshop: “typing a bunch in
the search and then clearing the search is still a really slow
experience. We need concurrent rendering!”
Q: How is it different from debouncing?
A: A debounce always waits a fixed time (say 300ms), even on a fast
machine. useDeferredValue doesn’t wait at all. It starts the background
render immediately and simply lets urgent updates (typing) interrupt it.
On a fast device the list updates almost instantly.
Q: Does it make the first render faster?
A: No. On the first render there’s no “old” value to show, so the slow
list renders at full cost. It only helps updates. The workshop: “it’s
better to just ‘make it faster’ if you can.”
The idea in one picture
A search box on top of a slow list. Each keystroke has to update both.
Without useDeferredValue, one render does everything, and the letter
you typed appears only after every card is done:
keystroke → [ input + ALL slow cards ] → screen updates
             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ 300ms, input feels frozen

With useDeferredValue, the update is split in two:
keystroke → [ input ] → screen updates (letter appears immediately)
                 └──→ [ slow cards, in the background ] → list updates
                         ↑ if you type again, React drops this and restarts

The simplest example
This is the example from the workshop’s README, adapted from the React
docs. It has the whole pattern in 15 lines:
function App() {
	const [text, setText] = useState('')
	const deferredText = useDeferredValue(text)
	return (
		<>
			<input value={text} onChange={(e) => setText(e.currentTarget.value)} />
			<SlowList text={deferredText} />
		</>
	)
}
 
const SlowList = memo(function SlowList({ text }) {
	// something really slow happens here...
	return <div>{text}</div>
})

The input gets text, the fresh value, so it always shows what you
typed.
The list gets deferredText, the lagging value, so it catches up
later.
memo on SlowList lets React skip it when deferredText hasn’t
changed yet.

What happens when you type “a”

































MomenttextdeferredTextWhat React doesOn screenbefore""""–empty input, full listrender 1 (urgent)"a""" ← still oldApp runs. SlowList gets text="" again, the same as last time, so memo skips itinput shows “a” immediatelyrender 2 (background)"a""a"App runs again. SlowList gets text="a", which is new, so it renders (slow)list updates a moment later
If you type “b” while render 2 is running, React throws render 2 away,
does a new fast render 1 for “ab”, then starts a new render 2 with “ab”.
You never wait for a list that’s already out of date.
What happens without memo




















MomentWhat React doesResultrender 1 (urgent)App runs, and SlowList isn’t memoized, so it re-renders with the old ""slow, input freezes anywayrender 2 (background)SlowList renders again with "a"slow again
So the slow work happens twice instead of once. The workshop’s
warning: “You must memo-ize the slow component … if you don’t use memo
on the component, React is forced to rerender the entire component with
the old value anyway which defeats the purpose of useDeferredValue.”
The workshop’s version
The workshop app is the same pattern with more files. A Form (search
input and checkboxes) and a MatchingPosts list both read the search
query from a shared context. Each Card is artificially slow: it renders
one SlowThing per character of the post title, and each one busy-waits:
function SlowThing() {
	// This artificially slows down rendering
	const now = performance.now()
	while (performance.now() - now < 0.01) {
		// Do nothing for a bit...
	}
 
	return null
}
The problem: the list filters by the live query, and Card isn’t
memoized. “Every time we type in the search the characters are not
responsive.”
The fix is two changes in posts.tsx:
export function MatchingPosts() {
	const [searchParams] = useSearchParams()
	const query = getQueryParam(searchParams)
	const deferredQuery = useDeferredValue(query)        // ← change 1
	const matchingPosts = getMatchingPosts(deferredQuery)
 
	return (
		<ul className="post-list">
			{matchingPosts.map((post) => (
				<Card key={post.id} post={post} />
			))}
		</ul>
	)
}
 
const Card = memo(function Card({ post }: { post: BlogPost }) {   // ← change 2
	const [isFavorited, setIsFavorited] = useState(false)
 
	return (
		<li>
			{/* ...favorite button, image, title and description... */}
			{post.title.split('').map((c, index) => (
				<SlowThing key={index} />
			))}
		</li>
	)
})
The input in Form keeps using the fresh query, so the checkboxes and
typing respond immediately.
Why memo can skip the cards here
memo compares each prop with Object.is. A Card’s only prop is
post, so the question is whether it’s the same post object as last
time.
getMatchingPosts filters one fixed, module-level array of posts. A
filter gives you a new array, but the items inside are the same
objects:
const all = [p1, p2, p3]
const a = all.filter(() => true)   // [p1, p2, p3]
const b = all.filter(() => true)   // [p1, p2, p3]
 
a === b          // false: different arrays
a[0] === b[0]    // true: both are p1, the same object
So in the fast render, where the deferred query is still the old one,
every card gets exactly the post object it had before, and memo skips
all of them.
Two different kinds of “same”
It’s easy to mix these up:




















What it isWho decides it’s “the same”The Card instancethe mounted card on screen, with its own state (isFavorited)React, by matching key={post.id} with the previous renderThe post propa plain data object from the posts arraymemo, by checking Object.is(oldPost, newPost)
For every <Card> in a render, React does this:
1. Is there already a Card with this key?
     no  → MOUNT a new Card (must render: slow)
     yes → reuse that instance (its state is kept), then go to 2
2. memo: Object.is(old post, new post)?
     same object → SKIP, don't call Card() (free)
     different   → call Card() again (slow)
3. Keys that were there last time but are missing now → UNMOUNT (cheap, no render)

Typing “cat” and deleting it, step by step
A simplified example. The real app has more posts, but the mechanics
are identical. Imagine only 4 posts, filtered by whether the title
contains the query:
const p1 = { id: 'cat-care',    title: 'Cat care' }
const p2 = { id: 'caterpillar', title: 'Caterpillar life' }
const p3 = { id: 'dog-walks',   title: 'Dog walking' }
const p4 = { id: 'cooking',     title: 'Cooking tips' }
const blogPosts = [p1, p2, p3, p4]   // created ONCE, never copied

























QueryMatching posts""p1, p2, p3, p4"c"p1, p2, p4 (no “c” in “Dog walking”)"ca"p1, p2"cat"p1, p2
Every keystroke causes two renders: first a fast one (the input uses
the fresh query, the list still uses the old deferredQuery), then a
background one (the list catches up). This assumes you type slowly enough
for each background render to finish. Fast typing is covered at the end.
Legend: skip = memo saw the same post object, so Card() isn’t
called (free). mount = new card, must render (slow). unmount =
card removed (cheap).
Typing
Start. The query is "", and all 4 cards are on screen.
Type “c”



































RenderquerydeferredQueryListp1p2p3p4fast"c""" ← oldp1 p2 p3 p4skipskipskipskipbackground"c""c"p1 p2 p4skipskipunmountskip
In the fast render the list is filtered with "" again. That returns the
same 4 objects, so all 4 cards skip. The input shows “c” instantly.
In the background render, p3 disappears and the other three still get the
same objects, so they skip. Slow cards rendered: 0.
Type “a” (query “ca”)
































RenderquerydeferredQueryListp1p2p4fast"ca""c" ← oldp1 p2 p4skipskipskipbackground"ca""ca"p1 p2skipskipunmount
Slow cards rendered: 0.
Type “t” (query “cat”)
