RenderquerydeferredQueryListp1p2fast"cat""ca" ← oldp1 p2skipskipbackground"cat""cat"p1 p2skipskip
Slow cards rendered: 0. Typing forward only ever removes cards, and
removing is cheap.
Deleting one letter at a time
Delete “t” (query “ca”)





























RenderquerydeferredQueryListp1p2fast"ca""cat" ← oldp1 p2skipskipbackground"ca""ca"p1 p2skipskip
Slow cards rendered: 0.
Delete “a” (query “c”)
































RenderquerydeferredQueryListp1p2p4fast"c""ca" ← oldp1 p2skipskip–background"c""c"p1 p2 p4skipskipmount (slow)
The input shows “c” immediately, because the fast render skipped
everything. p4 comes back as a brand-new card, since its old instance
was unmounted earlier. It must render all its SlowThings, which happens
in the background.
Delete “c” (query "")



































RenderquerydeferredQueryListp1p2p3p4fast"""c" ← oldp1 p2 p4skipskip–skipbackground""""p1 p2 p3 p4skipskipmount (slow)skip
The input empties immediately, and p3 mounts in the background.

💬 This is exactly the workshop’s “clearing the search is still a really
slow experience”. With the real data, clearing brings back many cards at
once. Without useDeferredValue those mounts happen inside the
keystroke’s render and freeze the input. With it, the input updates
first.

What if you type fast?
Say you type “c”, “a”, “t” quickly, before any background render
finishes:
"c" → fast render (all skip) ✅ → background render for "c" starts…
"a" → React ABANDONS the "c" background render
      → fast render (all skip) ✅ → background render for "ca" starts…
"t" → ABANDONS "ca" → fast render ✅ → background render for "cat" runs to the end

Every keystroke gets its cheap fast render, so the input never lags.
Only the last background render finishes. The work for “c” and “ca”
is thrown away, which is fine, since those lists were already out of date.
The same walkthrough without memo
Take “Delete ‘a’” again (query "ca" → "c") and remove memo from
Card:


























RenderListp1p2p4fastp1 p2render (slow)render (slow)–backgroundp1 p2 p4render (slow)render (slow)mount (slow)
Without memo, React never compares the post objects. A plain
component re-renders whenever its parent does, so every visible card
re-renders in both renders. The fast render isn’t fast anymore, and
the input lags again. memo is what makes the fast render cheap:
same post object → skip.

💬 If getMatchingPosts returned copies (posts.map(p => ({ ...p }))),
every post would be a new object, memo would never skip, and the fast
render would be slow again. memo only works when the props are truly
the same objects.

useDeferredValue + memo, step by step
The workshop test’s scenario is to check “caterpillar”, then uncheck
it and require the checkbox to update in under 50ms. Unchecking is the
slow direction, because the full list has to come back:








































StepquerydeferredQueryWhat React doesOn screen0'caterpillar''caterpillar'–box checked, 2 cards1'''caterpillar' ← oldFast render. Form updates the checkbox. MatchingPosts runs with the old query, so it gets the same 2 posts and memo skips both cardsbox unchecked immediately (test passes, < 50ms)2''''Background render. MatchingPosts runs with '', so it gets all posts. The 2 existing cards skip, and all the others mount (slow). React pauses between cards so the browser stays responsivefull list appears a moment later2′––If the user clicks again during step 2, React drops step 2 and goes back to step 1 with the newest valuealways shows the latest click
Rules and caveats

Put the pieces in the right places. Call useDeferredValue where
the slow part reads the value (MatchingPosts), give the fresh value to
whatever must feel instant (the input), and wrap the slow child in memo
(Card).
Props must stay the same objects. Primitives (strings, numbers) are
always fine. Objects must be the same references, as the filtered posts
are here. New objects on every render break memo.
You can show that the list is behind. query !== deferredQuery
means the background render hasn’t finished. Use it to dim the list,
for example style={{ opacity: isStale ? 0.5 : 1 }}.
First make it faster. useDeferredValue doesn’t reduce the work.
It only schedules it better. In real code, find out why a component is
slow first. SlowThing is only a stand-in.

Sources

EpicWeb React Performance workshop, exercise 03.concurrent-rendering (README, step deferred: posts.tsx, form.tsx, params.tsx, concurrent.test.ts), shared/blog-posts.tsx

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: Context
Element Optimization
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
Element Optimization

Notes from EpicWeb’s React Performance
workshop by Kent C. Dodds (exercise 1, “Element Optimization”) plus his
posts One simple trick to optimize React re-renders
and What is JSX?, the react.dev
memo reference, and the React
19.2.5 source the workshop installs. This is the overview note for the
exercise. It holds the shared mental model: what an element is, how strict
equality works, and when React skips a render. Each workshop step has its
own note:

Reusing Elements: hoist a static element out of the component
Element Props: pass the element in as a prop
Context: move the dynamic value into context so the element can be hoisted again
Memoize Elements: useMemo an element that depends on a prop
Memoize Components: memo the component itself

Background on when React re-renders at all: React Re-rendering. The
same trick powers Composition and Layout Components. My own notes and
clarifications are marked with > 💬.

The whole exercise rests on one sentence of Kent’s:

If you give React the same element you gave it on the last render, it
won’t bother re-rendering that element.

Every step in the exercise finds a different way to hand React the same
element (or, in the last step, props that compare equal) across renders.
If you understand what “the same” means here, memoization stops being
magic. That meaning is JavaScript’s strict equality, not “looks the same”.
Interview Q&A
Q: When a parent re-renders, why do its children re-render too, even when nothing about them changed?
A: Re-rendering the parent means calling the parent function again. Every
JSX expression inside it runs again and creates a brand-new element
object with a brand-new props object. React sees a props object it has
never seen before. It can’t prove the child would render the same output,
so it calls the child. This isn’t a bug: the default is correct, just not
minimal.
Q: What exactly does React compare to decide to skip a child?
A: Two different checks, depending on the component:

Plain component: React checks whether the props object is the same
object as last time: oldProps !== newProps (see the React source
below). No deep comparison and no per-key comparison happens. Same object
means skip. New object means render.
memo component: React runs shallowEqual(oldProps, newProps). It
walks every key and compares each value with Object.is.

In both cases the child still re-renders when its own state changes or a
context it reads changes.
Q: Why does <Footer /> === <Footer /> evaluate to false?
A: JSX is function-call syntax. <Footer /> compiles to jsx(Footer, {}),
which returns a new object literal on every call. Two separate object
literals are never ===, even when every field inside them matches. The
same goes for {} === {} and [] === [].
Q: How can you avoid unnecessary re-renders without React.memo
A: Hand React the same element reference on every render, so its
identity check passes. The exercise shows four ways to do that:

Create it outside the component, so it’s created once at module load
(Reusing Elements).
Create it in a parent that doesn’t re-render as often
(Element Props).
Remove its dynamic props, for example by reading them from context, so
it can be hoisted (Context).
Cache it with useMemo so it’s only recreated when its deps change
(Memoize Elements).

The fifth step, memo (Memoize Components), is different. It accepts a
new element but compares its props key by key.
Q: If the element is reused, does the component never re-render?
A: No. Element reuse only removes the parent-caused re-render. The
component still re-renders when its own state changes or when a context it
reads changes. That’s why Context works: Footer skips on count clicks
and still updates on color changes.
Q: Isn’t useMemo/memo everywhere the safe default, then?
A: No. Every comparison has a cost, every deps array can go stale or never
match, and the code gets harder to read. The workshop’s own warning is
“Sometimes you may inadvertently make things slower when applying a
performance optimization! Don’t optimize prematurely.” Restructure first
(steps 1 to 3). Reach for useMemo/memo (steps 4 and 5) when the
structure can’t do it. With the React Compiler enabled, much of this is
done for you. See the react.dev memo page.
What a React element actually is
JSX is sugar for a function call (What is JSX?):
<Footer name={name} />
// compiles to
jsx(Footer, { name: name })
And jsx returns a plain object. This is the real implementation from
react/cjs/react-jsx-runtime.production.js in the workshop’s React 19.2.5:
function jsxProd(type, config, maybeKey) {
  var key = null;
  void 0 !== maybeKey && (key = "" + maybeKey);
  void 0 !== config.key && (key = "" + config.key);
  if ("key" in config) {
    maybeKey = {};
    for (var propName in config)
      "key" !== propName && (maybeKey[propName] = config[propName]);
  } else maybeKey = config;
  config = maybeKey.ref;
  return {
    $$typeof: REACT_ELEMENT_TYPE,
    type: type,
    key: key,
    ref: void 0 !== config ? config : null,
    props: maybeKey
  };
}
So <Footer name="Kody" /> is just this:
{
  $$typeof: Symbol.for('react.transitional.element'),
  type: Footer,            // a reference to the function itself
  key: null,
  ref: null,
  props: { name: 'Kody' }  // the object React will compare
}

💬 In development builds the element also carries _owner, _store and
debug fields, but the ones that matter here are type and props. Note
that props is the config object the compiler passed in. A new
{ name: name } literal on every render means a new props object on
every render.

An element is a description (“render Footer with these props”), not the
rendered output. Creating one is cheap. What costs something is React
calling Footer() to find out what that description turns into.
Strict equality in 60 seconds
React’s comparisons use Object.is, which behaves like === except for
NaN and ±0:
// Primitives compare by VALUE
'Kody' === 'Kody'            // true
42 === 42                    // true
Object.is(NaN, NaN)          // true  (=== says false)
 
// Objects, arrays and functions compare by REFERENCE (identity)
({}) === ({})                // false: two different objects
[] === []                    // false
(() => {}) === (() => {})    // false
 
const a = { name: 'Kody' }
const b = a
a === b                      // true: same object, two names
 
// Elements are objects
<Footer /> === <Footer />    // false
const footer = <Footer />
footer === footer            // true
The mental model: primitives are values, and everything else is a
pointer. === on objects asks “same pointer?”, never “same contents?”.
Memoization in React is the craft of keeping the pointer the same
across renders when the contents haven’t meaningfully changed.
How React decides to skip a child
During reconciliation React has the previous fiber (with the props it
rendered with, memoizedProps) and the new element (with its props,
which becomes pendingProps). In react-dom-client.development.js
(beginWork) the check for an ordinary component is literally:
current.memoizedProps !== workInProgress.pendingProps ||
If that’s true (a different props object), React marks the fiber as having
received an update and calls the component. If it’s false (the same
props object, which only happens when the same element was handed back),
and the fiber has no pending state update or context change, React bails
out. It reuses the previous result and doesn’t call the function.
For a memo component, React swaps that identity check for a comparison
function (Component.compare, defaulting to shallowEqual), again straight
from the source:
function shallowEqual(objA, objB) {
  if (objectIs(objA, objB)) return !0;
  if ("object" !== typeof objA || null === objA ||
      "object" !== typeof objB || null === objB)
    return !1;
  var keysA = Object.keys(objA), keysB = Object.keys(objB);
  if (keysA.length !== keysB.length) return !1;
  for (keysB = 0; keysB < keysA.length; keysB++) {
    var currentKey = keysA[keysB];
    if (!hasOwnProperty.call(objB, currentKey) ||
        !objectIs(objA[currentKey], objB[currentKey]))
      return !1;
  }
  return !0;
}
The whole exercise, as one picture:
Parent re-renders → new element for child?
│
├─ SAME element reference (hoisted / passed in / useMemo)
│     props === props  → bail out (unless own state/context changed)
│
└─ NEW element
      ├─ plain component → render (new props object, always !==)
      └─ memo component  → shallowEqual(prev, next)
            ├─ every key Object.is-equal → bail out
            └─ any key differs          → render

useMemo vs memo: the same idea at two places






























useMemo(() => <Footer name={name} />, [name])const Footer = memo(FooterImpl)What is cachedthe element objectthe component’s last rendered resultWhere it livesin the parent (the one rendering Footer)on the component (applies wherever it’s rendered)What is comparedthe deps array [name], each item with Object.isthe props object, each key with Object.isOn a matchreturns the same element, so React’s plain !== check passesskips calling FooterImpl even though the element is new
The workshop’s own phrasing: memo “effectively turns the props object
into a dependency array a la useMemo”.
What breaks memo (and useMemo deps)
Because each prop is compared with Object.is, anything created inline
during render is a new reference every time:























































Prop passed to a memo componentEqual on next render?Whyname="Kody" / name={name} (string)✅ yesprimitive, compared by valuecount={3}✅ yesprimitivestyle={{ color }}❌ nonew object literal each renderitems={[1, 2]}❌ nonew array literalonClick={() => setX(1)}❌ nonew function each renderchildren={<span />} / JSX children❌ nonew element objectstyle={styleFromUseMemo}✅ if deps unchangedsame reference returnedonClick={handlerFromUseCallback}✅ if deps unchangedsame reference returnedsetX (a useState setter)✅ yesReact guarantees a stable identity
One ❌ prop is enough to make memo pure overhead: React does the
comparison, it fails, and then React renders anyway. This is why
react.dev’s advice is to minimize props changes: pass primitives, or
stabilize objects and functions with useMemo/useCallback.
Where this optimization stops

Context bypasses it by design. A reused element, and a memo
component, still re-render when a context they read changes. react.dev:
“Memoized components will still re-render when a context they consume
changes.” In this exercise that’s the desired behavior: Footer should
update when color changes.
Own state bypasses it. Element identity only blocks renders that come
from the parent.
It doesn’t make the first render faster. Kent’s post notes it doesn’t
help initial mount or forced top-down updates.
Structure first, memo second. Kent’s post argues for moving the
element to where it’s created less often before reaching for memo:
“the trick works best when the extracted component is genuinely static.”
The workshop’s closing reminder: “focus more of your efforts on making it
easier for humans to understand your code than on making it faster for
the computer to run unless you have a specific performance problem.”

Rules and caveats

The identity of the props object is what React checks, never its
contents, unless you opt into memo.
A hoisted, module-level element can’t use props that come from
component state. Move the dynamic data into context, pass the element
in, or memoize it.
useMemo for elements is legitimate but, in Kent’s words, “a bit of an
unconventional approach”. memo is the conventional tool for the same
job.
memo is only as good as the stability of its least-stable prop. Audit
for inline objects, arrays, functions, and JSX children.
Always measure with the React DevTools Profiler (“Highlight updates when
components render”) before and after. The workshop tests do the
equivalent by recording which components were called.

Sources

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
Optimize Context

Notes from EpicWeb’s React Performance
workshop by Kent C. Dodds (exercise 2, “Optimize Context”) plus his post
How to optimize your context value
and the react.dev useContext
reference. This is the overview note for the exercise. Each workshop step
has its own note:

Memoize Context: useMemo the provider value
Provider Component: move context state into a provider component that takes children
Split Context: separate the state context from the setters context

It builds directly on Element Optimization (element identity,
Object.is, memo) and on Context, where context first appeared as a
way around element props. My own notes and clarifications are marked with
> 💬.

Interview Q&A
Q: When does a context consumer re-render?
A: Whenever the nearest provider’s value changes, compared with
Object.is. Every component that reads that context re-renders, whether or
not it’s wrapped in memo. The workshop: context “triggers a re-render of
all the consuming components (which will re-render whether or not they’re
memoized).” In our example, Footer is memo-ized, yet it re-renders
every time FooterContext’s value changes.
Q: Why is <Ctx value={{ state, setState }}> a performance problem?
A: The object literal is created on every render of the component that
renders the provider. Object.is(prevValue, nextValue) is then always
false, so every consumer re-renders every time that component renders,
even when state didn’t change. In our example, clicking the unrelated
app counter re-rendered Footer until the value was memoized.
Q: What are the ways to reduce context-driven re-renders?
A: Three, and this exercise does all of them in order:

Stabilize the value with useMemo (and useCallback for functions).
Put the state in a provider component that takes children, so a
state change re-renders only the provider and its consumers, not the
whole tree.
Split contexts by how often values change, typically state vs
setters/dispatch, so setter-only consumers never re-render.

Q: Should you do this for every context?
A: No. Kent’s own verdict: “I personally feel like this is more
complicated of an API than is necessary for most situations, so I wouldn’t
bother optimizing most of my contexts.” It pays off when the value changes
often, there are many consumers, and you’ve measured a problem. The
workshop’s closing line: use these “whenever you run into performance
problems (and not before!!).”
Q: Does memo protect a component from context updates?
A: No. memo only compares props. react.dev: memoization “does not
prevent children from receiving updated context values.” To make a
component skip context updates, it must not read the context that changes.
That’s the idea behind Split Context.
How context updates actually propagate
A context provider is just another fiber holding a value. When the
component that renders it re-renders, React compares the provider’s old
and new value with Object.is. The possible outcomes:
Provider re-renders
│
├─ Object.is(prev, next) === true   → nothing extra happens.
│     Consumers only render if something else (parent, own state) makes them.
│
└─ Object.is(prev, next) === false  → React walks the subtree, finds every
      fiber that read this context, and schedules it, skipping memo checks.

Two things follow:

Value identity is everything. A { color, name } literal is a new
object every render, so it’s “changed” every render, even with identical
contents. This is the same trap as inline props on a memo component
(see Memoize Components), except that every consumer falls into it
at once.
Context and props are separate update paths. A consumer can skip
its parent’s render (element reuse or memo) and still be woken by
context. That’s the behavior we want when the value really changed, and
the one we’re removing when it didn’t.

The value objects across two renders
The workshop’s intro example, as [count, setCount]:
function CountProvider(props) {
	const [count, setCount] = useState(0)
	const value = [count, setCount]
	return <CountContext value={value} {...props} />
}
// render 1:  value = [0, setCount]   /* V1 */
// render 2 (parent re-rendered, count unchanged):
//            value = [0, setCount]   /* V2 */
Object.is(V1, V2)   // false → every consumer re-renders
 
// memoized: useMemo(() => [count, setCount], [count])
// render 2: deps [0] vs [0] → return V1
Object.is(V1, V1)   // true → consumers untouched
setCount is the same function across renders, because React guarantees
stable identity for useState setters. So only count needs to be in the
deps. That fact also makes Split Context possible.
Which components re-render, step by step
These are the exact expectations from the workshop’s tests. “App count”
means clicking the unrelated App counter. “Color” means clicking a color
button.






























StepApp count clickColor clickProblem (inline { color, name })App, FooterSetters, Main, FooterImplApp, FooterSetters, Main, FooterImplMemoize ContextApp, FooterSetters, MainApp, FooterSetters, Main, FooterImplProvider ComponentApp, FooterProvider, FooterSetters, MainFooterProvider, FooterSetters, FooterImpl (not App or Main)Split Context (+ memo on setters)App, FooterProvider, MainFooterProvider, FooterImpl (not FooterSetters)
Read down a column to see what each technique removes:

useMemo removes the consumer re-render when the value didn’t
change.
The provider component removes the tree re-render when the value
did change.
Splitting removes the setter-only consumer re-render.

Rules and caveats

Memoize every object or array you pass as a context value. Also wrap
functions you define in useCallback. useState setters and
useReducer dispatch are already stable.
Keep contexts small and cohesive. One huge “app state” context
re-renders every consumer on any change. Split by update frequency.
A component can’t consume a provider it renders itself. react.dev:
providers must be above consumers. That’s another reason the provider
lives in its own component.
Measure first. Kent’s post opens with “No seriously, if you’re going
to do this stuff just because you think your code might be slow,
then don’t bother.”

Sources

EpicWeb React Performance workshop, exercise 02.context (README, steps
memo-context, provider-component, split-context, their tests,
FINISHED)
Kent C. Dodds: How to optimize your context value
react.dev: useContext, “Optimizing re-renders when passing objects and functions”

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
React Performance
Notes on making React apps render less and respond faster, from EpicWeb’s
React Performance
workshop by Kent C. Dodds, plus outside research.
The workshop’s framing: “there’s nothing faster than not doing anything at
all”. The target is “fast enough for our users”, reached by measuring
rather than guessing, because “sometimes you may inadvertently make things
slower when applying a performance optimization.”
The first exercises build on one idea: React skips work when it can
prove nothing changed, and “nothing changed” means Object.is-equal
references. Exercise 1 applies that to elements and props, and exercise
2 applies it to context values. Exercise 3 changes the question: when
the work can’t be skipped, it can at least be made interruptible and
lower priority.
Element Optimization (skip a child's render)
  hoist a static element        → Reusing Elements
  create it in a calmer parent  → Element Props
  move dynamic data to context  → Context
  cache it by its deps          → Memoize Elements   (useMemo)
  compare props key-by-key      → Memoize Components (memo)

Optimize Context (skip a consumer's render)
  stabilize the provider value  → Memoize Context    (useMemo)
  own state below the tree      → Provider Component (children reuse)
  separate state from setters   → Split Context      (+ memo)

Concurrent Rendering (can't skip → deprioritize)
  render urgent first, rest later → useDeferredValue + memo

Notes


Element Optimization: the shared mental model for the whole
exercise. What a React element object looks like, ===/Object.is on
primitives vs objects, React’s props identity check vs memo’s
shallowEqual, and a table of which props break memoization.

Reusing Elements: hoisting a static element so React receives the
identical object on every render.
Element Props: passing an element down so its identity follows
the creating component’s renders, not the receiver’s.
Context: routing dynamic data around the element through context,
so the element can be hoisted again and still update.
Memoize Elements: useMemo returns the same element until a
dependency changes (Kent: “a bit of an unconventional approach”).
Memoize Components: memo turns the props object into a
dependency array. Covers what silently defeats it, and where the React
Compiler fits.



Optimize Context: how context propagation works (the provider
value is compared with Object.is, and consumers re-render even when
memoized). Includes a table of which components each technique stops
re-rendering.

Memoize Context: useMemo the provider value so an unrelated
parent re-render doesn’t wake every consumer.
Provider Component: move context state into an XProvider({ children })
so updates start below the app and children is reused.
Split Context: separate state from setters (stable identity), so
setter-only consumers, plus memo, never re-render.



Concurrent Rendering: the 16ms frame budget, interruptible
rendering, urgent vs deferred updates, and how deferring differs from
debouncing.

useDeferredValue + memo: keep an input responsive over a slow
list. It explains why the slow component must be memo-ized for the
deferral to help.




Exercises 4–7 (code splitting, calculations, re-renders, windowing) are
not written up yet.

Line-by-line render trace
The notes above explain concepts. Render Trace is a companion set of
notes that trace execution order through the actual solution code:
which component function runs on each click, when each element object is
created, and which equality check lets React skip a render.

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
Concurrent Rendering — Render Trace (Exercise 3)

Line-by-line render/execution trace through the 1 solution step of
exercise 3 (“Concurrent Rendering”) of EpicWeb’s
React Performance
workshop by Kent C. Dodds. For the concept explanation see
Concurrent Rendering and useDeferredValue + memo. This note is
about invocation order: which render is urgent and which is
background, what value useDeferredValue returns in each, which Cards
memo skips, and when React yields or abandons work.

Notation: p1, p2, … are post objects from the module-level blogPosts
array. The same label means the same reference.
deferred — useDeferredValue + memo
Problem: Every card re-renders slowly (SlowThing busy loops), and
because the search input and the list update in the same synchronous
render, “every time we type in the search the characters are not
responsive.” memo alone still leaves “typing a bunch in the search and
then clearing the search … a really slow experience.”
export function MatchingPosts() {
	const [searchParams] = useSearchParams()
	const query = getQueryParam(searchParams)
	const deferredQuery = useDeferredValue(query)
	const matchingPosts = getMatchingPosts(deferredQuery)
 
	return (
		<ul className="post-list">
			{matchingPosts.map((post) => (
				<Card key={post.id} post={post} />
			))}
		</ul>
	)
}
 
const Card = memo(function Card({ post }: { post: BlogPost }) {
	const [isFavorited, setIsFavorited] = useState(false)
 
	return (
		<li>
			{/* ...favorite ButtonWithTooltip, gradient div, title/description link... */}
			{post.title.split('').map((c, index) => (
				<SlowThing key={index} />
			))}
		</li>
	)
})
Render trace
Scenario: the workshop test’s second click. “caterpillar” is checked, so
the committed list is [p2, p3], and the user unchecks it.

The click fires Form’s checkbox onChange →
handleCheck('caterpillar', false) → setSearchParams({ query: '' }, { replace: true }).
Inside setSearchParams: setGlobalSearchParams calls
history.replaceState and returns new URLSearchParams. Then
setSearchParamsState compares prevParams.toString() with the new
string, and they differ, so it schedules an update on
QueryParamsProvider. This update comes from a discrete event (a
click), so it has urgent priority.
Urgent render starts. QueryParamsProvider() runs and builds a new
searchParamsTuple (a new array → new context value). React marks both
consumers, Form and MatchingPosts.
Form() runs: query = '', catChecked/caterpillarChecked are
recomputed, and the caterpillar checkbox gets checked={false}.
MatchingPosts() runs: query = ''. useDeferredValue('') sees the
render is urgent and returns the previous deferred value,
'caterpillar'. React schedules a background re-render for later.
getMatchingPosts('caterpillar') returns a new array [p2, p3] with the
same post objects as the last commit. .map creates new <Card>
elements.
Card p2: memo → shallowEqual({ post: p2 }, { post: p2 }) →
Object.is(p2, p2) → true → skip. The same happens for p3. No
SlowThing runs.
Commit. The checkbox is unchecked on screen. The test’s waitFor
resolves, and elapsed time is well under the 50ms limit.
Background render starts, at transition-like low priority.
MatchingPosts() runs again, and useDeferredValue('') now returns
''.
getMatchingPosts('') returns every post, [p1, p2, p3, p4, …].
p2 and p3 skip via memo. Every other card is new to the tree
and mounts, so Card() runs, then one SlowThing() per title
character.
React works in time slices. After each unit of work it checks whether
it should yield. If yes, it returns control to the browser (paint,
events), then continues where it left off.
If a new update arrives during step 10–11 (the user checks another
box), React abandons the in-progress background tree and goes back
to step 3 with the newest value. Nothing from the abandoned work was
committed.
Otherwise, once the whole tree is ready, React commits the full list at
once, and the user sees all cards appear together.

Contrast — without useDeferredValue (problem code, memo on or off)

Steps 1–4 are the same.
MatchingPosts() runs with getMatchingPosts(query) = getMatchingPosts('')
→ every post.
In the same urgent, non-interruptible render, every newly visible
card mounts and runs its SlowThings. memo can only skip p2 and
p3. The new cards have no previous props to compare against.
Only after all of that finishes does React commit, so the checkbox’s
visual update is stuck behind the slow cards. The test fails (> 50ms).

Contrast — with useDeferredValue but Card not memoized

Steps 1–6 are the same: deferredQuery = 'caterpillar', and the list is
[p2, p3].
Step 7 changes. Card is a plain component, and the new <Card post={p2}/> element has a new props object, so newProps !== oldProps and React renders p2 and p3 fully, SlowThings included,
in the urgent pass.
With only two cards the urgent pass costs little here. When typing into
a broad search, though, the urgent pass re-renders the whole old list
on every keystroke, which is exactly what the workshop warns about:
“React is forced to rerender the entire component with the old value
anyway which defeats the purpose.”
Then the background pass renders the list again with the new value. The
total work is higher than without the hook.

Why
useDeferredValue turns one update into two renders at different
priorities. It can only pay off if the urgent one is cheap, and the urgent
render is cheap only because memo plus stable post references
(blogPosts.filter returns the same objects) let every existing Card
skip. The expensive work, mounting new cards, is moved into the background
render. There React can yield every few milliseconds and throw away stale
attempts, so the checkbox, which is updated in the urgent render, never
waits for it.
Sources

EpicWeb — React Performance workshop, exercise 3 (step + solution, concurrent.test.ts)
react.dev — useDeferredValue
React v18 release post — What is Concurrent React?

JavaScript Promises
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
JavaScript Promises

Foundational JS — not React-specific — but scoped inside React Suspense/
because the rest of that folder (The use Hook,
Suspense and ErrorBoundary for Data Fetching) leans on exactly the
mechanics documented here. Notes and clarifications by me are marked with
> 💬.

Interview Q&A
Q: What is a Promise?
A: A built-in JS object standing in for the eventual result of any
asynchronous operation — network requests, file I/O, timers, worker
messages — so you can attach “when this finishes” behavior without knowing
in advance whether or when it’ll actually happen. It’s the foundation
async/await, fetch, and most async Node/browser APIs are built on. In
this note’s examples, getShip(name) returns exactly this kind of value: a
promise standing in for ship data that hasn’t arrived yet.
Q: What states can a Promise be in, and can it change state more than once?
A: Exactly one of pending, fulfilled, or rejected at a time, for any promise
regardless of what async work it wraps. Once it settles (fulfilled or
rejected) that’s permanent — it never transitions again — which is a
general guarantee that makes a promise safe to hand to multiple independent
consumers without them racing or disagreeing about the outcome. In this
folder specifically, Promise Caching leans on that permanence: once a
cached promise settles, every consumer that reads it later gets the same
answer for free.
pending ──resolve(value)──▶ fulfilled
   │
   └──────reject(reason)──▶ rejected

Q: Are .then/.catch callbacks run synchronously?
A: No, never — this is true of every promise in JS, not just ones tied to
network calls. Even an already-settled promise queues its callback on the
microtask queue, which only drains after the currently executing
synchronous code finishes and before the next macrotask (a setTimeout, an
event, I/O). In this note’s Promise.resolve().then(...) example, that’s
why "synchronous code" logs before "promise callback" even though the
promise is resolved instantly.
Q: What’s the relationship between async/await and .then?
A: async/await is just syntax sugar over .then chains, available for
any promise-returning code, not a separate mechanism — an async function
always returns a promise, and a throw inside one (sync or not) becomes
that promise rejecting with the thrown value instead of an uncaught
exception. In this note, the async function getShip example and its
hand-written .then equivalent produce identical behavior:
// async/await
async function getShip(name) {
  const response = await fetch(`/ships/${name}`)
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`No ship named ${name}`)
  return response.json()
}
 
// equivalent .then chain
function getShip(name) {
  return fetch(`/ships/${name}`).then((response) => {
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`No ship named ${name}`)
    return response.json()
  })
}
Q: Why does it matter that a Promise is “just a value”?
A: Because nothing in the language restricts what you’re allowed to
throw — a string, an Error, or a Promise are all fair game, and any
catch block (or React’s internal render loop) that receives one can
inspect it and attach its own .then to find out later when it settles.
This is a general JS fact useful anywhere you want custom control-flow
around thrown values, not something React invented. In our folder, this is
the entire mechanism `use` and Suspense exploit: use
throws a pending promise, React’s reconciler catches it and attaches its
own .then to know when to retry rendering.
The state machine
A promise is always in exactly one of three states:

pending — the initial state; neither fulfilled nor rejected yet.
fulfilled — the operation succeeded; the promise has a value.
rejected — the operation failed; the promise has a reason (usually an
Error).

A promise is settled once it’s fulfilled or rejected. Settling is
one-way and permanent — a promise can only transition out of pending
once, and never changes state again after that. This guarantee is what makes
a promise safe to hand to multiple consumers (like React’s Suspense
machinery) without worrying that its outcome will flip on you later.
pending ──resolve(value)──▶ fulfilled
   │
   └──────reject(reason)──▶ rejected

Creating one: the executor function
const promise = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  // this function — the "executor" — runs immediately and synchronously
  doSomethingAsync((err, result) => {
    if (err) reject(err)       // → settles as rejected
    else resolve(result)       // → settles as fulfilled
  })
})

💬 The executor itself runs synchronously the instant new Promise(...) is
called — it’s the resolve/reject callbacks that get invoked later,
asynchronously. This is why you can’t just wrap new Promise(...) in a
try/catch to catch a later rejection: the executor’s synchronous portion
has already returned by the time reject fires.

Consuming one: .then / .catch / .finally
promise
  .then(
    (value) => console.log('fulfilled with', value),
    (reason) => console.log('rejected with', reason), // optional 2nd arg
  )
  .catch((reason) => console.log('shorthand for .then(undefined, onRejected)'))
  .finally(() => console.log('runs either way, for cleanup'))
Each of .then/.catch/.finally returns a new promise, which is what
makes chaining work — if a handler throws, or returns a rejected promise, the
promise returned by that link in the chain becomes rejected too, and the
error propagates down the chain until something’s .catch handles it (or
nothing does, and you get an unhandled rejection).

💬 A promise’s outcome isn’t synchronously inspectable from the outside —
there’s no public .state or .value you can just read. The only way to
learn it is asynchronously, by attaching a .then and waiting for it to
fire once the promise settles. And you can attach more than one: multiple
independent .then calls, from different pieces of code, on the same
promise, don’t interfere with each other — each just gets invoked (in the
order it was attached) once the promise settles. The use Hook leans on
both halves of this fact: it’s why use has to track status/value/
reason manually instead of asking the promise for them, and it’s why
React’s internal pseudocode and use itself can each attach their own
separate .then to the same promise without stepping on one another.

Timing: the microtask queue
.then/.catch/.finally callbacks never run synchronously, even if the
promise is already settled by the time you attach them:
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('promise callback'))
console.log('synchronous code')
// logs: "synchronous code" then "promise callback"
Promise callbacks are queued on the microtask queue, which the JS engine
drains only after the currently executing synchronous code finishes (and
before it goes on to the next macrotask, like a setTimeout or an event).
This is why a promise resolving doesn’t interrupt whatever’s running right
now — including, as covered in The use Hook, why a component that throws
a pending promise gets to fully unwind first before React’s own .then
handler on that promise ever fires.
async/await is sugar over this
async function getShip(name) {
  const response = await fetch(`/ships/${name}`)
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`No ship named ${name}`)
  return response.json()
}
is equivalent to:
function getShip(name) {
  return fetch(`/ships/${name}`).then((response) => {
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`No ship named ${name}`)
    return response.json()
  })
}
async functions always return a promise, and a throw inside one
(synchronous or not) becomes that promise rejecting with the thrown
value, rather than an uncaught synchronous exception.
The fact the rest of this folder depends on
A promise is just a JavaScript value — an object like any other. Nothing
in the language restricts what you’re allowed to throw. You can throw
a string, a number, an Error… or a Promise. Nobody awaits a thrown
promise, so throwing one doesn’t pause anything by itself — but a catch
block that receives it can inspect it, and in particular can attach its own
.then to it to find out later when it settles. That’s the entire trick
behind React’s use hook and Suspense: see The use Hook for exactly how
React exploits this.
Sources

MDN — Promise
javascript.info — Microtasks

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: Suspense and ErrorBoundary for Data Fetching
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
Suspense and ErrorBoundary for Data Fetching

Notes from EpicWeb’s React Suspense
workshop by Kent C. Dodds (exercise 1, “Data fetching”), code pulled
directly from the exercise solutions. Companion to The use Hook (the
mechanism that triggers all of this) and Error Boundaries (the general
ErrorBoundary API — composition, showBoundary, resetErrorBoundary,
not repeated here). Notes and clarifications by me are marked with > 💬.

Interview Q&A
Q: What does <Suspense> actually catch, and what’s it generally used for?
A: A thrown pending promise — any component under it that “suspends” (i.e.
throws a not-yet-settled promise, whether from use, a framework’s data
layer, or React.lazy) gets its fallback rendered instead of its children
until that promise settles. It’s React’s general-purpose mechanism for
declaring “this subtree isn’t ready yet” for any async reason — lazy-loaded
code, data fetching, or streaming SSR — not something built only for one
kind of fetch. In our example, ShipDetails throws the in-flight
shipPromise, so <Suspense fallback={<ShipFallback />}> shows the
fallback until that specific promise resolves:
<Suspense fallback={<ShipFallback />}>
  <ShipDetails />
</Suspense>
Q: How far up the tree does React look for a Suspense boundary, and why does that matter for layout?
A: As far as it needs to — React walks up to the nearest <Suspense>
ancestor regardless of how deeply nested the suspending component is, and
treats everything under that boundary as one unit (any child suspending
shows the whole boundary’s fallback). This lets you control loading
granularity generally: one boundary around a whole page for an all-or-
nothing spinner, or several nested boundaries for staggered, progressive
reveal. In our example there’s a single boundary around ShipDetails, so
only that piece of UI shows a fallback rather than the whole page.
Q: Why does ErrorBoundary wrap Suspense, and not the other way around?
A: This follows the general rule for any error boundary in React: a
boundary can’t catch an error thrown from within itself, only from its
children. So ErrorBoundary has to sit outside Suspense to also catch
errors from Suspense’s own internal machinery, not just a rejected fetch. In
our example that’s why the JSX nests ErrorBoundary → Suspense →
ShipDetails, not the reverse — a ship-fetch rejection and any hypothetical
Suspense-internals bug both get caught by the same outer boundary.
Q: Is React’s “throw to suspend” mechanism just a teaching simplification?
A: No — it’s close to literal, and it’s the same mechanism regardless of
what triggers the suspend (data fetching, React.lazy, a framework’s
cache). React’s render work loop wraps each unit of work in a real
try/catch; on catch it duck-types the thrown value
(typeof value.then === 'function') to decide whether it’s a suspend
(thenable) or a real error, then walks up the fiber tree to find the
matching Suspense or error-boundary fiber. In our example, that’s
precisely what happens when ShipDetails throws shipPromise versus when
it throws a fetch-rejection Error — same reconciler code path, different
branch.
Q: Why must ErrorBoundary be a class component?
A: This is a general React constraint, not specific to Suspense: the
reconciler’s upward walk for non-thenable errors specifically looks for a
component with getDerivedStateFromError/componentDidCatch, and there’s
no function-component equivalent of those lifecycle hooks — so any error
boundary anywhere in React, including react-error-boundary’s
ErrorBoundary used in our example, wraps a class component under the
hood.
<Suspense> and ErrorBoundary are the declarative shell around
`use`: use throws either a pending promise or a rejection
reason, and these two components are what actually catch those throws and
turn them into UI.
<Suspense fallback={...}>

Lesson video

“Suspending” means a component threw a pending promise. <Suspense> catches
that throw and renders its fallback instead of its children, for as long as
the promise stays pending:
import { Suspense, use } from 'react'
 
function App() {
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<ShipFallback />}>
      <ShipDetails />
    </Suspense>
  )
}
React looks up the component tree for the nearest <Suspense> ancestor
of whatever suspended — it doesn’t matter how deep the suspending component
is nested, as long as some <Suspense> sits above it. All the boundary’s
children are treated as one unit: if any of them suspends, the whole boundary
shows its fallback until every suspending child is ready. Boundaries can be
nested for progressive/staggered loading — an outer boundary can reveal
its content while an inner one keeps showing its own fallback for a slower
piece of data.
ErrorBoundary, and why it wraps Suspense (not the other way around)

Lesson video

If the promise rejects, use throws the rejection reason instead of the
promise — a real error, not something <Suspense> knows what to do with. An
ErrorBoundary from react-error-boundary
catches that:
import { ErrorBoundary } from 'react-error-boundary'
 
function App() {
  return (
    <ErrorBoundary fallback={<ShipError />}>
      <Suspense fallback={<ShipFallback />}>
        <ShipDetails />
      </Suspense>
    </ErrorBoundary>
  )
}
The convention — put ErrorBoundary outside Suspense, not inside — is
the same reasoning as any other error boundary: a boundary can’t catch an
error that happens within itself, only errors from its children. If
Suspense (or its own internal machinery) were to error, only a boundary
sitting above it could catch that. Putting ErrorBoundary outermost means
it covers both “the data fetch rejected” and “something went wrong in the
suspending/loading machinery itself.” (This mirrors general ErrorBoundary
placement rules — see Error Boundaries.)
How React actually implements this (fiber internals)
The use Hook’s pseudocode says “React wraps the rendering of your
component in a try/catch.” That’s not just a teaching simplification — it’s
close to literal. The real mechanism, from React’s fiber reconciler:

There genuinely is a try/catch, just not one you write. React’s
render work loop (renderRootSync for sync work, renderRootConcurrent
for concurrent/transition work) wraps the loop that renders each unit of
work — each fiber, roughly one component — in a real try/catch. Your
ShipDetails function itself never has a try/catch in it; the
reconciler has one around the call to it.
On catch, handleError → throwException inspects what was thrown.
The check is exactly the duck-typing you’d expect from
JavaScript Promises: typeof value === 'object' && typeof value.then === 'function'.
A thrown promise (or anything else “thenable”) is treated as a suspend;
anything else is treated as a real error.
Thenable → find the nearest <Suspense> fiber. React walks up the
fiber tree via each fiber’s .return pointer (getNearestSuspenseBoundaryToCapture)
until it hits a SuspenseComponent fiber, marks it with a ShouldCapture
flag, and calls attachPingListener(root, wakeable, lane) — which is
essentially promise.then(ping, ping). Notice: both the fulfilled and
rejected callbacks are the same ping — either way, it just means “this
fiber’s work is unblocked, try rendering it again.”
Non-thenable → find the nearest error-boundary fiber. Same upward
walk, but this time looking for a class component whose type has
getDerivedStateFromError or whose instance has componentDidCatch.
That’s precisely what ErrorBoundary from react-error-boundary is
under the hood: a class component implementing those two lifecycle
methods. React queues a CaptureUpdate that will call
getDerivedStateFromError(error) to compute the boundary’s next state.
The “unwind” phase turns the mark into a re-render. During
completeUnitOfWork, the ShouldCapture flag becomes DidCapture, and
the matched boundary (Suspense or the error-boundary class component)
re-renders showing its fallback instead of its previous children.
When the ping fires, React retries — from scratch, not from where it
left off. The suspended fiber’s subtree renders again as a fresh render
pass. This is why use(promise) doesn’t need to “remember its place” —
it just re-runs the component, and this time the promise (or the workshop’s
hand-rolled usePromise.status) is settled, so use returns synchronously
or throws the rejection reason — a plain error now, which takes the
non-thenable path above straight to the ErrorBoundary.


💬 This is also why ErrorBoundary has to be a class component (or wrap
one) and can’t be a plain function: getDerivedStateFromError/
componentDidCatch are the actual hooks the reconciler’s upward walk is
searching for. There’s no function-component equivalent — it’s baked into
this fiber-walking mechanism, not a limitation react-error-boundary
could work around.

The workshop’s progression, in real code
The exercise builds this up in five steps, each one a real diff on the same
ShipDetails component. All snippets below are the actual solution code.
1. Throw the promise, add <Suspense>. Remove the await; keep a module-level
promise; if the data isn’t in yet, throw the promise:
let ship: Ship
const shipPromise = getShip(shipName).then((result) => (ship = result))
 
function ShipDetails() {
  if (!ship) throw shipPromise
  return <h2>{ship.name}</h2>
}
<Suspense fallback={<ShipFallback />}>
  <ShipDetails />
</Suspense>
2. Handle rejection, add ErrorBoundary. Track the rejection reason
alongside the resolved value, and throw it when present:
let ship: Ship
let error: unknown
const shipPromise = getShip(shipName).then(
  (result) => (ship = result),
  (err) => (error = err),
)
 
function ShipDetails() {
  if (error) throw error
  if (!ship) throw shipPromise
  return <h2>{ship.name}</h2>
}
<ErrorBoundary fallback={<ShipError />}>
  <Suspense fallback={<ShipFallback />}>
    <ShipDetails />
  </Suspense>
</ErrorBoundary>
3. Formalize the status. Replace the implicit “is ship set? is error
set?” checks with an explicit, single source of truth:
let ship: Ship
let error: unknown
let status: 'pending' | 'rejected' | 'fulfilled' = 'pending'
const shipPromise = getShip(shipName).then(
  (result) => { ship = result; status = 'fulfilled' },
  (err) => { error = err; status = 'rejected' },
)
 
function ShipDetails() {
  if (status === 'rejected') throw error
  if (status === 'pending') throw shipPromise
  return <h2>{ship.name}</h2>
}

💬 The workshop explicitly cites Kent C. Dodds’ own
“Make Impossible States Impossible”
and “Stop using isLoading booleans”
for this step. The argument: separate booleans (isLoading, isError,
plus the data itself) can be combined into states that shouldn’t be
possible — e.g. isLoading: true and stale data both present at once.
A single status enum with one value at a time makes those combinations
structurally impossible instead of just “shouldn’t happen.” You can still
derive convenience booleans from it (const isLoading = status === 'pending')
without losing the guarantee.

4–5. Extract use, then swap in React’s own. This is exactly the
progression documented in The use Hook — steps 3’s three let variables
and if checks collapse into the hand-rolled use<Value> utility, and the
component becomes:
const shipPromise = getShip(shipName)
 
function ShipDetails() {
  const ship = use(shipPromise)
  return <h2>{ship.name}</h2>
}
…then the hand-rolled use is deleted in favor of import { use } from 'react'
— identical call site, React’s real implementation underneath.
Sources

react.dev — <Suspense>
Kent C. Dodds — Make Impossible States Impossible
Kent C. Dodds — Stop using isLoading booleans
EpicWeb React Suspense workshop, exercise 01.fetching (all 5 steps)
jser.dev — How does ErrorBoundary work internally in React? —
throwException, getDerivedStateFromError/componentDidCatch lookup,
ShouldCapture/DidCapture flags
jser.dev — How Suspense works internally in Concurrent Mode —
thenable detection, getNearestSuspenseBoundaryToCapture, attachPingListener

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: The use Hook
Promise Caching
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
Promise Caching

Notes from EpicWeb’s React Suspense
workshop by Kent C. Dodds (exercise 2, “Dynamic Promises”). Builds directly
on The use Hook and Suspense and ErrorBoundary for Data Fetching —
read those first if use(promise) throwing a pending promise doesn’t
already make sense.

Interview Q&A
Q: Why does calling a fetch function directly inside a component body break Suspense?
A: This is a general consequence of how use/Suspense identifies “the same”
async operation across renders: it goes purely by promise object identity,
not by what the promise represents. Every render that calls a fetch function
inline creates a brand-new Promise object, so React has no way to know two
calls are “the same fetch” — every re-render (even one triggered by
unrelated state) re-suspends the component. In our example, calling
getShip(shipName) directly inside ShipDetails on every render was
exactly this trap — clicking an unrelated counter button re-triggered the
ship fetch.
Q: How do you fix it, generally?
A: The general technique — usable for any resource, not just this app’s
ships — is to cache the promise itself, not just the eventual data, so
the same promise object is returned across renders for the same input: a
module-level variable for a single value, or a Map keyed by id/parameter
for parameterized fetches. In our example that’s the shipCache Map:
const shipCache = new Map<string, Promise<Ship>>()
 
function getShip(name: string): Promise<Ship> {
  const shipPromise = shipCache.get(name) ?? getShipImpl(name)
  shipCache.set(name, shipPromise)
  return shipPromise
}
Q: Why should the caching function not be declared async?
A: This is a general JS fact about async functions, not specific to
React: an async function wraps its return value in a new promise on
every call, even if the underlying work is already cached — so a strictly
correct cache guards the call with a plain (non-async) function to
guarantee one promise object per cache entry. In our example, getShipImpl
is written as a plain async function, but the outer getShip that
actually gets called by components is not async — it just returns
whatever promise is already in (or newly added to) the cache.
Q: Does this pattern handle cache invalidation?
A: No, deliberately — and this is a real limitation of the general
technique, not just this example: it caches forever for the page’s
lifetime, with no notion of staleness. Real invalidation, eviction, and
cache keys are a much bigger topic on their own; in production you’d
typically reach for a data-fetching library (React Query, SWR, or a
framework’s cache) instead of hand-rolling this Map. Our example’s
shipCache explicitly punts on this — refreshing the page is the only way
to clear it.
The problem: a new promise on every render
In the Data Fetching examples, the promise passed to use was created
once, outside the component, so it never changed. But real apps need to
fetch dynamic data — e.g. “whichever ship the user currently has selected.”
The naive way to do that is to call the fetch function directly inside the
component:
function ShipDetails({ shipName }: { shipName: string }) {
  const ship = use(getShip(shipName))
  return <h2>{ship.name}</h2>
}
This looks reasonable, but getShip(shipName) runs on every render of
ShipDetails — and every call creates a brand-new Promise object. use
doesn’t know two promises are “the same fetch,” so:

Clicking an unrelated button that re-renders this component re-triggers
the fetch and re-suspends the component, even though shipName didn’t
change.
React actually detects this pattern and warns about it — creating promises
during render like this is unsupported unless something is caching them
for you.

The fix: cache the promise, not just the data
The trick is to make the fetch function return the exact same promise
object for the same input, so use (and Suspense) can recognize “this is
already in flight / already settled” instead of starting over.
Single value, no parameters — a module-level variable is enough:
let userPromise: Promise<User> | undefined
 
function fetchUser() {
  userPromise = userPromise ?? fetchUserImpl()
  return userPromise
}
 
async function fetchUserImpl() {
  const response = await fetch('/api/user')
  return response.json()
}
The first call creates and stores the promise; every call after that returns
the same cached promise instead of calling fetchUserImpl again.
Parameterized fetches (e.g. fetch by id/name) need a Map keyed by that
parameter instead of a single variable:
const shipCache = new Map<string, Promise<Ship>>()
 
function getShip(name: string): Promise<Ship> {
  const shipPromise = shipCache.get(name) ?? getShipImpl(name)
  shipCache.set(name, shipPromise)
  return shipPromise
}
 
async function getShipImpl(name: string): Promise<Ship> {
  const response = await fetch(`/api/ships/${name}`)
  return response.json()
}
Now ShipDetails can stay simple and dynamic:
function ShipDetails({ shipName }: { shipName: string }) {
  const ship = use(getShip(shipName))
  return <h2>{ship.name}</h2>
}
Every render with the same shipName returns the cached promise, so use
only ever suspends the first time a given ship is requested. Switching
back to a previously-loaded ship is instant, and unrelated re-renders no
longer trigger a fetch at all.

💬 One subtlety worth calling out: getShipImpl above should not be
declared async if you want to be strict about “only creating one promise
object” — an async function returns a new promise wrapper around its
body every time it’s called, even if the body itself resolves instantly.
Since getShip already guards the call with the cache check, this rarely
matters in practice, but it’s the difference between “definitely one
promise” and “one fetch, wrapped in a fresh promise shell each time.”

Cache invalidation is out of scope (on purpose)
This pattern caches forever — for the lifetime of the page. It deliberately
doesn’t address:

What happens when the underlying data changes on the server (stale cache).
Evicting old entries so the Map doesn’t grow unbounded.
Keying on more than one parameter, or partial/derived keys.

Kent C. Dodds calls this out explicitly in the workshop: caching correctly
(invalidation, staleness, cache keys) is a whole topic on its own — see his
talk Caching for Cash. In a
real app you’d typically reach for a data-fetching library (React Query,
SWR, or a framework’s built-in cache) rather than hand-rolling this Map.
This simple pattern exists here purely to make use/Suspense work correctly
with dynamic, parameterized data — not as a production caching strategy.
Sources

EpicReact — Promise Cache (exercise + solution)
Kent C. Dodds — Caching for Cash

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: useTransition and Avoiding Loading Flicker
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
useTransition and Avoiding Loading Flicker

Notes from EpicWeb’s React Suspense
workshop by Kent C. Dodds (exercise 2, “Dynamic Promises”, steps 2–3).
Assumes Promise Caching is already in place — this note is about
smoothing the experience of switching between already-cacheable data,
not about fetching itself.

Interview Q&A
Q: What does useTransition do?
A: It marks a state update as non-urgent/lower-priority rather than the
default “urgent” priority every state update gets. Concretely this means:
React can interrupt or delay that low-priority render if something more
urgent comes in (a keystroke, a click), which keeps the UI responsive
instead of janky/blocking on slow renders; and if the low-priority update
would cause a component to suspend, React keeps the currently-committed UI
on screen instead of tearing it down for a Suspense fallback, giving you an
isPending boolean to show your own lighter-weight loading state instead.
Avoiding the Suspense fallback is one visible consequence of that — the
underlying idea is “this update can wait, don’t block on it.” In our
example, wrapping setShipName in startTransition is what keeps the
previously selected ship visible (dimmed) instead of blanking out for the
fallback while the new ship loads:
const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition()
 
function handleShipSelection(newShipName: string) {
  startTransition(() => {
    setShipName(newShipName)
  })
}
Q: When would you use it, beyond avoiding a Suspense fallback?
A: Generally, any time a state update might cause an expensive re-render or
block the main thread long enough to feel janky — filtering a large list,
switching tabs that re-render a heavy chart, typing into a search box that
triggers a costly re-render on every keystroke (keeping the input itself
“urgent” while the results re-render as a lower-priority transition) — even
when nothing suspends at all. Suspense-avoidance (our example: switching
between already-cacheable ships) is just one common case of a broader
“don’t let this update block more important ones” tool.
Q: Does useTransition prevent the fetch/suspend from happening?
A: No, and this is true regardless of what’s inside the transition — it
never changes what work happens, only how React schedules and displays
it. The underlying use/<Suspense> mechanism, or any expensive
computation, still runs exactly the same; the transition just changes the
priority of the update and, if it suspends, suppresses the fallback UI in
favor of isPending. In our example, getShip(shipName) still actually
fetches — startTransition just changes what the user sees while it does.
Q: Why can transitions still show a flash of loading state, and how do you fix it?
A: This is a general UX problem with any asynchronous pending indicator,
not specific to useTransition: if the underlying work resolves very
quickly, a boolean like isPending can flip true then false fast enough
to register as an ugly flicker rather than useful feedback. The general fix
is to decouple “is it pending” from “should I show a spinner” with a
debounce-like rule — which is exactly what useSpinDelay (from the
spin-delay package) does: only show the pending UI if it lasts longer than
a delay, and once shown, hold it for at least a minDuration, so it never
flashes regardless of how fast the network is. In our example:
const showSpinner = useSpinDelay(isPending, { delay: 300, minDuration: 350 })
The problem: every suspend falls back to the Suspense fallback
With Promise Caching in place, switching to a ship you haven’t loaded
yet still suspends the component — that’s correct, there’s a real fetch
happening. But by default, any suspend bubbles up to the nearest
<Suspense> boundary and swaps the entire UI for the fallback, even for a
quick, minor update like picking a different item from a list. That’s a
jarring flash for what should feel like a small state change.
useTransition: keep the old UI, get an isPending flag instead
useTransition lets you mark a state update as a transition. React then
tries to render the new UI in the background while keeping the old UI (and
all its already-resolved data) visible, instead of tearing it down for the
Suspense fallback. You get an isPending boolean to show your own, more
subtle pending state while that happens:
function ShipPicker() {
  const [shipName, setShipName] = useState('dreadnought')
  const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition()
 
  function handleShipSelection(newShipName: string) {
    startTransition(() => {
      setShipName(newShipName)
    })
  }
 
  return (
    <div style={{ opacity: isPending ? 0.6 : 1 }}>
      <ShipDetails shipName={shipName} />
      {/* buttons call handleShipSelection(...) */}
    </div>
  )
}
What actually happens when setShipName runs inside startTransition:

React starts rendering ShipDetails with the new shipName in the
background, without committing it yet.
If that render suspends (the new ship isn’t cached yet), React does
not show the Suspense fallback. Instead, it keeps showing the
previously committed UI and sets isPending to true.
isPending drives your own inline loading treatment — here, just
dimming the details to opacity: 0.6 — instead of blowing away the UI.
Once the new ship’s promise resolves, React commits the new render and
isPending flips back to false.

The only two things that changed versus a plain setShipName(newShipName)
call: wrap the update in startTransition, and use the returned isPending
for a local loading indicator. Everything about use/<Suspense> from
Suspense and ErrorBoundary for Data Fetching keeps working exactly the
same underneath — useTransition only changes what the user sees while a
suspend is happening, not whether it happens.

📜 useTransition docs

The next problem: transitions can flash too
isPending solves the “replace the whole screen” problem, but it introduces
a smaller version of the same issue: if the fetch resolves very quickly
(say, 50ms), the user still sees a brief flicker of opacity: 0.6 and back.
Delaying the pending UI with a CSS transition doesn’t really fix
this — it just moves the threshold at which the flash happens (a request
that takes slightly longer than your CSS delay still flashes).
useSpinDelay: only show pending state if it’s actually worth showing
The spin-delay package solves this with two
rules:

If the pending state resolves in under delay ms, never show a spinner
at all.
If it takes longer than delay, show the spinner for at least
minDuration ms — even if the data arrives right after the delay window,
so the spinner itself doesn’t flash.

import { useSpinDelay } from 'spin-delay'
 
function ShipDetails({ shipName }: { shipName: string }) {
  const ship = use(getShip(shipName))
  const [isTransitionPending, startTransition] = useTransition()
  const showSpinner = useSpinDelay(isTransitionPending, {
    delay: 300,
    minDuration: 350,
  })
 
  return (
    <div style={{ opacity: showSpinner ? 0.6 : 1 }}>
      <h2>{ship.name}</h2>
    </div>
  )
}
With delay: 300, minDuration: 350:

Fetch takes 100ms → showSpinner never becomes true. No flash.
Fetch takes 400ms → showSpinner becomes true at the 300ms mark and
stays true until at least 300 + 350 = 650ms, even though the data was
ready at 400ms. No flash, just a clean, deliberate loading state.

useSpinDelay doesn’t replace useTransition — it just wraps the
isPending boolean useTransition gives you with debounce-like timing
rules, so what the user actually sees stays smooth regardless of how fast
or slow the network happens to be.
Sources

EpicReact — useTransition (exercise + solution)
EpicReact — Pending Flash (exercise + solution)
react.dev — useTransition
spin-delay on npm

40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.title: useFormStatus
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
useFormStatus

Notes from EpicWeb’s React Suspense
workshop by Kent C. Dodds (exercise 3, “Optimistic UI”, step 2). Pairs
with useOptimistic Hook — both are about giving the user feedback
while a form action is in flight, but they solve different parts of it:
useOptimistic updates data, useFormStatus reports the status of
the submission itself.

Interview Q&A
Q: What does useFormStatus do?
A: For any <form> anywhere in a React app, it reports the status of that
form’s action while it’s running in the nearest ancestor <form> —
giving you pending, the data (FormData) being submitted, the method,
and the action reference — without you having to wire up your own state
for any of it. It’s a general building block for any form-pending UI
(disabling a submit button, showing a spinner, reading what was submitted),
not tied to one specific form. In our example it’s used to power the create
button’s own pending state:
function CreateButton() {
  const { pending } = useFormStatus()
  return (
    <button type="submit" disabled={pending}>
      {pending ? 'Creating...' : 'Create'}
    </button>
  )
}
Q: Where does useFormStatus come from, and where must it be called?
A: This is a hard, general requirement regardless of what the form does:
it’s imported from react-dom (not react), and it must be called from a
component that is a child of the <form> — never the component that
renders the <form> itself, since it looks to its nearest form ancestor for
status. Think of <form> as a context provider and useFormStatus as the
consumer. In our example this is exactly why CreateButton is its own
component instead of a plain <button> inline in CreateForm — the button
needs to sit underneath the <form> it’s reporting on.
Q: Why do you often see a submit button extracted into its own small component?
A: This is a direct, general consequence of the previous rule, useful
anywhere you build a reusable submit-button/spinner component: a component
that both renders the <form> and tries to call useFormStatus in the same
scope won’t get a form to read from, so the button has to be pulled into a
sibling/child component underneath the <form>. In our example that’s
CreateButton, extracted specifically so it can call useFormStatus from
inside CreateForm’s rendered <form>.
Q: How is useFormStatus different from useOptimistic?
A: This distinction holds for any form, not just ours: useFormStatus is
read-only and answers “is this form submitting, and what was submitted?”
automatically, with no state management on your part. useOptimistic (see
useOptimistic Hook) is for showing your own custom state during the
transition — a preview of data being created, or a multi-step progress
message — something useFormStatus can’t give you since it only reports
the form’s built-in submission status. In our example, useFormStatus
drives the button’s disabled/“Creating…” state while a separate
useOptimistic call drives the optimistic ship preview shown elsewhere on
the page.
The problem: no built-in way to know a form is submitting
A form with an action doesn’t automatically disable its submit button or
show a “submitting…” state — nothing stops the user from clicking submit
again while the first submission is still in flight, which can trigger the
action multiple times.
useFormStatus: read the status of the nearest parent <form>
useFormStatus (from react-dom, not react) reports on the form action
currently running in the nearest ancestor <form>:
import { useFormStatus } from 'react-dom'
 
function CreateButton() {
  const { pending } = useFormStatus()
  return (
    <button type="submit" disabled={pending}>
      {pending ? 'Creating...' : 'Create'}
    </button>
  )
}
function CreateForm() {
  return (
    <form action={createShip}>
      {/* other inputs */}
      <CreateButton />
    </form>
  )
}

💬 Think of <form> as a context provider and useFormStatus as the
consumer. That’s also why it has a hard requirement: the component
calling useFormStatus must be a child of the <form>, not the
component that renders the <form> itself. Calling it directly inside
CreateForm above (the component rendering the form) won’t work — it
has to be called from a component nested underneath it, like
CreateButton. This is a common reason to extract a submit button into
its own small component, purely so it can sit inside the form as a child.

What else useFormStatus gives you
Besides pending, the returned object also has:

data — the FormData currently being submitted (or null when idle).
method — the HTTP method of the submission.
action — the action function reference itself.

Since data is the live FormData being submitted, you can read individual
fields out of it to make the pending message more specific:
function CreateButton() {
  const { pending, data } = useFormStatus()
  return (
    <button type="submit" disabled={pending}>
      {pending ? `Creating ${data?.get('name')}...` : 'Create'}
    </button>
  )
}
Before any submission, useFormStatus() returns
{ pending: false, data: null, method: null, action: null }.
useFormStatus vs. useOptimistic
They’re complementary, not competing:

useFormStatus answers “is this form currently submitting, and what
was submitted?” — read-only, derived automatically from the nearest
<form>, no state management on your part.
useOptimistic (see useOptimistic Hook) is for showing your
own custom state during the transition — like an optimistic version of
the data being created, or a custom multi-step progress message —
something useFormStatus alone can’t give you because it only reports on
the form’s built-in submission status, not arbitrary app state.

A button showing “Creating…” from pending and a page showing an
optimistic preview of the new ship from useOptimistic are typically used
side by side in the same feature, as in the workshop’s ship-creation form.
Sources

EpicReact — Form Status (exercise + solution)
react.dev — useFormStatus

React Suspense
40-resources/engineering/javascript/reac.content:
React Suspense
Notes on Suspense-based data fetching in React — from EpicWeb’s
React Suspense workshop
by Kent C. Dodds, plus outside research.
The short version of how the pieces fit together: a component calls
`use(promise)`. If the promise is still pending, use
throws it; React catches that throw and renders the nearest
`<Suspense>` fallback until
the promise settles. If the promise rejects, use throws the rejection
reason instead, and the nearest ErrorBoundary catches that. Both of these
throws only work because a Promise is just a regular
JS value — nothing stops you from throwing one.
use(promise)
  ├─ fulfilled → return value synchronously
  ├─ pending   → throw promise   → caught by <Suspense fallback>
  └─ rejected  → throw reason    → caught by <ErrorBoundary fallback>

Notes
Notes are grouped into a subfolder per workshop module.
Data Fetching (exercise 1)

JavaScript Promises — what a Promise is, its state machine, .then/.catch,
the microtask queue, and the “a promise is just a throwable value” fact
everything else here depends on.
The use Hook — how use synchronously unwraps a promise by throwing,
React’s implicit try/catch around rendering, and a hand-rolled
implementation built step-by-step in the workshop.
Suspense and ErrorBoundary for Data Fetching — the declarative
boundary components that catch what use throws, why ErrorBoundary
wraps Suspense rather than the reverse, and the full workshop code
progression.

Dynamic Promises (exercise 2)

Promise Caching — why calling a fetch function directly during render
breaks use/Suspense, and how caching the promise itself (a module-level
variable, or a Map keyed by id) fixes it.
useTransition and Avoiding Loading Flicker — keeping the old UI visible
during a suspending update with useTransition, and eliminating flash of
loading state on top of that with useSpinDelay.

Optimistic UI (exercise 3)

useOptimistic Hook — updating state during a transition (which
useState can’t do) to show a provisional result immediately, with a
built-in fallback/rollback once the transition settles.
useFormStatus — reading a <form>’s submission status (pending,
data, method) from a child component, and how it complements
useOptimistic.

See also use and createContext (use for context, not promises) and
Error Boundaries (the general ErrorBoundary API beyond the
Suspense-specific usage covered here).
Line-by-line render trace
The notes above explain concepts. Render Trace is a companion set of
notes that instead trace execution order through the actual solution code
of all 6 exercises (17 steps) of the workshop — what renders first, what
throws, what catches it, and what waits on what — including exercises 4–6
(image Suspense, useDeferredValue, and performance optimizations), which
aren’t covered by the concept notes above yet.
